01 DEF · Product Definition

DEF-01Market and customer requirements consolidation

Takes4ww0–w4 of the stage
Costs4.0 M/M~4.3 people while it runs
OwnerRequirements leadStage lead approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Consolidate what customers and the market are asking for into a single, ranked and approved set of product requirements that the entire program is measured against.

Everything that follows is driven by these product requirements—from the PPA targets and cost model to the feasibility assessment and the architecture itself. Until the requirements are baselined and approved, all downstream decisions remain provisional. Changes introduced late in the program are significantly more expensive, often resulting in costly silicon redesigns.

What it delivers

DEF-D1Product requirements document (PRD)

The requirements list built here becomes the body of the PRD. This activity does not contribute to the PRD—it produces its content.

Needs first

  • Customer RFI / RFQ responses
  • Field feedback and errata from the previous generation
  • Analyst forecasts and segment sizing
  • Competitor datasheets and public benchmarks
  • Sales pipeline and committed-volume view

Done when

  • Every requirement has an owner, a priority and an acceptance measure
  • Conflicts resolved, or deferred with a named decision owner
  • Register baselined and signed by product, engineering and sales

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w0w1w2w3w4

Main sequence

12457

In parallel

36
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Stakeholder map and interview plan Stakeholder map and interview schedule 0.5w
2 Anchor-customer interviews — two accounts, six sessions Interview notes, per account 1.5w
3 Market and analyst input, segment sizingruns in parallel Market and analyst input with segment sizing 1w
4 Requirement extraction, de-duplication and requirements list build Requirements list — ID, owner, priority, acceptance measure 1w
5 Conflict resolution and priority ranking — must-have, should-have, nice-to-have Conflict and deferral log · Priority ranking record 0.5w
6 Traceability tagging to candidate KPIs and PPA targetsruns in parallel Requirement-to-KPI traceability tags 0.5w
7 Stakeholder review and baseline signoff Baseline signoff sheet 0.5w

The seven steps total 5.5 weeks of work inside a 4-week window because steps 3 and 6 run in parallel with the main sequence. This is why the activity TAT does not equal the sum of its step durations. If either parallel step has to move onto the critical path, the activity takes 1.5 weeks longer.

Watch out for

  • Requirements not signed off by all stakeholders. Verbal agreement from sales is not a signature, and the Go / No-Go gate review checks for signatures. Missing approvals surface at the gate, when there is no time left to resolve them.
  • Late customer additions after baseline. If no change-control process is agreed at signoff, requirements continue to change and no downstream activity can freeze its own inputs.
  • Requirements written as solutions. "Use HBM3E" specifies an implementation; "819 GB/s sustained bandwidth" specifies a requirement. Writing the solution into the requirement removes the architecture team's options in ARCH-02.
  • Requirements without an acceptance measure. A requirement that cannot be tested is never verified during the program and resurfaces at qualification, when the only remaining options are a respin or a customer waiver.
  • A single anchor account dominating the requirement set. Requirements that serve one customer rather than a market segment produce a custom part that still carries a full product's development cost.

01 DEF · Product Definition

DEF-02Workload / use-case profiling and target KPI derivation (TOPS, TOPS/W, tokens/s)

Takes5ww1–w6 of the stage
Costs6.0 M/M~5.2 people while it runs
OwnerWorkload architectArchitecture liaison approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

The product requirements define what customers expect from the product. This activity defines what the silicon must actually do—the workloads it will run and the KPI targets derived from those workloads.

A KPI without a representative workload is just a marketing number. During ARCH-01, the architecture team spends fourteen weeks optimizing the design based on the workloads defined here. If those workloads do not reflect real customer usage, the silicon will be optimized for scenarios that customers never actually run. Verification will not catch this issue, because it only checks that the design functions correctly—not that it was optimized for the right workloads.

What it delivers

DEF-D2Target specification — PPA and KPI table

This activity derives the KPI half of the deliverable; DEF-03 derives the PPA half. The two are published as a single table.

Needs first

  • Requirement register from DEF-01
  • Customer-supplied models and traces, where the NDA allows
  • Previous-generation silicon and its lab platform
  • Public model zoo and framework benchmarks
  • Deployment mix estimates from the segment sizing

Done when

  • Every KPI traces to a named workload and stated conditions
  • Workload suite runs end to end on the reference platform
  • Architecture has accepted the handoff as modellable

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w1w2w3w4w5w6

Main sequence

12467

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Use-case shortlist drawn from the requirement register Use-case shortlist with deployment weights 0.5w
2 Workload trace capture — LLM inference, vision, recommendation Captured workload traces per use case 1.5w
3 Reference runs on the previous generation for a baselineruns in parallel Baseline measurements on the previous generation 1w
4 KPI derivation — TOPS, TOPS/W, tokens/s, time-to-first-token, batch scaling KPI derivation worksheet, one row per requirement 1.5w
5 Precision and quantization policy — INT8, FP8, mixedruns in parallel Precision and quantization policy note 1w
6 Sensitivity study — which KPI moves with which architectural knob Sensitivity table — KPI against architectural knob 1w
7 Workload suite packaging and handoff to architecture Workload suite — traces, models, and the harness to run them 0.5w

The main sequence fills the 5-week window exactly. Steps 3 and 5 run in parallel: the reference runs need lab time rather than analyst time, and the precision policy can be settled while traces are still being captured.

Watch out for

  • Workload traces that flatter the design. A workload suite assembled from benchmarks that already run well on the previous generation will not expose the cases that break the new architecture.
  • Customer models unavailable under NDA. Substituting a public proxy workload is acceptable practice. Not recording that a proxy was used is not, because downstream teams will treat the results as customer data.
  • Deployment mix estimated rather than measured. The architecture is tuned to the workload mix, so an incorrect mix allocates silicon area to the wrong functions. That area cannot be recovered after tapeout.
  • Precision policy left undecided. The choice between INT8 and FP8 changes the datapath, the memory footprint and the KPI targets at the same time, and the cost of changing it increases every week it is deferred.
  • KPIs quoted without operating conditions. A TOPS number with no batch size, sequence length or precision stated cannot be designed against and cannot be verified.

DEF-03PPA target definition — max frequency, power, die area

Takes4ww3–w7 of the stage
Costs3.0 M/M~3.3 people while it runs
OwnerPPA leadStage lead approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Convert the KPI set into the three numbers the design is actually held to—max frequency, power and die area—and allocate them so that every block owner inherits a specific budget rather than a program-level goal.

An unallocated target does not constrain anyone's design work. A board power target of 75 W does not bind any block owner until it is decomposed into a die-level budget, a per-domain budget and a per-block budget, each with a named owner. That decomposition is what makes a budget overrun visible in week 20 rather than in week 60, when the only remaining responses are reducing the speed bin or committing to a respin.

What it delivers

DEF-D2Target specification — PPA and KPI table

This activity produces the PPA half of the deliverable. DEF-02 produces the KPI half, and the two are published as a single table.

Needs first

  • KPI table from DEF-02
  • Block list and reuse inventory from the architecture sketch
  • Node PPA data from TECH-03
  • Previous-generation power and area actuals
  • Thermal and board constraints from the requirement register

Done when

  • Frequency, power and area targets each carry a stated assumption
  • Every block has an allocated budget and a named owner
  • Architecture and physical design have signed the review

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w3w4w5w6w7

Main sequence

12367

In parallel

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Frequency target from the KPI set and expected IPC Frequency target with the IPC assumption behind it 0.75w
2 Power envelope decomposition — board, package, die, per-domain Power budget tree — board to per-domain 1w
3 Die area budget from the block list and the reuse inventory Die area budget by block 1w
4 Multi-Vt and operating voltage strategy, first passruns in parallel Voltage and multi-Vt strategy note 0.5w
5 PPA sensitivity against the candidate nodesruns in parallel PPA sensitivity table per candidate node 0.75w
6 Per-block allocation with a named owner against each budget Per-block allocation sheet with owners 0.75w
7 Target review with architecture and physical design Target review record with architecture and physical design 0.5w

Allocation is the step that matters, and it sits late in the sequence because it cannot begin until the block list is stable. Steps 4 and 5 run in parallel with the budget work; both feed the review rather than the budgets themselves.

Watch out for

  • Targets set from ambition rather than from process capability. A max frequency target the standard cell library cannot reach leads to an extended timing closure effort that ends in either a respin or a reduced speed bin.
  • Power budget allocated with no margin. A budget fully committed at definition leaves nothing for the ECO activity during physical design, where power consistently increases rather than decreases.
  • Area budget set without the IP reuse inventory. Budgets set before the reuse decisions are known allocate area to blocks that will be reused and starve blocks that must be designed from scratch.
  • Budgets allocated without named owners. A budget with no owner is not defended during implementation, and the available area or power is consumed by whichever block closes first.
  • Targets frozen before DEF-07 reports. Feasibility can only be assessed against stated targets. Freezing targets that the selected node cannot support makes the feasibility verdict meaningless.

DEF-04Die size, yield and product cost model (wafer, mask, package, test, ASP)

Takes4ww3–w7 of the stage
Costs3.0 M/M~3.3 people while it runs
OwnerProduct cost analystFinance partner approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Determine what the product will cost before the program commits to building it. Wafer, mask, package, test and yield are combined into a single model that states the cost per unit at volume and whether the resulting margin is acceptable.

The cost model also functions as a veto. A design that meets every KPI target but exceeds the cost ceiling is not a viable product, and the least expensive point to discover that is here, while the die size is still an estimate rather than a completed floorplan.

What it delivers

DEF-D3Product cost and margin model

This activity produces the deliverable. The workbook and its assumptions are handed over in full rather than summarized, because downstream teams need to re-run the model when inputs change.

Needs first

  • Die area budget from DEF-03
  • Wafer, mask and NRE quotations from TECH-04
  • Package architecture assumption from the requirement register
  • HBM and substrate price indications
  • Volume forecast and ASP from the segment sizing

Done when

  • Cost model closes at the forecast volume with stated margin
  • Every assumption is named, sourced and dated
  • Sensitivity identifies the three exposures and their range

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w3w4w5w6w7

Main sequence

12367

In parallel

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Die area estimate from the block list and the reuse inventory Die area estimate with its tolerance 0.75w
2 Wafer cost and gross die per wafer, per node candidate Gross die and yield curves per node candidate 0.5w
3 Defect density and yield model per node candidate Defect density and yield curve per node 1w
4 Package and substrate cost — interposer, substrate layers, HBM stacksruns in parallel Package and substrate cost breakdown 0.75w
5 Test cost model — sort and final, with a test-time assumptionruns in parallel Test cost model with its test-time assumption 0.5w
6 Volume, ASP and margin roll-up Cost model workbook — wafer, package, test, yield · Margin roll-up at the forecast volume · Cost ceiling statement for the design 1w
7 Sensitivity — the three assumptions the model is most exposed to Sensitivity analysis on the three dominant assumptions 0.75w

The sensitivity analysis in step 7 is not optional. On a 2.5D product, cost is dominated by yield, interposer supply and HBM pricing, and at this point in the program all three are assumptions rather than quoted prices.

Watch out for

  • Yield assumed from a mature process node. Defect density during early node ramp is significantly worse than the mature figure quoted by the foundry, and the entire difference is absorbed by product margin.
  • Package cost treated as a minor adder. On a 2.5D product with two HBM stacks, package cost can approach die cost. Modeling it as a percentage adder hides the largest cost line the program can still influence.
  • Test cost estimated without a test time assumption. Test cost is test time multiplied by the tester rate. Without a test time estimate from the DFT team, the test cost line carries no information.
  • A single-point ASP assumption. An ASP with no downside scenario produces a margin number that cannot be committed to.
  • Die size estimate carried without a tolerance. An area estimate that later grows by 15% reduces gross die per wafer non-linearly, but the model reports the change as a small input adjustment.

DEF-05Memory and interface bandwidth requirements (HBM stacks, PCIe/CXL lanes, D2D)

Takes3ww2–w5 of the stage
Costs2.0 M/M~2.9 people while it runs
OwnerMemory systems architectArchitecture liaison approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Determine the bandwidth the target workloads require at each level of the memory hierarchy, and convert that into the interface count the package and floorplan must physically support.

Bandwidth requirements are where the specification becomes a physical commitment. Selecting two HBM stacks rather than one is not a documentation change; it determines interposer size, substrate construction, power delivery and product cost. Making this decision during product definition is inexpensive. Revisiting it during architecture is not.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Workload traces and KPI table from DEF-02
  • Requirement register — capacity and latency requirements
  • HBM generation availability and roadmap
  • Interface standard revisions in flight (PCIe, CXL, UCIe)
  • Previous-generation bandwidth utilization data

Done when

  • Bandwidth stated as sustained, per workload, with conditions
  • Memory configuration and interface count recommended with a reason
  • Bump budget accepted as buildable by package

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w2w3w4w5

Main sequence

1256

In parallel

34
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Bandwidth demand per workload, from the DEF-02 traces Bandwidth demand table, per workload and per hierarchy level 0.75w
2 Memory hierarchy sizing — on-die SRAM, HBM capacity and channels Memory configuration recommendation — capacity, stacks, channels 1w
3 Host interface sizing — PCIe / CXL generation and lane countruns in parallel Host interface sizing — generation and lane count 0.5w
4 Die-to-die interface requirement, if a chiplet split is a candidateruns in parallel Host and die-to-die interface requirement 0.5w
5 Translation into a pin and bump budget Pin and bump budget estimate 0.75w
6 Requirement review with architecture and package Review record with architecture and package 0.5w

Step 5 is the step that creates the commitment. A bandwidth figure stated in GB/s does not constrain any downstream team. The same figure expressed as a bump count constrains the floorplan, the package design and the cost model at the same time.

Watch out for

  • Bandwidth sized on peak rather than sustained demand. Peak figures size an interface the workload never reaches and add cost the product does not need.
  • Capacity and bandwidth requirements conflated. HBM stack count is frequently set by capacity requirements while the discussion is conducted in GB/s. The two constraints do not scale together, and confusing them produces the wrong stack count.
  • Interface standard still under revision. Committing to an interface generation whose specification is not yet ratified transfers the standards body's schedule risk into the program schedule.
  • Bump budget never derived. A bandwidth requirement that is not translated into a bump count is discovered as a floorplan problem during PD-04, by which time the package has already been ordered.
  • Chiplet decision deferred. A die-to-die interface is a major architectural commitment. Leaving the decision open past architecture freeze forces the program to adopt the monolithic option by default.

DEF-06Competitive benchmarking and product positioning

Takes4ww0–w4 of the stage
Costs2.0 M/M~2.2 people while it runs
OwnerProduct marketing leadStage lead approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Establish where the product will land against the parts that will be shipping when it ships, rather than against the parts available today.

Benchmarking against the current generation produces a favorable comparison with no predictive value. The program's silicon reaches customers roughly thirty months from now, so the relevant comparison is against products launching in that window. Those figures have to be projected from public roadmaps and process node cadence rather than measured directly.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Competitor datasheets, disclosures and conference material
  • Public benchmark submissions (MLPerf and equivalents)
  • Foundry node cadence and process roadmaps
  • Analyst launch forecasts
  • Field intelligence from sales

Done when

  • Every comparison is normalized to stated conditions
  • Field projected to our launch window, not read from today
  • Gap list handed to DEF-01 as candidate requirements

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w0w1w2w3w4

Main sequence

12456

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

5 Positioning statement and capability gap list Positioning statement · Capability gap list, ranked 1w
6 Review with product and sales Product and sales review record 0.5w

Normalization runs in parallel because it is time-consuming and independent of data collection. Vendors quote TOPS at different precisions, batch sizes and power points, and none of the published figures are comparable until they have been restated on a common basis.

Watch out for

  • Benchmarking against currently shipping parts. The comparison that determines the product's position is against parts launching thirty months out, and those numbers have to be projected rather than measured.
  • Vendor figures accepted without normalization. A TOPS figure quoted at a precision, batch size and power point chosen by the vendor is not comparable until it has been restated at common conditions.
  • Capability gaps recorded without an owner. A gap that does not become a requirement with a named owner remains an observation, and observations do not change the silicon.
  • Positioning based on a single metric. A product positioned only on TOPS/W competes poorly against one positioned on total cost of ownership, and that comparison is not made until launch.
  • Competitor launch dates treated as fixed. A schedule slip in the competitive field affects the product's position as much as a slip in this program, and neither can be predicted to within a quarter.

Why it exists

Assess the requirement set, the PPA targets and the cost model against real process nodes, and return a verdict: buildable as specified, buildable with named concessions, or not buildable.

Feasibility is the only activity in this stage whose output can be "no", and its value depends entirely on that answer being available. A feasibility study run after the node has been selected and the budget committed documents a decision rather than informing one, and it cannot stop a program that should be stopped.

What it delivers

DEF-D4Feasibility report

This activity produces the deliverable. The verdict, the assessment matrix and the concession list are published together, because the verdict on its own cannot be acted on.

Needs first

  • Requirement register from DEF-01
  • PPA targets from DEF-03
  • Cost model from DEF-04
  • Node characterization and DTCO study from TECH-03
  • IP availability indications from vendors and internal inventory

Done when

  • Every target has an achievability finding per candidate node
  • Concessions named and costed, not described
  • Verdict recorded with a recommendation and a dissent record

The concession list is the part of the deliverable that actually gets used. A binary verdict gives the decision review nothing to act on. A list stating "this node, at 200 MHz below target, with the PHY licensed rather than developed internally" gives the review a decision it can make.

Watch out for

  • Feasibility assessed after the node has been selected. The study then documents an existing decision rather than informing one, and its independence is lost.
  • Optimistic assessment at the boundary. A target described as reachable "with aggressive timing closure" is reachable in a presentation and not in a timing report.
  • IP availability taken from the vendor roadmap. An IP block promised on the target node but not yet ported is a schedule risk, and recording it as available converts that risk into a hidden dependency.
  • Thermal feasibility checked at typical rather than maximum power. Feasibility at average power says nothing about the part at its rated power, which is the condition the product is sold at.
  • No concession list produced. A yes-or-no verdict gives the decision review no third option, and in practice the concession option is the one most often taken.

Takes4ww4–w8 of the stage
Costs3.0 M/M~3.3 people while it runs
OwnerProgram managerFinance partner approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Convert the milestone profile into a dated plan for this program, state what it requires in engineering headcount, and compare that requirement against the resources the organization actually has.

A schedule built on a headcount curve the organization cannot staff is not a plan; it is a slip that has already been committed to. The value of this activity is the comparison between required and available capacity, not the Gantt chart itself.

What it delivers

DEF-D5Program charter, staffing and budget plan

The schedule, the headcount curve and the effort roll-up are the operative content of the charter.

Needs first

  • Milestone profile and stage baselines
  • Effort figures per activity from the template
  • Organization capacity and current program commitments
  • Supplier lead times — substrate, interposer, probe card, IP, shuttle
  • Feasibility concessions from DEF-07

Done when

  • Schedule dated from a committed kickoff
  • Headcount curve reconciled against real capacity, gaps named
  • Critical path derived and buffers placed against the fixed gates

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

Main sequence

57
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

The supplier lead-time overlay runs in parallel and changes more dates than the internal plan does. A probe card and an advanced substrate each carry roughly twenty weeks of lead time, they are ordered against dates this activity sets, and once ordered they are outside the program's control.

Watch out for

  • A headcount curve the organization cannot staff. A peak requirement of 200 engineers in a 120-engineer organization is a schedule slip recorded as a plan.
  • Template baselines used without adjustment. The profile describes a typical program. A derivative product or a first program on a new node is not typical, and the differences belong in the plan.
  • Supplier lead times discovered rather than planned. Probe card and substrate lead times run to twenty weeks. Discovered late, they move the wafer-out date rather than the purchase order date.
  • Schedule buffer placed at the end of the program. A buffer after the final stage protects nothing. Buffers belong immediately before the gates that cannot move.
  • Critical path assumed rather than derived. On a 23-stage profile with parallel enablement work, the critical path frequently runs through technology or package enablement rather than through the design flow, and assuming otherwise directs management attention to the wrong stages.

Watch out for

  • Base case presented alone. A business case that closes at forecast volume and is never shown at downside volume transfers the risk to whoever inherits the program.

  • Feasibility concessions softened before the review. A concession list edited on its way into the decision pack makes the entire feasibility activity worthless.
  • Decision authority unclear. A gate review where no individual is identified as able to decline the program is a gate review that cannot decline it.

Why it exists

Build the model the architecture is argued with. Every partitioning, sizing and interface decision in this stage is settled by simulation against the DEF-02 workload suite rather than by opinion.

Fourteen weeks and 28 M/M make this the largest activity in the stage by a wide margin, and that is the right shape. Being wrong in a model costs a re-run; being wrong in RTL costs a quarter; being wrong in silicon costs a respin. The model's credibility is the stage's credibility—the moment nobody trusts it, every decision reverts to seniority.

6 Interconnect and NoC topology studiesruns in parallel Interconnect and NoC topology study results 2w

8 Bottleneck analysis and roofline characterizationruns in parallel Bottleneck and roofline analysis 1.5w
9 Sensitivity analysis and a stated confidence interval Sensitivity analysis with a confidence statement 3w
10 Model handoff and regression harness for later stages Performance model and its source · Regression harness for downstream re-runs 1w

Correlation sits early on purpose. A model that has never been checked against silicon produces numbers, not answers, and every sweep run before correlation has to be re-run afterwards.

Watch out for

  • Model never correlated against silicon. An uncorrelated model has an unknown error bar, and every decision taken on it inherits that error silently.
  • Fidelity chosen for comfort. An analytical model that runs in seconds will answer the wrong question quickly; a cycle-accurate model that takes a week per sweep will answer nothing in time to matter.
  • Sweeps run on an unrepresentative workload. The model inherits whatever bias DEF-02 built into the suite, and amplifies it across every architectural decision.
  • Power model bolted on at the end. TOPS/W is a KPI; a performance model with no power overlay cannot answer the question the product is sold on.
  • No confidence statement. A projection quoted as a single number invites the organization to plan against a precision the model does not have.

Takes8ww2–w10 of the stage

Why it exists

Decide what sits on which die and where the block boundaries fall—including whether this is one die or several.

The monolithic-versus-chiplet call is the most expensive decision in the stage. It sets the package, the die-to-die interface, the test strategy, the yield model and the cost model at once, and after Architecture Freeze it is effectively irreversible: unwinding it means redoing the floorplan, the package design and the test hardware together.

The partitioning half of the deliverable; ARCH-06 supplies the budget half against these blocks.

  • Package architecture options from the requirement register
  • Test strategy assumptions from DFT-01

Done when

  • Partitioning decided and recorded with the alternatives it beat
  • Every boundary carries a bandwidth and latency budget
  • Test and yield implications priced, not deferred

Boundary definition takes three of the eight weeks because it is the part that gets skipped. Deciding "two dies" is quick; deciding exactly which signals cross at what bandwidth and latency is the work that makes the decision real.

Watch out for

  • Chiplet chosen for the roadmap rather than for this product. A die-to-die interface costs area, power and a test strategy; taking it on to be ready for the next program charges this one.
  • Boundaries drawn without bandwidth. A partition that names blocks but not the traffic between them is redrawn at PD-02 when the floorplan cannot carry it.
  • Reticle limit checked against the estimate, not the growth. Die area grows through implementation; a partition that fits at architecture and not at signoff is a partition that fails late.
  • Test implications deferred. Known-good-die coverage on a chiplet part is a DFT and test-hardware program of its own, and it is priced after the decision is taken.
  • Decision recorded without the dissent. The objection nobody minuted resurfaces at first silicon with nothing to point at.

ARCH-03Dataflow and memory hierarchy definition (on-die SRAM capacity, HBM channels)

Takes8ww4–w12 of the stage
Costs12.0 M/M~6.5 people while it runs
OwnerMemory systems architectWorkload analyst approves

Why it exists

Define how data moves and where it lives—dataflow, on-die SRAM capacity and organization, HBM channel count—for each workload class the product serves.

An inference accelerator is a memory system with arithmetic attached. A hierarchy that does not match the reuse pattern of the workload shows up as a utilization number nobody can lift afterwards: not by clock speed, not by more compute, and not by any amount of software.

What it delivers

ARCH-D1Architecture specification

The memory hierarchy chapter is authored here and lands in the specification whole; ARCH-09 assembles rather than rewrites it.

Needs first

  • Workload traces and reuse analysis from DEF-02
  • Bandwidth requirements from DEF-05
  • Design-space results from ARCH-01
  • Partition boundaries from ARCH-02
  • Memory compiler capability from PDK-04

Done when

  • Capacity and bandwidth justified by simulation, not by precedent
  • Dataflow chosen per workload class with the trade recorded
  • Memory instance requirements handed to PDK and AMS

How it gets there 8 steps · 2 lanes

w4w6w8w10w12

Main sequence

12478

In parallel

356
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Dataflow selection per workload class — weight-stationary, output-stationary, hybrid Dataflow specification per workload class 1.5w
2 On-die SRAM capacity sizing against measured reuse distance SRAM capacity sizing with reuse-distance evidence 2w
3 SRAM banking, port and bandwidth organizationruns in parallel SRAM capacity, banking and port organization 1.5w
4 HBM channel count and address interleaving scheme HBM channel count and interleaving scheme 1.5w
5 Cache and scratchpad policyruns in parallel Cache and scratchpad policy note 1w

Sizing precedes simulation and simulation revises sizing—the two weeks in step 7 include at least one full turn back through step 2. A hierarchy accepted on its first simulation has almost certainly not been swept.

Watch out for

  • SRAM sized on average reuse. Reuse distance has a tail; a capacity chosen at the median misses the workloads that define the product's worst case.
  • Banking decided after capacity. Capacity and bandwidth are separate constraints, and a bank organization that cannot feed the compute wastes the area it took.
  • Memory compiler capability assumed. The instance the hierarchy needs may not exist on the node—PDK-05 is where that is found, and it is found after this decision unless someone asks early.
  • Dataflow chosen once for all workloads. A single dataflow optimized for one class starves another, and the deployment mix decides which mistake is cheaper.
  • Interleaving left to implementation. Address interleaving decides whether HBM channels are actually parallel; deferred, it becomes a bandwidth shortfall nobody predicted.

The handoff in step 7 is what makes this activity urgent rather than merely important. <code>IPR-04</code> cannot evaluate a PHY vendor against a generation nobody has chosen, and PHY license lead times run to a quarter.

Watch out for

  • Specification not ratified at selection. Designing to a draft revision transfers a standards-body schedule into the program, and the transfer is invisible until compliance testing.
  • PHY assumed available on the node. A PHY proven on the previous node is not a PHY on this one; IPR-05 is where that is confirmed, and it is confirmed after this choice.
  • Compliance requirements written late. Interoperability testing needs hardware, test suites and lab time booked against dates set here.
  • Lane count set by bandwidth alone. Lanes cost bumps, area and power; a count chosen without ARCH-08 in the room is a count the floorplan will renegotiate.
  • Die-to-die selection deferred past ARCH-02. The interface is a large architectural commitment, and deferring it forces the conservative default.

Why it exists

Define the power and clock structure the whole implementation inherits—domains, rails, DVFS operating points, clock crossings, reset topology—and write the first UPF intent.

Power intent is one of the few architectural artifacts consumed literally by tools. A domain boundary drawn here becomes isolation and level-shifter cells at SYN-06 and a verification obligation at DV-06. Drawn late, or drawn differently by two teams, it forces both to be redone.

What it delivers

This activity is the deliverable, and the UPF file is the part of it tools consume directly.

The crossing inventory in step 4 is the artifact <code>RTL-06</code> closes CDC against. An inventory that is incomplete at Architecture Freeze becomes a CDC finding in week 40, when the fix is an RTL change under change control.

Watch out for

  • Domains drawn for elegance rather than for control. Every domain boundary costs isolation cells, level shifters and verification states; a domain that is never independently gated is pure overhead.
  • Crossing inventory incomplete. A clock crossing missing from the inventory is a crossing nobody constrains and nobody verifies, and it fails intermittently in silicon.
  • DVFS policy without measured operating points. Operating points chosen from the library rather than from silicon leave either performance or margin on the table.
  • UPF drafted after RTL starts. Power intent that arrives mid-RTL forces retrofitting into blocks already written, and the retrofit is never as clean as the design.
  • Reset sequencing left to bring-up. A reset order discovered in the lab is discovered on silicon that cannot be changed.

Watch out for

  • Budgets allocated to 100%. A budget with no margin has nothing left for the ECO storm at physical design, where power and area always grow.

  • Reconciliation against DEF-03 skipped. If the architecture's total quietly exceeds the definition target, the cost model is wrong and nobody has been told.
  • Timing budget by clock domain only. Domains contain blocks with very different closure difficulty, and a flat budget hides which one is impossible.

ARCH-07Security and safety architecture — secure boot, root of trust, fusing

Takes6ww6–w12 of the stage
Costs7.0 M/M~5.1 people while it runs
OwnerSecurity architectCompliance liaison approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Define how the part boots trustworthily, protects its assets and identifies itself—secure boot chain, root of trust, key storage, fuse map and lifecycle states—and the debug lockdown that goes with them.

Security is architectural or it is absent. A root of trust cannot be retrofitted onto a design with no immutable boot path and no fuse plan. The tension worth naming early is that the debug access DFT and bring-up want is the same access an attacker wants, and only an architecture can resolve it.

What it delivers

ARCH-D1Architecture specification

The security chapter is authored here in full—boot chain, lifecycle states and lockdown policy—and lands in the specification whole.

Needs first

  • Security requirements from the requirement register
  • Customer and regulatory obligations
  • Block list and boot architecture from ARCH-02
  • eFuse and OTP capability from PDK-02
  • DFT access architecture intent from DFT-04

Done when

  • Threat model reviewed and every asset mapped to a control
  • Lifecycle states defined with their transitions and their tests
  • Debug lockdown agreed with DFT rather than imposed on it

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Threat model and asset inventory Threat model and asset inventory 1w

3 Root of trust and key storage selectionruns in parallel Root of trust and key storage architecture 1w
4 Fuse map, chip identity and lifecycle state definition Fuse map and lifecycle state definition 1w

6 Cryptographic accelerator requirementruns in parallel Cryptographic accelerator requirement 0.75w
7 Security architecture note and review Security architecture note and review record 2.5w

Step 5 is a negotiation, not a decision taken alone. <code>DFT-04</code> needs JTAG and trace access for silicon debug, and every path it opens is a path this activity has to close in production lifecycle states.

Watch out for

  • Security started after the block list is fixed. A root of trust needs its own reset domain, its own ROM and its own fuse path; adding them later disturbs three architectures at once.
  • Debug access left open in production. The lifecycle state that locks JTAG is the one nobody tests, because testing it makes the part undebuggable.
  • Fuse map without a lifecycle model. Fuses are one-time; a map with no defined state transitions produces parts that cannot be returned to a testable state.
  • Key storage decided by IP availability. Choosing the root of trust because a block was available is choosing a threat model by accident.
  • No named security owner past architecture. Security decisions get eroded one waiver at a time through implementation unless someone owns them all the way to qualification.

Watch out for

  • Bump budget derived after interfaces are fixed. Lane counts set without a bump budget produce a floorplan that cannot be built and an interface that has to be cut late.
  • Power delivery bumps underestimated. Too few power bumps is an IR-drop problem discovered at SIPI-04, when the bump map is already in the package design.
  • Placement intent treated as decoration. Physical design inherits this drawing; an intent that ignores routing feasibility is redrawn at PD-01 and the schedule pays for both.
  • Package feasibility checked against a generic assumption. Bump pitch and field size depend on the actual interposer and substrate technology, which PKGD-01 may not have settled yet.
  • HBM PHY placement left open. HBM PHYs must sit against the interposer edge facing their stacks; deciding this late constrains everything else on the die.

3 Consistency pass — every number traced to its source activityruns in parallel Consistency and traceability record 1.5w
4 Open-issue register and dispositionruns in parallel Open-issue register with disposition per item 1w
5 Internal technical review, two rounds Internal technical review findings, two rounds 2w
6 Downstream readiness review with RTL, DV, DFT and physical design Downstream readiness review findings 1.5w
7 Freeze package assemblyruns in parallel Architecture Freeze package and decision record 1w
8 Architecture Freeze gate Architecture Freeze gate decision 1.5w

The downstream readiness review in step 6 is the one that predicts the program. Architecture reviewing its own specification confirms it is coherent; RTL, DV and DFT reviewing it confirms it is implementable, and those are different questions.

Watch out for

  • Freeze declared with open issues undispositioned. An open issue carried past freeze is a decision deferred to whoever hits it first in RTL.
  • Consistency pass skipped under schedule pressure. The same number appearing differently in two chapters is the defect that costs the most and is found the latest.
  • Downstream teams reviewing after freeze. A readiness review that happens after the gate cannot change anything, and becomes a complaint rather than a review.
  • Specification written as a narrative. Implementable specifications are tables, interfaces and constraints; prose is where ambiguity survives review.
  • Freeze treated as a date rather than a condition. A gate that passes because it was scheduled to teaches the organization that gates do not mean anything.

ARCH-10Block microarchitecture specification kickoff

Takes6ww12–w18 of the stage

Why it exists

Turn each architectural block into a microarchitecture specification its RTL owner can implement from—pipeline structure, interfaces, control, register map and the verification hooks.

The architecture specification says what each block does; this says how. Starting it inside the architecture stage rather than at RTL kickoff is what lets RTL-02 begin with something to write against instead of a paragraph—and it is the cheapest place to find out that two blocks disagree about the interface between them.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Partitioning and boundaries from ARCH-02
  • Memory hierarchy specification from ARCH-03
  • PPA budget per block from ARCH-06
  • Verification strategy intent from DV-01

Done when

  • Every block has a specification and a named owner
  • Shared interfaces agreed by both sides, not by each
  • RTL leads have accepted the handoff as implementable

Step 4 runs in parallel and is where the interesting failures live. Two block owners each writing their side of a shared interface will disagree, and finding that here costs a meeting rather than an integration debug at <code>RTL-04</code>.

Watch out for

  • Block owners not assigned. A block whose specification has no author is a block whose RTL starts by inventing one, usually in week three of implementation.
  • Interfaces written from one side. Each owner specifying their own side of a shared interface produces two consistent documents that disagree with each other.
  • Register map deferred to RTL. The register map is the software contract; defining it late means firmware development starts late and the two never converge.
  • Verification hooks added after the design. Observability designed in is cheap; observability retrofitted costs area, timing and an RTL change under control.
  • Microarchitecture that ignores the budget. A pipeline designed without reference to ARCH-06's allocation is a budget overrun scheduled for synthesis.

03 TECH · Technology & Foundry Selection

TECH-01Foundry and node long-list to short-list evaluation

Takes5ww0–w5 of the stage
Costs4.0 M/M~3.5 people while it runs
OwnerTechnology strategistChief architect approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Narrow the field of foundries and nodes to a short-list the program can actually evaluate, and record why the others were dropped.

Every other decision in this stage is conditional on this one, and so is most of the enablement band: IP availability, PDK maturity, library qualification and capacity all become node-specific the moment the short-list closes. The screen has to be quick and it has to be written down—a selection nobody can reconstruct is one that gets reopened at every setback.

What it delivers

TECH-D1Technology selection report and decision record

This activity owns the deliverable; TECH-03 supplies the technical evidence it rests on.

Needs first

  • Product requirements and PPA targets from DEF-01 and DEF-03
  • Volume forecast and cost ceiling from the business case
  • Foundry public roadmaps and node cadence
  • Previous-program experience with each foundry
  • Export control and supply-continuity guidance

Done when

  • Short-list of at least two candidates, with the dropped options recorded
  • Criteria weighted before the responses were read
  • Recommendation carries availability windows, not only technical fit

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w0w1w2w3w4w5

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 3 is the pacing item and almost none of it is our work—information requests sit with the foundry's technical marketing team, and the response time is theirs. Starting the engagement in week one is the only lever the program has over it.

Watch out for

  • Short-list of one. A screen that arrives at a single candidate has no negotiating position on price, capacity or terms, and the foundry knows it.
  • Selection driven by relationship. The foundry the last program used is a legitimate input and a poor criterion; making it the criterion means the screen was theatre.
  • Availability window not checked. A node that is right for the product but reaches risk production after the tapeout date is not a candidate, however good the numbers are.
  • Export control screened late. A candidate that fails compliance after technical evaluation has consumed weeks of the stage for nothing.
  • Criteria written after the data arrives. Weighting the screen once the responses are in produces the answer somebody already wanted.

03 TECH · Technology & Foundry Selection

TECH-02Process option and flavor selection (HPC/HD, multi-Vt menu, backside PDN, RF/HV adders)

Takes5ww4–w9 of the stage
Costs4.0 M/M~3.5 people while it runs
OwnerTechnology strategistFoundry technical account manager approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Choose the flavor of the node, not just the node—performance or density library, the multi-Vt menu, the metal stack, backside power delivery, and any analog or high-voltage adders the product needs.

A node name is not a specification. Two programs on the same node with different flavor sheets get different density, different leakage and different routing resource, and the difference is larger than most architectural decisions. This sheet is also what the foundry prices against, so it has to close before TECH-04 can finish.

What it delivers

TECH-D2Process option / flavor sheet agreed with foundry

This activity is the deliverable, and it is contractual rather than advisory.

Needs first

  • Short-list from TECH-01
  • PPA targets from DEF-03
  • DTCO findings as they emerge from TECH-03
  • Reticle and die size direction from ARCH-02
  • Analog and PHY requirements from ARCH-04

Done when

  • Flavor sheet agreed and signed, not merely discussed
  • Metal stack backed by a congestion study rather than by precedent
  • Every analog and adder requirement captured before agreement

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w4w5w6w7w8w9

Main sequence

1257

In parallel

346
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Process flavor options against the PPA targets — HPC, HD, or mixed Flavor option comparison against the PPA targets 1w
2 Multi-Vt menu selection and its leakage implication Multi-Vt menu selection with leakage projection 1w
3 Backside power delivery evaluation, where the node offers itruns in parallel Backside power delivery evaluation 0.75w
4 RF, high-voltage and analog adder requirementsruns in parallel Analog, RF and high-voltage adder list 0.5w
5 Metal stack selection and routing resource implication Metal stack selection and routing resource note 1w

Two of the five weeks sit in step 7, which is signature time rather than engineering time. The sheet is a contractual artifact: once agreed it governs what the PDK contains and what the wafer costs, and changing it later reopens both.

Watch out for

  • Flavor chosen for density alone. A high-density library that cannot reach the frequency target trades an area saving for a performance failure, and the trade is discovered at trial synthesis.
  • Metal stack chosen without a congestion study. Too few routing layers is the defect that surfaces at PD-06, when the only remaining fix is a floorplan change.
  • Multi-Vt menu wider than the flow supports. Every extra Vt is a library to characterize, qualify and maintain; menus are chosen for leakage and paid for in methodology.
  • Backside power taken for the roadmap. A first-generation backside PDN buys power integrity and costs schedule risk, and the trade belongs to this product rather than the next one.
  • Adders discovered after the sheet is agreed. An analog or high-voltage requirement that arrives late is a sheet amendment, a price change and a PDK delta at once.

03 TECH · Technology & Foundry Selection

TECH-03Density / performance / leakage benchmarking against product targets (DTCO study)

Takes7ww3–w10 of the stage
Costs6.0 M/M~3.7 people while it runs
OwnerDTCO leadFoundry technical contact approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Measure the candidate nodes against this product's targets rather than against the foundry's brochure—density, achievable frequency, leakage, SRAM Vmin and routing resource, on circuits that resemble the design.

This is the technical evidence the selection stands on. Published node comparisons are made on somebody else's circuits at somebody else's operating point; a DTCO study run on representative structures is the only way to know whether the PPA targets survive the node, and it is what DEF-07 tests feasibility against.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Short-list from TECH-01
  • PPA targets from DEF-03
  • Foundry-supplied preliminary libraries and models
  • Previous-generation design as a benchmark reference
  • Memory compiler capability indications

Done when

  • Every target has a measured result per candidate node
  • Findings state margin, not only pass or fail
  • Benchmark set documented well enough to re-run on a later PDK

How it gets there 8 steps · 2 lanes

w3w5w7w9w10

Main sequence

12378

In parallel

456
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Benchmark circuit set definition, representative of the design Benchmark circuit set and its rationale 0.75w
2 Standard cell density and area scaling study Density and area scaling results per node 1.5w
3 Ring oscillator and critical-path frequency study Ring oscillator and critical-path frequency study 1.5w
4 Leakage and dynamic power characterization across the Vt menuruns in parallel Frequency and leakage characterization per Vt 1.25w
5 SRAM bitcell density and Vmin studyruns in parallel SRAM density and Vmin findings 1.25w
6 Routing congestion proxy study on the candidate metal stacksruns in parallel Routing congestion proxy results 1w
7 Node comparison against the DEF-03 targets Node comparison against the PPA targets 1.5w
8 DTCO findings and recommendation DTCO findings and node recommendation 1.75w

Three of the eight steps run in parallel because they use different data and different people—power characterization, SRAM and congestion are separable studies. What cannot be parallelized is step 7: comparison needs all three to have landed.

Watch out for

  • Benchmark circuits unrepresentative. A study run on ring oscillators alone measures the node and not the design; the answer is precise and irrelevant.
  • Preliminary libraries treated as final. Early PDK models move, sometimes by more than the difference between the candidates, and a comparison made on 0.5 data can invert.
  • SRAM left out. On an accelerator the array is a large fraction of the die; a node comparison without a bitcell and Vmin study has skipped the dominant area and the dominant Vmin constraint.
  • Congestion never modelled. Density that cannot be routed is not density, and the routing resource question is decided by the metal stack chosen in TECH-02.
  • Results reported without margin. A target met exactly in a DTCO study will not be met in implementation, and reporting the number without the margin invites the wrong conclusion.

03 TECH · Technology & Foundry Selection

TECH-04Wafer price, mask and NRE quotation; MPW and volume pricing

Takes6ww5–w11 of the stage
Costs3.0 M/M~2.2 people while it runs
OwnerProcurement leadProgram manager approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Put a price on the technology—wafers at the forecast volume, the mask set, the NRE, the MPW shuttle, and every adder the flavor sheet carries—and hand it to the cost model as quotations rather than estimates.

The cost model in DEF-04 is only as good as this activity. A model built on published estimates produces a margin nobody can defend at the funding gate; a model built on quotations produces one that survives the first conversation with finance.

What it delivers

TECH-D3Wafer, mask and NRE cost sheet

This activity is the deliverable, and its value is that the numbers are quoted rather than estimated.

Needs first

  • Short-list and flavor sheet from TECH-01 and TECH-02
  • Volume forecast and ramp profile from the business case
  • Die size estimate from DEF-04
  • Mask layer count implied by the metal stack
  • MPW shuttle calendar from the foundry

Done when

  • Every cost line quoted, with a validity period and currency term
  • Tier structure reflects the actual ramp, not a notional volume
  • Cost sheet loaded into the DEF-04 model, not summarized into it

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w5w7w9w11

Main sequence

1267

In parallel

345
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Volume and wafer-start forecast from the business case Volume and wafer-start forecast 0.5w
2 Wafer price request and negotiation Wafer price quotations per foundry 2w
3 Mask set and NRE quotation per node and flavorruns in parallel Mask set and NRE quotation per candidate 1.5w
4 MPW shuttle pricing and slot costruns in parallel MPW shuttle pricing and slot cost 0.5w
5 Option adder pricing against the TECH-02 sheetruns in parallel Option adder pricing 0.5w
6 Volume tier and price-break structure Wafer price quotation with tier structure 2.5w
7 Cost sheet publication into the DEF-04 model Cost sheet published into the DEF-04 model 1w

The tier structure in step 6 is worth more than the headline price. A wafer price that only applies above a volume the product will not reach in its first year is a price the cost model should not be using.

Watch out for

  • Price quoted at a volume the product will not reach. Tier structures are where the real cost lives, and a headline price at ten times the forecast volume is a number the model should reject.
  • Mask cost estimated from layer count alone. EUV layers dominate mask cost, and the count of them depends on the flavor sheet rather than on the total layer count.
  • Adders priced after the sheet is agreed. Once TECH-02 closes, the adders are committed; pricing them afterwards removes the option of dropping one.
  • Currency and term exposure ignored. A quotation with no validity period or currency term is not a quotation the cost model can carry to a funding gate.
  • Second-source pricing never requested. Without a comparison the negotiation has no floor, and the first price is the last price.

03 TECH · Technology & Foundry Selection

TECH-05Fab capacity and tapeout slot reservation; hot-lot policy agreement

Takes5ww8–w13 of the stage
Costs2.0 M/M~1.7 people while it runs
OwnerFoundry relationship managerProduct engineering liaison approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Convert the program's schedule into reserved fab capacity—a wafer-start profile, a tapeout slot, hot-lot terms and an engineering-lot allocation—and get it committed in writing.

Capacity is not bought at tapeout; it is reserved a year before, against a date that will move. The commitment matters most in its escalation path: when the schedule slips or the market tightens, what the program has is whatever was written down, and a verbal understanding is worth exactly nothing at that moment.

What it delivers

TECH-D5Capacity and tapeout slot commitment

This activity is the deliverable, and it is worth only as much as the escalation path written into it.

Needs first

  • Program schedule and tapeout date from DEF-08
  • Wafer volume forecast and ramp profile
  • Foundry capacity availability at the node
  • Hot-lot policy terms offered by the foundry
  • Engineering and risk-lot requirements from the test plan

Done when

  • Capacity committed in writing, with an escalation contact named
  • Hot-lot terms explicit rather than understood
  • Engineering and risk lots allocated separately from production

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w8w9w10w11w12w13

Main sequence

1236

In parallel

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

4 Hot-lot policy and priority termsruns in parallel Hot-lot policy and priority terms 1w
5 Engineering-lot and risk-wafer allocationruns in parallel Engineering and risk-lot allocation 0.75w
6 Capacity commitment letter and escalation path Capacity commitment letter with an escalation path 2w

Steps 4 and 5 look like details and behave like insurance. Hot-lot priority is what turns an 18-week fab cycle into an 11-week one at <code>FAB-04</code>, and it is only available to programs that negotiated it before they needed it.

Watch out for

  • Slot reserved against a date that has not been committed. A tapeout slot booked against an optimistic schedule is a slot that will be missed and re-queued behind whoever is ready.
  • Hot-lot terms left informal. Priority granted by relationship evaporates when a larger customer needs the same capacity in the same week.
  • No escalation path. A commitment with no named escalation contact is a commitment enforced by goodwill, which is not a mechanism.
  • Engineering lots forgotten. Test-program development and characterization need silicon before the production ramp, and those wafers have to be allocated separately.
  • Capacity sized to the base case only. An upside scenario the fab cannot supply is a revenue forecast the program cannot deliver on.

Why it exists

Put the legal frame in place that everything technical depends on—NDA, design agreement, PDK and library licensing, the foundry IP frame, and liability terms—and execute it.

This is the longest activity in the stage at eight weeks and one of the smallest at 2 M/M, which is exactly the shape it should have: the elapsed time belongs to two legal departments and almost none of the work belongs to the program. It is on the critical path anyway, because production PDK access, memory compilers and foundry IP all sit behind the design agreement.

What it delivers

TECH-D4Executed foundry design agreement (DA) and NDA

This activity is the deliverable, and until it executes the enablement band cannot legally start.

Needs first

  • Short-list from TECH-01
  • Corporate legal templates and negotiation positions
  • Foundry standard agreement terms
  • Export control and compliance guidance
  • IP requirements from ARCH-04 and IPR-01

Done when

  • NDA and design agreement executed, not merely agreed
  • PDK, library and foundry IP access all covered by scope
  • Access distributed to the teams that need it, and tracked

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 1 is deliberately first and deliberately short. Nothing technical can be discussed before the NDA executes, so every week it takes is a week subtracted from <code>TECH-03</code>—which is why the NDA is chased separately from the agreement it precedes.

Watch out for

  • NDA treated as a formality and queued behind the agreement. Technical evaluation is blocked until it executes, and every week lost here is taken out of the DTCO study.
  • Foundry IP frame left out of scope. Memory compilers and IO libraries are licensed separately from the PDK; discovering that at PDK-04 stops library qualification.
  • Distribution not tracked. An executed agreement nobody circulated leaves engineers unable to download the PDK they are waiting for, and the delay looks technical.
  • Yield responsibility left ambiguous. Who owns a process excursion is a term, not a conversation to have after it happens.
  • Redline cycles unbudgeted. Two legal departments will take longer than either forecasts, and the program's plan should assume the longer number.

03 TECH · Technology & Foundry Selection

TECH-07Foundry roadmap and risk-production timing alignment

Takes4ww1–w5 of the stage
Costs1.5 M/M~1.6 people while it runs
OwnerTechnology strategistProduct cost analyst approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Establish where each candidate node actually is on its maturity curve—risk production timing, defect density trend, yield learning rate, capacity ramp—and turn that into a risk assessment the program plans against.

A node chosen at the right time is a node in volume production when the program taped out. A node chosen too early gives the program the foundry's learning curve as a yield problem, and the schedule to absorb it was never in the plan.

What it delivers

TECH-D6Node risk assessment — maturity, defect density, yield learning curve

This activity is the deliverable, and it is what the yield assumption in the cost model should be built on.

Needs first

  • Foundry roadmap and node cadence under NDA

Step 2 asks for data the foundry treats as sensitive, and how much of it arrives is itself a signal. A foundry that will not share a defect density trend under NDA is telling the program something about the trend.

Watch out for

  • Marketing defect density used as a planning number. The published curve is a target; the yield the program gets is the curve at its own tapeout date, which is a different point.
  • Risk production date taken as the availability date. Risk production is when the node exists, not when it is ready for a large die at volume, and the gap can be two quarters.
  • Roadmap alignment checked once. Foundry roadmaps move; an alignment done at selection and never revisited is a stale assumption by tapeout.
  • No mitigation options developed. Identifying a maturity risk without a mitigation—a later slot, a shuttle, a conservative design rule set—leaves the program with a finding and no action.
  • Large-die yield inferred from small-die data. Defect density scales against area brutally, and a curve measured on small test die flatters a 600 mm² part.

TECH-08Second-source and node-migration strategy assessment

Takes4ww9–w13 of the stage
Costs1.5 M/M~1.6 people while it runs
OwnerTechnology strategistProgram manager approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Decide, deliberately, whether the program accepts single-source risk—and if it does not, what dual-sourcing or migration readiness would cost in area, schedule and IP.

Most leading-edge programs end up single-source, and that is a defensible answer. What is not defensible is arriving there by default. This activity prices the alternative so that the acceptance is a decision with a number attached rather than a shrug.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Selected node and flavor from TECH-01 and TECH-02
  • IP bill of materials direction from IPR-01
  • Design rule sets for alternative foundries
  • Migration experience from previous programs
  • Supply-continuity findings from TECH-01

Done when

  • Migration cost estimated with IP portability included
  • Recommendation recorded, including the option of accepting single source
  • Accepted exposure entered on the program risk register with an owner

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

4 Design rule and library delta analysisruns in parallel Design rule and library delta analysis 0.75w

Migration readiness is a design-time choice, not a later option: it constrains which IP can be used and how aggressively design rules can be pushed. Deciding after RTL starts means the decision has already been made by everyone who chose an IP.

Watch out for

  • Single-source accepted by default. A decision nobody made is a decision nobody owns, and it surfaces during a supply disruption as a surprise.
  • Migration cost estimated without IP portability. Foundry-specific memory compilers, IO and PHY are the expensive part of a migration, and they are usually the part left out of the estimate.
  • Migration readiness assumed to be free. Designing to the intersection of two rule sets costs density and frequency on the node actually used.
  • Decision taken after IP selection. Once IPR-03 has committed to foundry-specific IP, migration readiness is no longer available at the price this study quotes.
  • Second source screened on capability alone. Capability without allocated capacity is not a second source; it is a phone number.

Why it exists

Open the backend supply chain early—OSAT capability and capacity, substrate and interposer suppliers, the foundry-to-OSAT logistics model, and who owns known-good die—so package design starts against real constraints.

On a 2.5D part the backend is not a downstream detail; it is a second supply chain with its own lead times, its own capacity constraints and its own qualification. Advanced packaging capacity in particular is allocated far ahead, and a program that starts asking at PKGD-10 is asking late.

What it delivers

  • Interposer technology options from the foundry

Done when

  • Advanced packaging capacity indicated, not assumed
  • Known-good-die responsibility model agreed in principle
  • Findings handed to PKGD before package architecture is chosen

Step 5 decides an argument before it happens. When a packaged unit fails, whether the die or the assembly is responsible is a contractual question, and settling it while nobody has lost money is far easier than settling it afterwards.

Watch out for

  • Advanced packaging capacity assumed available. CoWoS-class capacity is allocated quarters ahead and to a small number of customers; assuming access is the single most common backend planning error.
  • OSAT chosen after package design starts. Assembly process capability constrains the package design; choosing the OSAT afterwards means redesigning to fit.
  • Known-good-die responsibility left open. The first failed assembly lot is the wrong moment to discover that nobody agreed who owns the die.
  • Substrate lead time discovered rather than planned. Twenty-week substrate lead times set the order date, and the order date is derived from a wafer-out date nobody has committed yet.
  • Logistics model ignored. Wafers crossing borders between fab, sort and assembly carry customs, export control and transit time that the schedule rarely shows.

04 PDK · PDK & Design Enablement

PDK-01PDK version roadmap tracking (0.1 → 0.5 → 1.0 → production) and delta impact analysis

Takes34w cont.w0–w34 of the stage
Costs14.0 M/M~1.8 people while it runs
OwnerPDK ownerPhysical design liaison approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Track what the foundry actually ships, version by version, and turn each release into a delta the program can act on—what changed, what it costs, and whether anything already done has to be redone.

A PDK is not a thing you receive; it is a sequence. Design starts on 0.5 because waiting for production would cost two quarters, and the 0.5-to-1.0 delta then arrives in the middle of physical design. Whether that delta is a two-week re-characterization or a reopened timing signoff depends entirely on whether anyone was watching.

What it delivers

PDK-D1PDK readiness dashboard — version, release date, open gap list

This activity is the deliverable, and it is a living document rather than a report—its value is entirely in being current.

Needs first

  • Foundry PDK release calendar and notes
  • Selected node and flavor sheet from TECH-01 and TECH-02
  • Design agreement access from TECH-06
  • Library and deck versions in use across the teams
  • Design status — what has been characterized against which version

Done when

  • Every version transition assessed before adoption, not after
  • All teams on one recorded version, with exceptions logged
  • Production PDK adopted and frozen with an exception path defined

How it gets there 8 steps · 2 lanes

w0w7w14w21w28w34

Main sequence

12468

In parallel

357
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Release calendar and version tracking framework Release calendar and version tracking framework 1w
2 0.1 to 0.5 delta impact analysis 0.1-to-0.5 delta impact analysis 4w
3 Gap list maintained against what the design actually needsruns in parallel Open gap list against the design's requirements 3w
4 0.5 to 1.0 delta impact analysis Delta impact analysis per version transition 5w
5 Library and deck re-qualification per versionruns in parallel Re-qualification record per library and deck 6w
6 Production PDK adoption and version freeze decision Production PDK adoption and freeze decision 4w
7 Version freeze policy and exception handlingruns in parallel Version freeze decision and exception log 3w
8 Readiness dashboard maintenance across the stage PDK readiness dashboard, maintained 20w

Step 8 runs for twenty of the thirty-four weeks and is the activity most likely to be dropped when the team is busy. It is also the only artifact that tells the program which of its assumptions have quietly expired.

Watch out for

  • Design starts on a version the foundry calls preliminary and nobody re-checks. The gap between 0.5 and production has reopened timing signoff on more than one program.
  • Delta analysis done on the release notes alone. Foundry notes describe what changed; only re-running the design's own characterization says what it costs here.
  • Teams on different versions. Synthesis on one library revision and physical design on another produces a mismatch that looks like a tool bug for weeks.
  • Freeze declared without an exception path. A hard freeze with no route for a critical fix gets broken quietly, which is worse than breaking it openly.
  • Dashboard maintained until the team gets busy. A stale readiness dashboard is more dangerous than none, because it is still trusted.

04 PDK · PDK & Design Enablement

PDK-02Design rule manual review; restricted and recommended rule disposition

Takes6ww1–w7 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~3.6 people while it runs
OwnerCAD methodology leadFoundry technical contact approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Read the design rule manual as a constraint on this design rather than as a document—identify which restricted rules bite, dispose of every recommended rule, and get the exceptions requested early.

Restricted and recommended rules are where a node's real density lives. A design that adopts every recommended rule is safe and large; one that ignores them is dense and fails DFM. The disposition is a series of deliberate trades, and making them here is far cheaper than discovering them as violations at physical verification.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Design rule manual for the selected node and flavor
  • Previous-node DRM for comparison
  • Floorplan intent from ARCH-08
  • Custom and analog design intent from AMS-01
  • Foundry exception request process

Done when

  • Every recommended rule dispositioned with a reason, not defaulted
  • Exception requests submitted, with expected response dates
  • Disposition distributed to digital and custom teams alike

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Exception requests in step 5 run in parallel because the foundry's response time is measured in weeks. Submitting them at the end of the review rather than as each one is identified adds a month to the answer.

Watch out for

  • Recommended rules adopted wholesale. Safe, and it costs density the product was sized against; the trade should be made per rule, not once.
  • Restricted rules discovered at physical verification. A restricted rule that bites is a layout change, and finding it at SO-02 means finding it after routing closed.
  • Exception requests batched to the end. Foundry turnaround runs to weeks per request; batching them converts a parallel wait into a serial one.
  • Analog rules read only by the digital team. Pushed-rule and analog-specific sections matter to AMS-07, and they are the sections a digital-led review skips.
  • Disposition never distributed. A decision the layout engineers never saw is a decision that does not exist.

04 PDK · PDK & Design Enablement

PDK-03Standard cell library selection and qualification (track height, multi-Vt, multi-bit flops)

Takes8ww4–w12 of the stage
Costs9.0 M/M~4.9 people while it runs

Why it exists

Choose the standard cell libraries the design will be built from and qualify them rather than assume them—track height, Vt menu, multi-bit flops, and the timing models every downstream tool will trust.

Library selection is a PPA decision disguised as a procurement one. Track height sets density and drive strength; the Vt menu sets leakage; multi-bit flops set clock power. And a timing model that is wrong at one corner produces a design that closes in the tool and fails in silicon, which is the failure mode nobody catches until bring-up.

What it delivers

PDK-D2Qualified library list with .lib / LEF / GDS views

The standard cell half of the deliverable; PDK-04 adds memory and PDK-07 adds IO.

Needs first

  • Flavor sheet from TECH-02
  • DTCO findings from TECH-03
  • PDK release under tracking from PDK-01
  • PPA targets and clock power budget from ARCH-06
  • Foundry library release notes and characterization data

Done when

  • Timing models checked at this design's corners, not only the foundry's
  • Vt menu frozen with a maintenance owner per corner
  • Abstract and layout views confirmed consistent

356
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

7 Qualification record and library freeze Library qualification record and freeze 3.5w

Step 4 is the step that earns the activity. Foundry timing models are qualified by the foundry against the foundry's test cases; checking them at this design's corners and slew ranges is what catches the model error before it becomes a silicon failure.

Watch out for

  • Timing models trusted without a quality check. A model error at one corner produces a design that closes in the tool and fails on silicon—the most expensive class of library defect.
  • Track height chosen from the previous program. Density and drive strength trade differently at each node; inheriting the choice inherits an answer to a question nobody asked here.
  • Vt menu wider than the flow can maintain. Every Vt is a characterization, a qualification and a maintenance burden across every version transition.
  • Multi-bit flops evaluated after synthesis starts. Clock power is largely decided by flop banking, and retrofitting it means re-running synthesis and re-closing timing.
  • LEF and GDS inconsistency. An abstract that disagrees with the layout produces DRC violations at the very end, after routing has been built on the abstract.

Why it exists

Get the memory compiler licensed, evaluate what it can actually produce, and generate the instances the design asked for—with every view a downstream tool needs.

On an inference accelerator the memory array is a large fraction of the die, and the compiler decides most of it. What the compiler can generate is a hard boundary on the architecture: a configuration outside its range is not a compiler setting, it is a custom design program in AMS-05 costing four months.

Step 3 is the one with a schedule consequence. A capability gap found here opens the <code>PDK-06</code> decision with fifteen weeks of runway; found at instance generation, it opens the same decision with three.

Watch out for

  • Compiler license assumed to be covered by the PDK agreement. Memory compilers are licensed separately, and discovering that here stops the activity for weeks.
  • Capability screened after generation starts. The gap is the same size either way; what differs is how much runway the custom path has.
  • Views generated but never checked. A missing or inconsistent view surfaces at PD-02 when the macro cannot be placed, and the compiler run has to be repeated.
  • Redundancy chosen without DFT. Repair schemes have to match the BISR architecture in DFT-03, and a mismatch is found at pattern generation.
  • Instance count explosion. Generating every configuration a block owner asks for produces a library nobody can characterize or maintain; consolidation is cheaper here than later.

PDK-05Compiler instance PPA characterization against block budgets — density, Vmin, access time, leakage

Takes6ww14–w20 of the stage
Costs7.0 M/M~5.1 people while it runs
OwnerMemory characterization engineerBlock owners approves

Why it exists

Measure what the generated instances actually deliver—density, Vmin, access time, leakage—and set it against the budget each block was allocated.

This is the activity that decides whether the custom memory path opens. The compiler produces an instance that meets the specification; the question here is whether it meets the budget, and the answer is frequently no by a margin large enough to matter but small enough to be argued about.

What it delivers

PDK-D3Memory PPA gap analysis and custom-instance decision record

The gap analysis half—PDK-06 adds the decision that follows from it.

Needs first

  • Generated instances from PDK-04
  • Block memory budgets from ARCH-06
  • Vmin and operating voltage requirements from ARCH-05
  • Access time requirements from the hierarchy specification
  • DTCO SRAM findings from TECH-03

Done when

  • Every instance measured against its block's budget
  • Gaps quantified in area, power and Vmin, not described
  • Results delivered with enough runway for PDK-06 to act

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

Main sequence

1236

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
