The gap analysis is quantified rather than described on purpose. "The compiler misses the budget" starts an argument; "the L2 array misses its density budget by 14%, which is 3.1 mm² of die" starts a decision.

Watch out for

  • Density measured on the datasheet rather than the instance. Compiler datasheets quote best-case configurations; the instance the design needs is rarely one of them.
  • Vmin characterized at nominal only. Vmin is a distribution, and the number that matters is at the corner and the sigma the product is sold at.
  • Gap described rather than quantified. A shortfall without a number in square millimetres cannot be traded against schedule in PDK-06.
  • Measurement late enough to remove the option. Characterization completing after the AMS window has closed makes the custom path unavailable regardless of the gap.
  • Access time measured without the wire load. An instance that meets access time standalone and misses it in place has not been characterized usefully.

Takes4ww19–w23 of the stage

Why it exists

Decide what to do about the memory shortfall—push rules, build a custom array, or change the architecture—and hand the chosen scope to AMS with a schedule attached.

This is a gate, not a study. The compiler instance missed the budget; the options each cost something different and one of them has to be taken. Deferring the decision does not preserve the options—the custom array path needs its full window in AMS-05 through AMS-10, and every week of deferral removes one from the end.

What it delivers

The decision half of the deliverable, and the record downstream stages will point at.

Needs first

  • AMS capacity and window from the program schedule
  • Foundry pushed-rule policy and approval process
  • Architecture flexibility from ARCH-03
  • Cost impact of the die area at stake from DEF-04

Done when

  • Decision taken and recorded with the rejected options priced
  • Foundry approval path confirmed if pushed rules are chosen
  • Scope handed to AMS with a date, not only a requirement

  • Decision deferred to preserve options. Deferral removes the custom option rather than preserving it, because the window is fixed at the far end by physical design.
  • Pushed rules chosen without foundry commitment. Approval is a process with its own duration, and an unapproved pushed-rule array is a layout nobody can tape out.
  • Architecture change dismissed too quickly. Reducing the array is sometimes cheaper than building it; the option deserves the same costing as the other two.
  • Scope handed to AMS without a schedule. A custom instance request with no date is a request that competes with the SerDes for the same engineers and loses.
  • Decision taken without the block owner. The owner who accepted the budget in ARCH-06 is the one who has to accept the concession here.

Why it exists

Qualify the IO, ESD and latch-up collateral—the library that sits at the die edge and decides whether the part survives handling, and whether its interfaces meet their electrical specifications.

IO qualification is unglamorous and it is where parts die. An ESD strategy chosen late constrains the pad ring after the bump map is fixed; a latch-up rule missed produces a part that fails qualification for reasons no functional test would ever find.

The ESD strategy in step 3 has to precede pad ring layout, which in turn precedes the bump map freeze in <code>ARCH-08</code>. Late ESD is a pad ring change, and a pad ring change is a bump map change.

Watch out for

  • ESD strategy chosen after the pad ring. Clamp placement and rail topology constrain the ring; retrofitting means redoing the ring and the bump map with it.
  • IO models unchecked. IO timing models feed both STA and the channel simulation in SIPI-07; an error propagates into two signoffs at once.
  • Latch-up rules read as a formality. Guard ring strategy affects area at the die edge, and a late change competes with the interfaces for the same space.
  • Package and board ESD requirements ignored. The part's ESD rating is a system property; qualifying only the die produces a rating the system cannot use.
  • Library selected per interface with no consolidation. Several IO families in one ring multiplies the qualification and the pad ring complexity for little gain.

Why it exists

Decide which tool at which version each flow step runs on, qualify that combination on the node, and freeze it—so that a result from one team means the same thing as a result from another.

Tool versions are a correctness question, not an IT one. A node this advanced needs certified versions for extraction, timing and physical verification, and mixing versions across teams produces disagreements that consume weeks before anyone suspects the tools rather than the design.

This activity is the deliverable, and the freeze is the part that matters.

  • Existing internal tool estate and licences
  • Flow step definitions from PDK-09

  • Freeze published with an exception route for critical fixes

Step 6 catches what per-tool qualification cannot. Each tool can be certified on the node and still disagree with the next one about a database format or a parasitic convention, and only a cross-tool check finds it.

Watch out for

  • Teams on different versions. Two teams with different STA versions will disagree about timing, and the disagreement is diagnosed as a design problem for weeks first.
  • Certification status assumed. Vendor node certification lags node release; an uncertified version produces results the foundry will not accept at signoff.
  • Interoperability never checked. Per-tool qualification passes and the handoff between them fails, usually on parasitic or database conventions.
  • Freeze with no upgrade path. A critical tool fix will arrive mid-program, and a policy that has no route to accept it will be broken informally.
  • Matrix published once. A matrix nobody re-reads after month three is a matrix that describes an estate nobody is running.

Why it exists

Take the foundry's reference flow, adapt it into a methodology this design can actually run, and prove it on a representative block before the whole team depends on it.

A reference flow is a starting point written for a generic design. This one has hierarchical partitions, hard macros, multiple power domains and a memory subsystem the reference never contemplated. The pilot in the last step is what turns an adapted flow into a trusted one.

Three of the ten weeks are the pilot, and it is the step under most pressure to be skipped. A flow that has never been run end to end on a real block is a flow whose first user is doing the debugging on the critical path.

Watch out for

  • Pilot skipped under schedule pressure. The flow's first real user then debugs it while on the critical path, which is the most expensive place to do it.
  • Reference flow adopted rather than adapted. A generic flow on a hierarchical design with hard macros produces results nobody can close.
  • Low-power flow bolted on late. UPF handling touches synthesis, placement and verification; adding it after the flow is built means rebuilding it.
  • Methodology deck written after the flow changes. A guide that lags the scripts teaches the wrong flow to every engineer who joins.
  • Pilot block unrepresentative. A small clean block pilots nothing; the pilot has to include a macro, a domain crossing and real congestion.

Why it exists

Put every rule deck, extraction file and verification runset under version control, validate them on known-good structures, and make deck changes a notified event rather than a surprise.

Decks are the quiet dependency. A DRC runset revision that arrives without notice changes what passes verification, and if two teams are running different revisions the disagreement looks like a layout problem. Version control here is what makes a signoff result reproducible six months later.

Validation on known-good structures in step 4 is what makes a deck trustworthy. A runset that has never been tested against a layout with a known answer will report both false positives and, far worse, false negatives.

Watch out for

  • Decks used from a shared directory. An unversioned deck makes every result unreproducible, and the problem is invisible until two results disagree.
  • Extraction deck unvalidated. Parasitic extraction errors move timing by amounts that look like design problems, and they are found after weeks of closure work.
  • Deck updates applied silently. A runset revision mid-closure changes what passes, and nobody can explain why yesterday's clean run is dirty today.
  • No known-good structures. Without a layout whose answer is known, deck validation is an assertion.
  • Tracking stops when the stage ends. Decks keep moving through signoff; a process that stops at PDK 1.0 leaves the most critical period unmanaged.

Why it exists

Agree with the foundry exactly which corners and derates signoff will be run at—PVT combinations, modes, and the OCV, AOCV or POCV methodology—and write it down before anyone closes timing against it.

A corner set is a contract. Sign off at corners the foundry does not recognize and the foundry will not accept the result; sign off at more corners than necessary and every closure iteration costs runtime and license capacity the program has not budgeted for.

What it delivers

Needs first

  • Operating conditions and DVFS points from ARCH-05
  • Library characterization corners from PDK-03
  • IO and ESD conditions from PDK-07
  • Foundry signoff requirements and recommended derates
  • Runtime and license capacity constraints

5 Signoff condition documentation Signoff condition document 1.5w
6 Corner count against runtime and license costruns in parallel Corner count impact on runtime and licences 1w

Step 6 exists because corner count multiplies. Nine corners across three modes is twenty-seven signoff runs per iteration, and the compute plan in <code>PDK-12</code> is sized against whatever number this activity settles on.

Watch out for

  • Corner set agreed after closure starts. Adding a corner mid-closure invalidates the work done, and the addition usually comes from the foundry.
  • Derate methodology chosen for margin. OCV is conservative and expensive in area and power; POCV is tighter and demands better data. Choosing without the data is choosing margin blindly.
  • Corner count unbounded. Every corner is a full signoff run per iteration; a set nobody trimmed becomes a schedule problem at SO-02.
  • Modes forgotten. Corners multiply by modes, and a mode discovered late—a test mode, a low-power mode—multiplies the whole set.
  • Library corners narrower than the signoff set. Signing off at a corner the library was never characterized at is signing off against extrapolation.

Why it exists

Model what the program will actually need in compute, EDA licences and storage across its peak, and procure it against a lead time rather than discovering it during timing closure.

The demand model is built per flow step rather than per team because that is how contention actually happens: three teams running the same tool at the same point in the schedule contend for one license pool, whatever the org chart says.

Watch out for

  • Demand modelled per team rather than per flow step. Contention happens when several teams hit the same tool at the same time, which an org-chart model cannot see.
  • Peak sized to the average. Signoff and closure peaks are several times the steady state, and a farm sized to the average flattens the burn-down exactly when it matters.
  • Licences procured without lead time. Additional seats are a commercial negotiation with a duration; needing them next week is needing them next quarter.
  • Storage forgotten. Multi-corner signoff databases are large, and a farm that runs out of storage stops as hard as one that runs out of cores.
  • Plan never reviewed against actual usage. A capacity plan is a forecast; without a comparison to actuals nobody learns that it was wrong until closure.

Watch out for

  • Released and then not maintained. Decks and PDK versions keep moving; an environment frozen at release drifts away from what signoff will require.

05 IPR · IP Strategy & Readiness

IPR-01Product requirement → IP requirement decomposition (IP bill of materials)

Takes5ww0–w5 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~4.3 people while it runs
OwnerIP strategistProgram manager approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Decompose the product into the IP it actually needs—every block, with its specification, its interfaces and the requirement it traces back to—and publish it as a bill of materials the program can be held to.

An IP-BOM derived from the last program's list is the most common way to arrive at the wrong one. What this product needs follows from its requirements and its architecture, and the blocks that differ from last time are exactly the ones with the longest lead times.

What it delivers

IPR-D1IP bill of materials with make / buy / reuse decision per block

The bill half of the deliverable; IPR-03 adds the decision against each line.

Needs first

  • Requirement register from DEF-01
  • Architecture sketch and block list direction from ARCH-02

Watch out for

  • Bill inherited from the previous program. The blocks that differ are the ones with the longest lead times, and inheriting the list hides exactly those.
  • Foundry IP omitted. Memory compilers, IO and standard cells are IP with licences and lead times, and a bill that lists only third-party blocks understates the procurement.
  • Specification stubs too thin to evaluate against. A vendor cannot be assessed against "a PCIe PHY"; the stub has to carry performance, interface and process detail.

Takes4ww1–w5 of the stage

Why it exists

Audit what the organization already owns and can actually reuse on this node—not what it owns in general, which is a different and much longer list.

Reuse is where the schedule is won, and it is also where optimism concentrates. A block proven on the previous node is not available on this one until it has been ported, re-characterized and re-verified, and that work is a project with a duration. The audit's job is to separate genuine reuse from hopeful reuse.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • IP bill of materials from IPR-01
  • Internal IP catalogue and repositories
  • Previous-program silicon results per block
  • Node and flavor selection from TECH
  • Team ownership records

Done when

  • Every internal block classified as direct reuse, port, or rebuild
  • Collateral gaps listed per block, not assumed away
  • Blocks with no maintainer flagged as such

Step 4 asks who still maintains each block, and the answer is often nobody. An unmaintained block is technically reusable and practically a rebuild, because the first bug found has no owner.

Watch out for

  • Reuse claimed on the previous node. Availability is node-specific; a block not yet ported is a porting project, not a reuse.
  • Collateral assumed complete. Missing multi-corner .lib files or an absent testbench turns reuse into re-characterization and re-verification.
  • Unmaintained blocks counted as reuse. A block with no owner has no one to fix its first bug, and the fix lands on the integration team.
  • Audit run on the catalogue rather than the repository. Catalogues describe intent; repositories contain what actually exists.
  • Silicon history ignored. A block that shipped with an erratum is reusable with that erratum, and the erratum belongs in the audit.

Why it exists

Take each line of the bill and decide, with a reason, whether it is made, bought or reused—and record what the rejected options would have cost.

Make/buy is a schedule decision more than a cost one. Building a PHY internally is cheaper on paper and costs nine months in AMS-03; buying it costs a license and a vendor dependency. Neither is wrong, and the program only gets to argue about it once.

Watch out for

  • Make decided on capability rather than capacity. The team can build it; whether it can build it alongside everything else it is already committed to is the real question.
  • Differentiating IP bought. Buying the block that is the product's actual advantage buys a product the competitor can buy too.
  • Commodity IP built. Building a standard interface consumes analog engineers who are the program's scarcest resource, for no differentiation.
  • Foundry-specific IP chosen without reference to sourcing strategy. It forecloses the migration option TECH-08 was pricing, and usually after that study concludes.
  • Decisions recorded without the alternatives. Every setback reopens a decision whose reasoning nobody can reconstruct.

Why it exists

Establish, for each bought and reused block, whether it has actually run in silicon on this node and this process option—and if not, what it would take to get it there.

"Silicon-proven" is the most abused phrase in IP procurement. It can mean proven on a different node, on a different process option, at a different speed grade, or in a test chip that was never characterized. This activity replaces the phrase with a fact, and the fact is what the integration schedule should be built on.

What it delivers

IPR-D3IP readiness report — silicon-proven status and maturity level per IP

This activity is the deliverable, and it is the one that replaces a claim with a fact.

Needs first

  • Vendor selections from IPR-04
  • Reuse classification from IPR-02
  • Node and process option from TECH-02
  • Vendor silicon evidence and characterization data
  • Errata from previous programs and vendor disclosures

Done when

  • Every block carries a maturity level backed by evidence, not by claim
  • Node and process option match verified per block
  • Findings available before licences are signed in IPR-07

Step 1 is not bureaucracy. Without an agreed evidence standard, every vendor's claim is accepted at its own definition, and the readiness report becomes a collection of adjectives.

Watch out for

  • Vendor claim accepted at the vendor's definition. Without an evidence standard, "silicon-proven" means whatever is most convenient.
  • Node matched, process option not. The same node with a different flavor sheet is a different library, different rules and often a different PHY.
  • Errata not requested. Every silicon-proven block has errata; a block presented with none has either not been characterized or is not being fully disclosed.
  • Assessment done after the license is signed. The finding has no commercial consequence once the PO is placed, and the leverage is gone.
  • Speed grade ignored. A PHY proven at a lower rate on the same node is an engineering project, not a proven block.

  • Checklist agreed after the PO. Once the commercial terms are closed, a missing view is a favor rather than an obligation.

  • Verification collateral omitted. A block delivered without its testbench has to be verified from scratch, and that effort was never in the DV plan.
  • No incoming inspection. Deliverables accepted without a check are found incomplete weeks later, when the vendor's engineer has moved on.
  • One checklist for all IP classes. A memory compiler, a PHY and a controller have genuinely different deliverable sets, and a single list serves none of them.

Watch out for

  • Hardening treated as vendor overhead. It is a project with a duration; leaving it off the plan means the block arrives on a date nobody derived.
  • Internal execution assumed available. The engineers who would port a PHY are the engineers building the PLL and the custom array, and they cannot do all three.
  • Re-verification omitted from scope. Porting changes the block; the verification collateral has to be re-run, and that effort belongs in the DV plan.
  • Characterization corners not matched to the program's. A block re-characterized at the vendor's corners still cannot be signed off at the program's.
  • Plan without dates. A hardening plan with owners and no dates does not integrate with the program schedule and is therefore not tracked.

  • Second source assessed on capability alone. An alternative vendor without a license, an evaluation and a delivery date is not a contingency.
  • Internal fallback assumed. A fallback that depends on engineers already committed to the critical path is not a fallback.
  • Register written and not reviewed. IP risk changes as deliveries land; a register reviewed once at IP Plan Freeze is stale by RTL integration.

AMS-01AMS IP specification and budget allocation (jitter, BER, PSRR, area)

Why it exists

Turn each custom block from a name on the make list into a specification with budgets—jitter, BER, PSRR, area, power—that a circuit designer can start against and a reviewer can hold them to.

Analog specifications are budgets before they are targets. Total jitter is divided between the PLL, the distribution network and the PHY; each owner gets a share, and a share nobody allocated becomes an argument at integration when the eye closes and no one can say whose fault it is.

What it delivers

AMS-D1AMS IP specifications and design review packages

This activity is the deliverable—the specifications every other AMS activity is executed and reviewed against.

  • Custom memory scope from PDK-06
  • Interface specifications from ARCH-04
  • Power and clock architecture from ARCH-05
  • Block PPA budgets from ARCH-06

Done when

  • Every system budget decomposed into per-block allocations
  • Each specification accepted by its named owner
  • Area and power allocations reconciled against ARCH-06

Step 2 is the one that prevents the integration argument. A jitter budget divided explicitly between PLL, distribution and PHY gives each owner a number; an unallocated total gives each owner a reason to believe the problem is somewhere else.

Watch out for

  • Budgets stated as totals rather than allocations. An unallocated jitter budget produces three designers each assuming the others left them room.
  • Specifications written without the PHY vendor. Where a PHY is bought, its jitter tolerance bounds what the PLL must deliver, and the two have to be written together.
  • Area allocated before the architecture is understood. Analog area is set by matching, isolation and routing, and an allocation made from a digital estimate is not usable.
  • PSRR requirements omitted. Supply sensitivity is what turns a working block into a failing one once the digital neighbors switch, and it is rarely specified up front.
  • No owner acceptance. A specification the designer has not accepted is one they will design around rather than to.

AMS-02PLL / clock generator design and closure

Takes26ww4–w30 of the stage

Why it exists

Design the clock generation the whole chip runs on—PLLs, their loop dynamics, their supply immunity and their jitter—and close them across process, voltage and temperature.

A PLL is small, slow to build and impossible to work around. Twenty-six weeks for a block of a few hundred microns square looks disproportionate until the first silicon that will not lock over temperature, at which point the entire program is waiting on a circuit nobody can patch.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Node device models and PDK from PDK-01
  • Supply and rail topology from ARCH-05

Done when

  • Jitter closed post-layout across PVT, not pre-layout
  • Lock time and startup sequence characterized and documented
  • Macro released with views and a behavioural model

Step 8 is where the schedule risk lives. Post-layout jitter is routinely worse than pre-layout by more than the margin, and the fix is a layout change that takes the six weeks of step 7 again.

Watch out for

  • Post-layout jitter worse than budget. The commonest analog schedule failure, and the fix is a layout iteration measured in weeks, not days.
  • PSRR ignored until integration. A PLL that meets jitter on a clean supply and fails beside switching digital logic has met a specification nobody can use.
  • Tuning range too narrow across corners. A VCO that cannot cover the DVFS range at the slow corner is a DVFS policy that has to be reduced in silicon.
  • Lock time and startup unspecified. Boot sequencing depends on lock time, and discovering it at bring-up delays every subsequent test.
  • One PLL designed for several very different uses. Sharing one design across HBM, SerDes and core clocking usually means it is optimal for none.

Watch out for

  • Bought PHY assumed to need no work. Hardening, integration and margin closure on this flavor sheet is a multi-quarter project regardless of who designed the circuit.
  • Lane pitch incompatible with the bump map. Discovered at layout, it forces a change at the die edge where there is least room to make one.
  • Compliance simulated late. A PHY that closes its own eye and fails the interface specification's compliance mask has to be reworked with no schedule left.
  • Channel budget not shared with SI. The PHY closes against an assumed channel; if SIPI-07 extracts a worse one, the margin was never real.
  • Vendor support model untested until integration. The first hard question is when a support relationship is discovered to be a ticketing system.

AMS-04LDO, bandgap and power-management cell design

Takes20ww6–w26 of the stage
Costs22.0 M/M~4.8 people while it runs

Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Build the power management cells everything else depends on—LDOs, bandgap references, bias generation—quietly and correctly, because every other block's specification assumes them.

These blocks are small, unglamorous and load-bearing. A bandgap that drifts moves every analog threshold on the die; an LDO with insufficient PSRR at the switching frequency turns the PLL's careful jitter budget into noise. They are specified against by everyone and reviewed by almost nobody.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Supply and rail topology from ARCH-05
  • PSRR requirements from AMS-01
  • Load profiles from the digital power estimate
  • Node device models and precision element availability
  • Test and trim capability from TEST-01

Done when

  • PSRR verified at the digital switching frequency, not only at DC
  • Stability held across the full load range post-layout
  • Trim procedure agreed with test engineering

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Supply topology and regulation requirement per domain Supply topology and regulation plan 1.5w

5 Startup, sequencing and brown-out behaviorruns in parallel Startup, sequencing and brown-out behavior definition 2.5w

7 Post-layout stability and PSRR verification across PVT Post-layout stability and PSRR results across PVT 4w

Step 8 is easy to leave until later and expensive to. A trim procedure that test engineering only sees at <code>TEST-05</code> becomes a test-time cost, and a bandgap with no defined trim is a part with a distribution nobody can tighten.

Watch out for

  • PSRR specified at DC. The frequency that matters is where the digital load switches, and a regulator flat at DC can be transparent at that frequency.
  • Stability verified only at nominal load. LDO compensation has to hold across the full load range including the transitions, which is where it usually does not.
  • Bandgap trim undefined. An untrimmed reference has a distribution wide enough to move every analog threshold, and there is no way to tighten it in production.
  • Brown-out and startup behavior unspecified. The part's behavior at supply ramp is discovered at bring-up, on silicon that cannot be changed.
  • Reviewed by nobody. Blocks everyone assumes and nobody reviews are the ones that fail in a way that looks like someone else's problem.

Why it exists

Architect the custom SRAM instance the compiler could not deliver—bitcell choice, array organization, sense amplifier topology and replica timing—against the density and Vmin the block budget demands.

This activity exists only because PDK-06 opened it. That decision came with a quantified gap and a fixed window, and the architecture chosen here determines whether the rest of the custom memory chain can close inside it. A conservative architecture will not recover the density; an aggressive one may not close Vmin.

Step 7 closes the loop with <code>PDK-05</code>. If the projected density still misses the budget, the answer is to reopen the architecture now rather than to discover it after sixteen weeks of layout in <code>AMS-07</code>.

Watch out for

  • Architecture that does not recover the gap. A conservative organization produces a custom array with the compiler's density and none of the compiler's maintenance advantages.
  • Bitcell pushed beyond foundry appetite. A cell the foundry will not approve is a layout that cannot tape out, and the approval path runs through PDK-06.
  • Sense amplifier offset budget optimistic. Offset drives Vmin more than any other single choice, and an optimistic budget is discovered in AMS-08 when it is far too late to change topology.
  • Replica timing not proven across corners. Self-timed paths that track at nominal and diverge at the corner produce read failures that look random.
  • Architecture frozen without the density projection. Freezing before step 7 means committing sixteen weeks of layout to an organization that may not close the gap.

06 AMS · Custom, AMS & Memory IP Development

AMS-06Read / write assist circuit design for Vmin — WL boost, negative bitline, VDD collapse

Takes10ww10–w20 of the stage
Costs12.0 M/M~5.2 people while it runs
OwnerMemory circuit designerMemory architect approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Design the assist circuits that buy Vmin—wordline boost, negative bitline, VDD collapse—and decide how much of each the array actually needs.

Assist is what makes an aggressive array workable, and it is not free: each technique costs area, power and complexity, and some of them interact badly. The design question is not which assist is best but which combination reaches the Vmin target at the least cost, verified statistically rather than at nominal.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Array architecture and Vmin budget from AMS-05
  • Vmin requirements from ARCH-05 operating points
  • Bitcell characterization data
  • Node assist circuit precedents from the foundry
  • Power budget for the array from ARCH-06

Done when

  • Vmin target met statistically, not at nominal
  • Assist interactions studied rather than assumed
  • Boost levels within the reliability limits AMS-14 will check

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w10w12w14w16w18w20

Main sequence

12567

In parallel

34
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Vmin gap analysis against the AMS-05 architecture Vmin gap analysis with assist requirement 1w
2 Assist technique selection and interaction study Assist technique selection and interaction findings 2w
3 Wordline boost circuit designruns in parallel Wordline boost circuit design 2w
4 Negative bitline circuit designruns in parallel Wordline boost, negative bitline and collapse circuits 2w
5 VDD collapse and read-assist timing VDD collapse and read-assist timing design 2w
6 Assist control, timing and calibration Assist control and calibration scheme 2w
7 Vmin verification with assist enabled, across corners Vmin verification results with assist enabled 3w

Steps 3 and 4 run in parallel and step 2 decides whether both are needed. Write assist and read assist pull in opposite directions on the cell, and enabling both without studying the interaction can leave Vmin worse than either alone.

Watch out for

  • Assist techniques combined without an interaction study. Read and write assist push the cell in opposite directions; enabling both blindly can make Vmin worse.
  • Assist verified at nominal. Vmin is a statistical quantity; verification at nominal proves nothing about the tail that decides yield.
  • Boost levels beyond reliability limits. Wordline boost stresses the cell, and a level chosen for Vmin alone shortens life in a way AMS-14 will find late.
  • Assist timing not calibrated. Fixed assist timing that works at one corner and misfires at another produces intermittent failures indistinguishable from a marginal cell.
  • Area cost of assist unbudgeted. Assist circuits sit in the periphery and can consume the density the custom array was built to recover.

Why it exists

Lay out the custom array at pushed rules, and get the foundry to approve it—because a layout the foundry will not sign is a layout that cannot tape out.

Sixteen weeks of layout is what the density recovery actually costs. Pushed rules are the mechanism, and they carry an approval process with its own duration and its own possibility of refusal. Running layout and approval in sequence would not fit the window, so they run together, which means designing against rules that are not yet certain.

This activity is the deliverable, and the approval is the half that cannot be produced internally.

Done when

Step 5 runs in parallel out of necessity rather than choice. Waiting for approval before laying out would not fit the window, so the array is laid out against rules that may still be refused—which is why step 1's pre-alignment matters more than its two weeks suggest.

Watch out for

  • Foundry refuses a pushed rule after layout is built on it. The mitigation is pre-alignment in step 1, and it is the single most valuable two weeks in the activity.
  • Density target missed despite the pushed rules. The array then costs sixteen weeks and delivers the compiler's density, which is the worst available outcome.
  • Approval iterations underestimated. Each foundry round trip runs to weeks, and the five-week allowance assumes no more than two.
  • Fill and density compliance left to the end. Fill interacts with the array's matching and can undo careful layout if applied late.
  • Layout frozen before extraction is proven. An array that extracts badly has to be re-laid out, and the extraction handoff is where that is found.

AMS-08Statistical margin and yield analysis — importance sampling, sigma-Vmin, bitcell variation

Takes10ww20–w30 of the stage
Costs12.0 M/M~5.2 people while it runs
OwnerStatistical analysis engineerAMS lead approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Prove the array works at the tail of the distribution rather than at nominal—sigma-Vmin, bitcell variation, sense amplifier offset—using importance sampling because brute-force Monte Carlo cannot reach six sigma.

A memory array of this size fails at the tail by definition: with hundreds of millions of cells, the six-sigma cell is not a hypothetical, it is present in every part. Nominal simulation says nothing about it, and the yield the cost model assumed depends entirely on where that tail sits.

What it delivers

AMS-D3Custom SRAM instance specification with Vmin and sigma-yield report

The yield half of the deliverable, and the half the cost model depends on.

Needs first

  • Array architecture from AMS-05
  • Assist circuits and Vmin results from AMS-06
  • Layout parasitics from AMS-07
  • Foundry variation models and silicon data
  • Redundancy scheme from AMS-09

Done when

  • Sigma targets met for read, write and retention
  • Variation model validated against silicon, not assumed
  • Yield projection handed to the cost model with its methodology

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w20w22w24w26w28w30

Main sequence

12367

In parallel

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Statistical methodology selection — importance sampling, scaled sigma Statistical methodology and its validation 1.5w
2 Bitcell variation model validation against silicon data Bitcell variation model validation record 2w
3 Sigma-Vmin analysis for read, write and retention Sigma-Vmin results for read, write and retention 3w
4 Sense amplifier offset distribution analysisruns in parallel Sense amplifier offset distribution analysis 2w
5 Peripheral and timing variation contributionruns in parallel Offset and peripheral variation contributions 1.5w
6 Array-level yield projection with redundancy applied Array yield projection with redundancy 2w
7 Statistical margin report and signoff Statistical margin report 1.5w

Step 2 is the step that makes the rest meaningful. A variation model that has not been validated against silicon produces a six-sigma number with an unknown error, and the number is then used to justify a yield assumption in the cost model.

Watch out for

  • Brute-force Monte Carlo used at the tail. Reaching six sigma by direct sampling is computationally impossible; a run that terminates has not reached the tail it claims.
  • Variation model unvalidated. The six-sigma answer inherits the model's error, and nobody knows its size.
  • Redundancy assumed to cover the tail. Repair fixes a bounded number of failing bits; a distribution problem produces more than the repair scheme can absorb.
  • Retention overlooked. Read and write Vmin get the attention; retention failures at low voltage and high temperature are found in qualification.
  • Result reported without the methodology. A sigma number quoted without stating how it was obtained cannot be compared or challenged.

AMS-09Redundancy and repair scheme integration with the BISR architecture

Takes6ww16–w22 of the stage
Costs6.0 M/M~4.3 people while it runs

Why it exists

Build redundancy and repair into the array and make it match the BISR architecture DFT is designing—spare rows and columns, fuse allocation, repair algorithm, and the interface between them.

Redundancy is worth several points of yield and only if the two halves agree. The array provides spares and a repair interface; DFT-03 provides the BIST engine and the repair analysis. A mismatch between them is found at pattern generation, when both are effectively frozen.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • BISR architecture intent from DFT-03

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w16w18w20w22

Main sequence

1236

In parallel

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Redundancy scheme selection — row, column, or both Redundancy scheme selection record 1w
2 Spare allocation against the projected defect distribution Redundancy scheme with spare allocation 1.5w
3 Repair interface definition with the BISR architecture Repair interface definition 1.25w
4 Fuse and repair storage allocationruns in parallel Fuse and repair storage allocation 1w
5 Repair algorithm agreement with DFTruns in parallel Repair interface specification, agreed with DFT · Repair algorithm agreement 1w
6 Redundancy verification and yield contribution analysis Redundancy yield contribution analysis 2.25w

Steps 3 and 5 are joint work with <code>DFT-03</code> rather than handoffs. Both sides can specify a repair scheme that is internally consistent and mutually incompatible, and only writing them together prevents it.

Watch out for

  • Repair interface specified independently by both sides. Two consistent specifications that disagree with each other, discovered at ATPG when both are frozen.
  • Spare allocation not matched to the defect distribution. Row spares against a column-clustered defect mode repair nothing.
  • Fuse capacity insufficient. Repair data has to be stored; an allocation made without counting the worst-case repair set produces parts that cannot be repaired.
  • Redundancy credited twice. Yield projections that apply repair in both the array analysis and the product model double-count the benefit.
  • Repair algorithm assumed rather than agreed. The BIST engine implements one algorithm; the array assumes another, and the mismatch is silent until silicon.

  • Abstract blockages wrong. Over-blocking wastes routing resource; under-blocking produces shorts found at SO-02.
  • Views released before the layout freezes. Characterizing against a layout that then changes means doing the whole activity twice.

Takes16ww6–w22 of the stage

Why it exists

Run the schematic-level design and pre-layout simulation that every analog block passes through—the common engineering discipline underneath the PLL, the PHY, the regulators and the array periphery.

This is the shared substrate rather than a block: topology exploration, device sizing, pre-layout corner simulation and the design reviews that gate a block into layout. Separating it makes the schedule honest—a block that has not passed pre-layout review is not ready for the sixteen weeks of layout that follow.

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 7 is a gate rather than a meeting. Layout is the longest and least reversible part of an analog block, and letting a schematic that has not closed at the corners enter layout guarantees that the corner failure is found after the layout is built.

Watch out for

  • Blocks entering layout without passing the gate. Sixteen weeks of layout on a schematic that fails at the corner is the most expensive way to discover a topology problem.
  • Corner simulation run at typical mismatch. Mismatch dominates analog corner behavior, and a corner run without it is a nominal run in disguise.
  • Testbenches written per block by different people. Inconsistent testbenches make results incomparable across blocks and unusable as a regression.
  • Device models used from an unfrozen PDK. Analog is far more model-sensitive than digital, and a model update mid-design can invalidate the sizing.
  • No regression suite. Every subsequent change is then verified by hand, and the coverage of that verification degrades under schedule pressure.

Step 5 is where careful layout is most often undone. Fill applied without regard to matching structures changes the parasitics the whole design was tuned against, and the effect is only seen in post-layout simulation.

Watch out for

  • Fill applied late and without care. It disturbs the parasitics the design was tuned against, and the damage appears only in post-layout results.
  • Matching implemented by intent rather than by construction. Common-centroid and dummy structures are a layout discipline; describing them in a review is not implementing them.
  • EM checked only at signoff. Analog supply routing carries high current density in small geometries, and an EM failure found at SO-03 is a layout rebuild.
  • Pin placement not agreed with physical design. A macro whose pins face the wrong way costs routing resource at the top level for the life of the design.
  • Layout frozen without an extraction check. A macro that extracts slowly or badly stalls every post-layout simulation that follows.

Why it exists

Simulate every block with its layout parasitics extracted, across process, voltage and temperature and across the Monte Carlo distribution—and close whatever the layout took away.

Post-layout is where analog designs are actually judged. Parasitics reduce bandwidth, add mismatch, degrade PSRR and move every margin in the wrong direction. The gap between pre- and post-layout is the real measure of layout quality, and closing it is what the sixteen weeks are for.

Step 6 is planned iteration rather than contingency. Analog blocks essentially always need at least one layout turn after post-layout simulation, and a schedule with no allowance for it is a schedule that will slip on the first block.

Watch out for

  • No layout iteration in the plan. At least one turn per block is normal; a schedule with none slips on the first block and never recovers.
  • Corner closure on a subset of blocks. The block skipped for time is the one that fails in silicon, and it is usually skipped because it looked simple.
  • Parasitic model too coarse. A model that misses coupling produces post-layout results that are optimistic in exactly the cases that matter.
  • Degradation not analyzed. Knowing a block passed post-layout is less useful than knowing how much margin the layout consumed, which is what predicts the next block.
  • Monte Carlo run at reduced sample count. Cutting samples to save runtime narrows the distribution and flatters the tail.

Step 4 is the one that needs the product's actual mission profile. Aging simulated at nominal conditions for a nominal lifetime says nothing about a part that runs at the top of its DVFS range continuously, which is exactly how an accelerator is used.

Watch out for

  • Aging simulated at nominal conditions. An accelerator runs near its limit continuously; a nominal mission profile understates the stress by a wide margin.
  • EM checked on supplies only. High-speed signal routing in a PHY carries current densities that matter, and signal EM is routinely omitted.
  • ESD path assumed from the strategy. The strategy defines the intent; only tracing the path through the actual layout confirms it exists.
  • Assist boost stress not fed back. The boost levels AMS-06 chose for Vmin have an aging cost, and the two activities have to reconcile.
  • Waivers granted without a lifetime calculation. A reliability waiver without a quantified life impact is a decision nobody can defend at qualification.

Watch out for

  • Behavioural models never correlated. Digital verification then passes against a model that does not match the circuit, and the mismatch reaches silicon undetected.

  • Support engineer unassigned. Integration questions arrive for months; without a named engineer they are answered by guesswork or not at all.
  • Errata captured in email. A limitation known to one integrator and nobody else is rediscovered by every other integrator in turn.
  • Calibration sequence not co-simulated. A calibration that works in the circuit and is never exercised from the digital side is first tried at bring-up.

TC-01Test chip objective definition and risk-item selection

Takes5ww0–w5 of the stage
Costs4.0 M/M~3.5 people while it runs
OwnerTest chip leadDevice and technology engineer approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Decide what the test chip is for—which specific risks it retires—and select the structures that will actually answer those questions rather than the ones that are easy to include.

A test chip with no objective becomes a collection of everything anyone wanted to try, and it answers nothing in time to matter. The discipline is subtractive: name the two or three uncertainties that would change a production decision, and carry only what measures them.

What it delivers

TC-D1Test chip specification and risk coverage matrix

This activity is the deliverable, and the matrix is what every later result is reported against.

Needs first

  • Node risk assessment from TECH-07
  • IP readiness gaps from IPR-05
  • Custom memory decision from PDK-06
  • AMS block risk list from AMS-01
  • Production design schedule from DEF-08

Done when

  • Every carried structure traces to a named risk and a decision rule
  • Schedule feasibility confirmed against the decision dates
  • Area and cost budget fixed before structures are finalized

Step 3 can cancel the activity, and should be allowed to. A test chip whose results land after the production design has committed is an expense with no decision attached, and finding that out in week three is far better than in week forty.

Watch out for

  • Scope grows until the shuttle is missed. Every team has something worth measuring, and a chip that carries all of them misses the slot that made it useful.
  • Results arrive after the decision. A test chip is only worth its cost if the answer lands while the production design can still act on it.
  • Structures chosen for measurability rather than for risk. Ring oscillators are easy and tell you about the node; the risk is usually in a specific circuit nobody has built before.
  • No decision rule attached to a result. Measuring something without agreeing in advance what each outcome would change produces data and no decisions.
  • Area budget set after structure selection. Shuttle die area is expensive and fixed; selecting first and budgeting second guarantees a painful subtraction later.

Why it exists

Design and integrate the vehicle itself—the IP under test, its access wrappers, the process monitors and the measurement structures—as a small chip that has to work first time.

A test chip gets one shuttle. There is no bring-up iteration and no respin, so the access paths, the monitors and the pad ring have to be right on submission. That makes it a small design with an unusually high verification burden relative to its size.

  • Every structure reachable through a verified access path

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 IP-under-test integration plan IP-under-test integration plan 1w

Step 8 gets two and a half weeks for a chip that is mostly structures, because an access path that does not work makes the structure behind it unmeasurable. Every mode has to be exercised in simulation, since there is no second chance in silicon.

Watch out for

  • Access paths unverified. A structure that cannot be reached is a structure that was not measured, and the failure is only discovered in the lab.
  • Pad count exceeded. Shuttle die have few pads; a measurement scheme needing more forces multiplexing that has to be designed and verified.
  • IP under test modified for the vehicle. A block wrapped or altered to fit the test chip is no longer the block the production design will use.
  • Monitors placed without regard to position. Process variation across the die is part of what is being measured, and monitors clustered in one corner cannot see it.
  • No redundancy in critical structures. A single instance of the structure that matters most means one defect loses the answer entirely.

TC-03MPW shuttle slot booking and data submission scheduling

Why it exists

Book the shuttle slot and work backwards from its submission date—because the shuttle calendar is fixed, and missing a slot costs a quarter rather than a week.

One man-month across four weeks: almost all of this is scheduling and paperwork. Its importance is out of proportion to its effort, because the submission date it fixes is what every other test chip activity is planned against.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Step 5 is the useful output. A shuttle slot is a date on which a compliant database must exist; scheduling backwards from it is what tells <code>TC-04</code> when physical verification actually has to finish.

Watch out for

  • Slot booked without checking the production decision date. An available slot that returns silicon too late buys nothing.
  • Submission requirements collected late. Shuttle submissions have their own format and layer rules, and discovering them near the date forces rushed rework.
  • Backward schedule not enforced. A submission date that is not translated into a physical verification deadline gets missed by exactly the amount by which signoff runs long.
  • No contingency slot identified. A missed shuttle costs a quarter, and knowing the next available date in advance changes how the schedule is managed.
  • Cost approved after booking. Shuttle die area is charged by area and layer count; booking before the budget is agreed produces an invoice nobody planned.

Why it exists

Implement the test chip physically and sign it off to shuttle submission standard—the same DRC, LVS and antenna closure a production die needs, on a fraction of the schedule.

The vehicle is small and the standard is not reduced. A shuttle rejects a non-compliant database, and the rejection costs the slot. What compresses the schedule is that timing closure is easy here; what does not compress is physical verification, which has to be as clean as production.

Step 3 exists because a test chip measures small signals. A power delivery network adequate for function but noisy in the measurement bands turns a characterization result into an argument about the vehicle rather than the device.

Watch out for

  • Submission rejected on frame or format compliance. Shuttle frames have their own rules, and a rejection costs the slot rather than a re-run.
  • PDN adequate for function and inadequate for measurement. The results then carry vehicle noise that cannot be separated from device behavior.
  • Physical verification compressed because the chip is small. Size does not reduce the standard, and a DRC violation is as fatal here as on a production die.
  • Structures placed without regard to the measurement plan. Placement affects what across-die variation can be seen, and it is decided here rather than in the lab.
  • No margin against the submission date. Everything before this activity can slip and this one cannot, so its schedule needs the buffer.

Watch out for

  • Board started when parts ship. The lab then waits, and the schedule advantage the test chip existed to buy is spent waiting for a PCB.

  • Instruments not reserved. A shared high-end instrument booked by another program stops characterization as effectively as a missing board.

Why it exists

Measure the silicon and correlate it against the models the production design is being built on—which is the only reason the chip exists.

Characterization without correlation produces a data set. Correlation produces a statement of the form "the model is optimistic by 8% on this parameter at this corner", and that statement is what TC-08 converts into margin decisions the production design can act on.

  • Measurement uncertainty stated alongside each correlation claim

This window overlaps the tail of fabrication because the stage as templated does not allow a clean sequence—PCM and e-test data are worked first, and device characterization follows once packaged parts arrive. It is worth noting that the stage's forty weeks are tight for its own chain.

Watch out for

  • Characterization without correlation. A data set with no comparison to prediction cannot change a design decision, and changing decisions was the point.
  • Sample size too small for variability. Across-wafer and lot-to-lot variation is often the question, and a handful of parts cannot answer it.
  • Measurement uncertainty larger than the effect. A correlation claim that sits inside the measurement error is not a finding.
  • Outliers discarded. The parts that behave unexpectedly are usually the informative ones, and discarding them removes the tail the yield model depends on.
  • Results delivered too late for TC-08. Correlation completed after the production design has committed is a report nobody can act on.

Why it exists

Convert correlation findings into changes the production design actually makes—corrected models, revised margins, methodology updates—and track that they were adopted.

This is where a test chip earns or wastes its cost. A correlation report that circulates and changes nothing has bought an expensive confirmation of what everyone assumed. The output has to be specific: this model corrected by this factor, this margin increased by this amount, owned by this person, adopted by this date.

What it delivers

TC-D5Design guidance and margin decisions for the production chip

This activity is the deliverable, and adoption tracking is what makes it more than a report.

Needs first

  • Correlation results from TC-07
  • Production design status and open margins
  • Model and library data from PDK-03
  • AMS post-layout results from AMS-13
  • Production design change control process from RTL-10

Done when

  • Every finding converted into a specific, owned action
  • Margin released where silicon beat the model, not only tightened where it did not
  • Adoption tracked to completion, not just published

Step 6 is the one that distinguishes a useful test chip from an expensive one. Publishing guidance is easy; tracking that physical design actually changed its margin and that the model was actually re-characterized is what turns the finding into a change.

Watch out for

  • Guidance published and not adopted. The most common way a test chip wastes its cost: everyone reads the report and nobody changes a margin.
  • Findings arrive after the design has committed. A margin decision for a block that has already closed is a decision that cannot be taken.
  • Model corrections requested but not scheduled. Re-characterization is work; a correction with no owner and no date does not happen.
  • Only bad news acted on. Where silicon is better than the model, the margin released is real and usually left on the table.
  • Guidance stated as observation. "Leakage is higher than modelled" is not actionable; "increase the leakage budget for the compute cluster by 12%" is.

Why it exists

Complete the microarchitecture specification for every block—pipeline, interfaces, control, register map—to the level of detail an implementer can write code against without inventing anything.

ARCH-10 started these inside architecture; this finishes them. The distinction matters: a block whose specification is still being written while its RTL is being written produces code that documents itself, and the specification then follows the code instead of leading it.

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Step 5 is the section most often left thin and the one verification spends the most time on. Corner-case behavior that the specification does not define is behavior the implementer chooses and the verification engineer has no basis to check.

Watch out for

  • Specification written alongside the code. The document then records what was built rather than defining it, and verification loses its independent reference.
  • Corner cases left undefined. The implementer decides, verification cannot check, and the disagreement surfaces at chip-level integration.
  • Interfaces specified from one side. Two blocks each documenting their own view of a shared protocol produces two consistent documents that disagree.
  • Entry gate skipped for schedule. Coding against an incomplete specification is faster for two weeks and slower for two months.
  • Observability requirements added later. Debug and coverage hooks designed in cost little; retrofitted they cost timing and an RTL change under control.

Watch out for

  • Specification churn arriving mid-implementation. Every upstream change lands here multiplied by the blocks affected, which is why RTL-10 exists.
  • Coding standard imposed after code exists. Retrofitting a standard across 180 man-months of code is a project nobody schedules and everyone half-does.
  • Assertions treated as verification's job. Assertions written by the implementer capture intent; written by someone else they capture observed behavior.
  • Blocks declared complete without verification feedback. First-pass code is not correct code, and a block frozen before its verification loop closes freezes its bugs.
  • Configurability added everywhere. Parameterization nobody uses multiplies the verification space at no benefit, and the cost lands on DV-03.

Watch out for

  • Deliveries accepted without inspection. Missing views and collateral then become the integration team's problem rather than the vendor's.
  • Boundary behavior assumed from documentation. Reset ordering, enable timing and calibration sequences are where IP integration actually fails.
  • Version manifest not maintained. An IP bug that cannot be traced to a version cannot be reported usefully or fixed reproducibly.
  • IP updates absorbed silently. A vendor drop applied without impact assessment can change behavior verification has already signed off.
  • Late IP compressing integration. The integration window is fixed at its far end by RTL-04; a late delivery does not move it, it shortens it.

Step 7—the first chip-level boot in simulation—is the moment the design becomes real. It is also slow, because the first boot exercises paths that no block test touched, and each failure takes a full-chip simulation to reproduce.

Watch out for

  • Connectivity checked by inspection. A chip this size has too many connections to review; automated connectivity checking is the only reliable method.
  • Integration started before blocks are stable. Integrating moving blocks produces defects that are re-found every time a block updates.
  • Address map assembled from block documentation. Generated maps agree with the code; hand-assembled maps agree with the documentation, which is a different thing.
  • First boot deferred. The boot path exercises reset, clocking, configuration and the fabric together, and delaying it delays every defect that only appears in combination.
  • Clock and reset distribution treated as a wiring task. It carries the crossing inventory from ARCH-05 and the CDC obligations that follow from it.

Why it exists

Implement the clock, reset and power intent the architecture defined—domain boundaries, isolation, retention, crossing synchronisers—and produce a UPF file the tools accept.

Power intent is where architecture becomes an obligation on every downstream tool. Synthesis inserts isolation cells from it, verification checks against it, and physical design implements it. An intent file that is wrong or incomplete propagates the same error into all three.

Step 5 includes a tool acceptance check because UPF that reads correctly to a human and fails to elaborate in synthesis is common. The file has to be exercised in the actual flow, not reviewed as a document.

Watch out for

  • UPF written as a document. Intent that has never been elaborated in synthesis is intent whose errors are found by the first person who runs the flow.
  • Crossings implemented without reference to the inventory. A synchroniser strategy chosen per crossing by each designer produces inconsistency CDC will flag hundreds of times.
  • Retention strategy decided late. Retention cells cost area and change the physical implementation; adding them after floorplan is expensive.
  • Reset sequencing implemented from the block view. Reset order is a chip-level property, and blocks each releasing in their own order produces a boot that works in simulation and not in silicon.
  • Intent reviewed only by its author. Synthesis, verification and physical design each consume it differently, and each has to confirm it works for them.

Step 4 is chip-level rather than block-level because most real crossings are between blocks. Block-level CDC finds the easy ones; the crossing that fails in silicon is usually one neither block owner considered theirs.

Watch out for

  • Waivers accumulated rather than reviewed. A waiver list nobody re-reads is where the surviving crossings hide, and they are the hardest silicon bugs to diagnose.
  • CDC run only at block level. The crossings that matter are usually between blocks, and neither owner runs the check that would find them.
  • Closure not regressed. Clean at one release and dirty at the next, with nobody noticing until the freeze package is assembled.
  • Rule set weakened to reduce noise. Turning off the rule that produces the most violations is the fastest way to a clean report and the slowest way to a working chip.
  • Crossing inventory not reconciled. Crossings found by the tool but absent from ARCH-05's inventory mean the architecture and the implementation disagree.

Why it exists

Define the register map—the software contract—and generate the RTL, headers and documentation from one source so they cannot disagree.

The register map is where hardware and firmware meet, and it is the interface most often maintained in three places. Generating the RTL, the C headers and the documentation from a single description is what makes them consistent; hand-maintaining them is what produces a driver that writes to the wrong offset.

What it delivers

RTL-D2Register map / RDL and generated headers

This activity is the deliverable, generated from one source rather than maintained in several.

  • Address map intent from ARCH-09

  • Verification model requirements from DV-01

  • RTL, headers and documentation generated from one source

  • Side effects and reset values specified for every register

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Register description language and tooling selection Register description source 1w
2 Address map allocation across blocks Address map allocation 1.5w

6 Software review of the mapruns in parallel Software review record 1.5w
7 Map release and change control Released register map with change control 3w

Step 6 is a review by the people who will use the map rather than the people who wrote it. A register set that is natural to the hardware and awkward to drive is a set the driver will work around, and the workaround becomes the real interface.

Watch out for

  • Map maintained in more than one place. RTL, headers and documentation drift apart, and the driver eventually writes to an offset that moved.
  • Software reviews the map after freeze. An awkward interface then gets worked around in the driver, and the workaround becomes the contract nobody documented.
  • Side effects undocumented. A read that clears a status bit is a behavior firmware has to know about, and discovering it in the lab costs days per instance.
  • Security access rules omitted. Registers that should be locked in production lifecycle states are locked late or not at all.
  • Reset values unspecified. Registers whose reset value is whatever the implementer chose produce a boot sequence that depends on undocumented behavior.

Step 7 is the activity's real shape—a weekly cadence rather than a one-off study. A single trial synthesis is a snapshot; a weekly one is a feedback loop, and only the loop changes how blocks are written.

Watch out for

  • Trial synthesis run once. A snapshot tells a block owner where they were; only a cadence tells them whether they are improving.
  • Feedback delivered without constraints. Timing results against bootstrap constraints that do not resemble the real ones send block owners chasing paths that do not matter.
  • Area overrun tolerated because it is early. Blocks rarely shrink after implementation, and an overrun accepted at trial synthesis is an overrun accepted permanently.
  • Congestion ignored. Routability problems are cheaper to fix in RTL structure than in placement, and the early indication is the only chance to do so.
  • Results not tied to the budget. QoR reported in absolute terms rather than against ARCH-06 tells nobody whether the block is acceptable.

Twenty-two of the thirty weeks are step 7, which is maintenance rather than construction. A CI system that is not maintained degrades into one everyone ignores, and an ignored red build is worse than no build at all.

Watch out for

  • Red builds tolerated. Once a broken build is normal, the signal is gone and every subsequent break is invisible.
  • Regression runtime exceeding the night. A nightly that takes thirty hours is not nightly, and the feedback loop silently doubles.
  • Releases produced by hand. An untagged release cannot be reproduced, and an IP bug found against it cannot be reported precisely.
  • Capacity not managed. Regressions competing with verification for the same licences slow both, usually at the point in the schedule where both matter most.
  • Triage unowned. Failures nobody is assigned to investigate accumulate until the regression result is meaningless.

RTL-10Specification change control and ECO board

Why it exists

Control what changes and when—specification change requests, ECO board decisions and the freeze itself—so the design converges rather than oscillates.

Every stage downstream assumes RTL stops moving at some point. Change control is how that point is created: not by refusing changes, but by making each one visible, costed and decided by people who can see what it affects. The freeze is this activity's output, and its credibility is the whole program's.

What it delivers

RTL-D7RTL Freeze package

This activity is the deliverable—the freeze, its criteria, its exceptions and the change history behind it.

  • Lint and CDC closure status from RTL-06
  • Freeze criteria from the program plan

Done when

  • Freeze declared against criteria, not against a date
  • Every change carries an impact assessment before approval
  • Post-freeze exception policy published and used

Step 3 runs for twenty weeks and is a standing meeting rather than a task. Its discipline is impact assessment: a change that looks like an afternoon in one block can invalidate a month of verification, and the board exists so that cost is visible before the change is approved.

Watch out for

  • Freeze declared by date rather than by criteria. A gate that passes because it was scheduled teaches everyone that gates mean nothing.
  • Impact assessment skipped for small changes. The cost of a change is rarely in the block that changes; it is in the verification that has to be re-run.
  • Post-freeze exceptions ungoverned. Changes will be needed after freeze; without a policy they happen informally and nobody knows what the design contains.
  • Board without downstream representation. Verification and synthesis are the ones who pay for most changes, and a board without them approves costs it cannot see.
  • Change log not reconciled with the release. A freeze package that does not match what was actually built is a package nobody can rely on.

09 DV · Verification

DV-01Verification plan and coverage model definition

Takes8ww0–w8 of the stage
Costs25.0 M/M~13.6 people while it runs
OwnerVerification leadProgram manager approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Write the plan that says what will be verified, how, and how anyone will know it is done—feature by feature, with a coverage model behind each claim.

Verification is the largest line of effort in the program, and without a plan it is 650 man-months of activity with no definition of completion. The coverage model is what turns "we tested it" into a measurable statement, and the features nobody writes into the plan are the features nobody verifies.

What it delivers

DV-D1Verification plan (vPlan) and coverage model

This activity is the deliverable, and the coverage model is what every later closure claim is measured against.

Needs first

  • Architecture specification from ARCH-09
  • Block specifications from RTL-01
  • Register map from RTL-07
  • IP verification collateral requirements from IPR-06
  • Compute capacity model from PDK-12

Done when

  • Every specified feature has a verification strategy and a coverage point
  • Closure criteria written and agreed before verification starts
  • Plan reviewed by architecture and design, not only by verification

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 6 is a review by the people who wrote the specification, and its purpose is to find features the plan missed. Verification reviewing its own plan confirms it is coherent; architecture reviewing it confirms it is complete, and incompleteness is the failure mode that matters.

Watch out for

  • Plan written from the RTL rather than the specification. It then verifies what was built rather than what was specified, and the two differ exactly where the bugs are.
  • Coverage model that measures activity rather than intent. Code coverage says lines were executed; functional coverage says features were exercised, and only the second answers the question.
  • Closure criteria left vague. "High coverage" is not a criterion anyone can sign, and it becomes whatever the schedule allows.
  • Architecture not in the review. The features the plan missed are exactly the ones only the specification's author would notice.
  • Resource model omitted. A plan that needs more compute or more engineers than exist is a plan whose closure date is fiction.

The environment is infrastructure with a long lead time and no visible output until it works. Step 4 is where verification quality is decided. A scoreboard that compares against a reference model finds bugs; one that only checks protocol legality confirms the design does something rather than the right thing.

Watch out for

  • Bring-up slower than planned and invisible. Environment work has no test-pass metric, so slippage is not visible until testing should have started.
  • Scoreboards that check protocol rather than function. A legal transaction carrying wrong data passes, and the bug survives to chip level.
  • No reuse strategy. Every block building its own environment multiplies effort and makes results incomparable across blocks.
  • Register model hand-written. A model that diverges from the RDL source produces tests that pass against the wrong offsets.
  • VIP licences short. Verification concurrency is capped by VIP seats, and the cap is discovered when regressions start queuing.

Watch out for

  • Constrained-random left unconstrained. Random stimulus without well-designed constraints spends compute exploring illegal or uninteresting space.
  • Corner cases skipped because the specification is silent. The gap belongs back in RTL-01, not quietly into the untested set.
  • Debug loop bottlenecked on block owners. Verification finds faster than design fixes, and the queue is where the schedule quietly goes.
  • Blocks signed off against different standards. Without enforced criteria from DV-01, each block closes to whatever its owner considered enough.

Why it exists

Verify the chip as one system running realistic scenarios—boot, configuration, traffic, power transitions, error recovery—rather than as a collection of verified blocks.

Blocks that each pass in isolation routinely fail together. Chip-level verification is where arbitration, ordering, deadlock, reset sequencing and end-to-end data integrity are actually tested, and none of those are visible from inside a block.

Step 7 uses the same workloads <code>DEF-02</code> assembled and <code>ARCH-01</code> modelled. Running them in simulation is slow and worth it: it is the only place the design, the model and the product's actual intent are compared against each other before silicon.

Watch out for

  • Started too late because blocks are not ready. Chip-level defects take longest to find and fix, and compressing the window pushes them into silicon.
  • Scenarios written by verification alone. Realistic use comes from the workload suite and from software; invented scenarios test what verification imagined.
  • Deadlock and arbitration untested. These fail only under contention, which random block-level stimulus does not create.
  • Power transitions verified functionally only. Retention, isolation and sequencing across a real power state change are where low-power designs actually fail.
  • Simulation too slow to run meaningful scenarios. If a boot takes a day, the scenario set shrinks to what fits, and emulation in DV-08 is the answer.

DV-05Formal property verification — control logic, connectivity, security

Takes16ww10–w26 of the stage
Costs40.0 M/M~10.9 people while it runs
OwnerFormal verification leadVerification lead approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Use formal proof where simulation is weak—connectivity, control logic, arbiters, security properties, register access—and prove exhaustively what testing can only sample.

Formal answers a different question. Simulation shows that the cases tried worked; a proof shows that no case exists that does not. For arbiters, protocol state machines and security isolation, the space is too large to sample and the failure modes are exactly the ones random stimulus misses.

What it delivers

DV-D4Formal proof reports with assumption list

This activity is the deliverable, and the assumption list is what makes the proofs auditable.

Needs first

  • Verification plan target selection from DV-01
  • Block RTL from RTL-02
  • Security architecture properties from ARCH-07
  • Interface protocol definitions from ARCH-04
  • Formal tool setup from PDK-08

Done when

  • Every proof reported with its assumptions and its bound
  • Assumptions reviewed for over-constraint, not just listed
  • Security properties proved rather than sampled

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

6 Assumption review and over-constraint checking Assumption review and over-constraint findings 2.5w

Step 6 is what separates a proof from a false claim. A property that passes because assumptions excluded the failing case has proved nothing, and reviewing assumptions is the only way to know which of the two happened.

Watch out for

  • Over-constrained proofs. Assumptions that exclude the failing case produce a green result and no information, and only assumption review catches it.
  • Formal applied where simulation is better. Datapath and workload behavior are poor formal targets; applying it there consumes specialist time for little return.
  • Bounded results reported as proofs. A property proved to depth twenty is not proved; the bound has to be stated with the result.
  • Properties written from the RTL. A property derived from the implementation proves the implementation matches itself.
  • Security properties omitted. Isolation and access control are exactly the properties simulation samples poorly and formal proves well.

Why it exists

Verify the design against its power intent—isolation, retention, level shifting, power sequencing—because none of it is visible in a normal functional simulation.

A design that passes every functional test can still corrupt state on a power-down, drive an isolated domain, or fail to retain what it needed. Low-power verification simulates the domains actually powering down, and it is the only place these failures appear before silicon.

What it delivers

DV-D5Low-power verification report

This activity is the deliverable, and it is the only evidence that the power architecture works as intended.

Needs first

  • UPF power intent from RTL-05
  • Power state definitions from ARCH-05
  • Verification environment from DV-02
  • Power management controller RTL from RTL-05
  • Low-power tool support from PDK-08

Done when

  • Domains simulated powering down, not only statically checked
  • Retention verified for both what is kept and what is not
  • Power-aware tests running in the regular regression

5 Power sequencing and controller verificationruns in parallel Power sequencing verification results 2w
6 Power-aware regression integrationruns in parallel Power-aware regression integration 1.5w

Step 4 is the one that finds real bugs. Retention verification requires actually powering a domain down in simulation and checking what survives; a design that has never been simulated through a power cycle has never been tested for the failure mode.

Watch out for

  • Only static checking performed. Structural UPF checks find missing cells; only simulation finds a design that corrupts state when the domain actually goes down.
  • Retention verified for the intended state only. What is not retained matters as much as what is, and a design that retains too little fails on resume.
  • Power sequences tested in isolation. The failure is usually a power transition during traffic, not a clean idle transition.
  • Power-aware simulation excluded from regression. It is slow, so it gets run once; a later RTL change then breaks it silently.
  • UPF used for verification differing from synthesis. Two versions of the intent means verifying one design and building another.

DV-07AMS / mixed-signal co-simulation

Takes12ww16–w28 of the stage
