Why it exists

Verify the boundary between the analog macros and the digital design—control interfaces, calibration sequences, startup ordering—with the analog represented by models correlated to its circuits.

Analog blocks fail where they meet digital. A PLL that locks perfectly and a controller that sequences perfectly can still disagree about when lock is valid. Co-simulation is where those disagreements appear, and the alternative is finding them at bring-up with an oscilloscope.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Behavioural models from AMS-15
  • Correlation results from AMS-16
  • Integrated AMS macros from RTL-03
  • Startup and sequencing requirements from ARCH-05
  • Verification environment from DV-02

Done when

  • Every model correlated against its circuit before being relied on
  • Calibration sequences exercised from the digital side
  • Degraded and fault behavior verified, not assumed

7 Co-simulation closure and findings report Co-simulation findings report 5.5w

Step 2 decides whether any of this is meaningful. Verification against a behavioural model that does not match the circuit proves the digital side works with a fiction, and the correlation in <code>AMS-16</code> is what makes the model a proxy rather than a guess.

Watch out for

  • Models never correlated. Digital passes against a fiction, and the mismatch reaches silicon as a bring-up failure nobody predicted.
  • Calibration sequences untested from the digital side. A calibration that works when the analog engineer drives it manually is first exercised by firmware at bring-up.
  • Ready and lock signaling assumed. When a lock signal becomes valid is a contract; each side assuming a different answer produces intermittent boot failures.
  • Degraded modes unverified. What the digital side does when a PLL fails to lock is behavior that only matters in the field, where it matters a great deal.
  • Co-simulation too slow to regress. Run once and never again, it cannot catch a later change on either side.

Why it exists

Stand up emulation and FPGA prototyping—partitioning, capacity, speed, debug—so that scenarios too long for simulation can actually be run.

A boot that takes a day in simulation takes minutes in emulation, and workload scenarios that are impossible in one are routine in the other. Emulation is also the platform firmware development runs on, which makes its availability date a dependency for a team outside this stage entirely.

Step 8 makes this activity a dependency for people outside verification. Firmware cannot start on real workloads until the platform runs, and the handover date belongs in the program schedule rather than in the verification plan alone.

Watch out for

  • Partitioning consuming more time than expected. Splitting a large design across emulator capacity is difficult and iterative, and it is routinely underestimated.
  • Capacity contended with another program. Emulator capacity is expensive and shared; a program without a booked allocation runs when the other one is not.
  • Debug visibility inadequate. A platform that runs fast and cannot be probed produces failures that cannot be diagnosed.
  • Handover date not in the program schedule. Firmware plans against it, and treating it as an internal verification milestone means nobody outside knows when it slips.
  • Models diverging from the design. Memory and interface models built for the platform can drift from the RTL, and results then reflect the model.

Watch out for

  • Performance treated as a bring-up activity. Discovered in silicon, a throughput shortfall has no remaining fix except software and marketing.
  • Measured only on synthetic traffic. Synthetic patterns exercise the interconnect; real workloads exercise the design, and only the second predicts the product.
  • Model and RTL disagreement left unresolved. Whichever is wrong, not knowing which means every downstream projection is unreliable.
  • Bottlenecks found without root cause. Knowing throughput is low is not actionable; knowing which queue saturates is.
  • No time left to act. Findings that arrive after RTL freeze can only be documented, not fixed.

Step 6 is unglamorous and load-bearing. A regression with intermittent failures trains everyone to ignore red results, and once that habit forms the regression has stopped being a signal.

Watch out for

  • Flaky regressions tolerated. Once red results are routinely ignored, the regression has stopped providing information and nobody notices when it matters.
  • Coverage merged without stability. Numbers from an unstable regression are noise presented as a trend.
  • Holes closed by waiving rather than testing. A hole waived without analysis is untested behavior recorded as covered.
  • Capacity insufficient at peak. Regression queues at the point of closure directly extend the closure date.
  • Closure signed with the curve still climbing. Coverage still rising at signoff means the plan's completion criteria were not what stopped the work.

Why it exists

Simulate the gate-level netlist, first functionally and then with real timing, to catch what RTL simulation structurally cannot—X-propagation, reset behavior, timing-dependent failures and synthesis or DFT-induced differences.

RTL simulation is optimistic about X and blind to timing. Gate-level simulation is slow, painful and the last check before the design becomes masks—it is also where scan insertion, clock gating and synthesis transformations are proved not to have changed behavior.

What it delivers

DV-D7Gate-level simulation report

This activity is the deliverable, and it is a tapeout checklist item rather than an optional confirmation.

Needs first

  • Gate-level netlist from SYN-01
  • SDF timing from PD-09
  • Scan-inserted netlist from DFT-06
  • Verification environment from DV-02
  • Power intent from RTL-05

Done when

  • X-propagation issues fixed rather than suppressed
  • Scan and test modes simulated, not only functional
  • Timing simulation run at the corners that matter

Step 3 finds the class of bug RTL simulation is structurally incapable of seeing. RTL X-optimism hides uninitialized state; at gate level the X propagates, and a design that boots in RTL can fail to come out of reset in gates.

Watch out for

  • Skipped because it is slow. The failures it finds—X propagation, reset, timing-dependent behavior—have no other pre-silicon detector.
  • Run only in functional mode. Scan and test modes are how the part is tested at ATE, and a scan mode that does not work makes the part untestable.
  • Started after netlist churn has settled. Waiting for a stable netlist means starting too late; running early on an imperfect netlist finds environment problems while there is time.
  • X failures suppressed rather than fixed. Forcing initial values to make the simulation run hides exactly the uninitialized state the check exists to find.
  • Timing simulation on a subset of corners. Timing-dependent failures appear at specific corners, and the corner skipped is the one that fails.

  • No escape analysis. The process that let a bug survive to week 34 will let the next one survive too.
  • Errata list assembled after tapeout. Bring-up needs the known-issue list on day one, and assembling it later means debugging problems that were already known.

10 DFT · DFT Architecture

DFT-01DFT architecture definition — scan style, compression ratio, hierarchical DFT

Takes8ww0–w8 of the stage
Costs12.0 M/M~6.5 people while it runs
OwnerDFT architectPhysical design liaison approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Decide how the chip will be tested before it is built to be testable—scan style, compression ratio, hierarchical partitioning, and the test modes the design will support.

Every one of these choices constrains the design rather than following it. Compression ratio decides pattern volume and therefore test cost; hierarchical DFT decides whether a block can be tested independently; and both have to be settled before SYN-01 writes constraints against them.

What it delivers

DFT-D1DFT architecture specification and coverage plan

This activity is the deliverable, and everything else in the stage is executed against it.

Needs first

  • Design hierarchy and partitioning from ARCH-02
  • Coverage and test-time targets from DFT-02
  • Memory list and BISR intent from ARCH-03
  • Test platform constraints from TEST-02
  • Debug access requirements from ARCH-07

Done when

  • Architecture fixed before synthesis writes constraints against it
  • Compression ratio chosen against a test cost model
  • Specification reviewed by test and product engineering

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w0w2w4w6w8

1236

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Test strategy definition — what is tested where and how Test strategy statement 1.5w

4 Hierarchical DFT partitioning against the design hierarchyruns in parallel Hierarchical DFT partitioning 1.5w
5 Test mode definition and mode controlruns in parallel Test mode definition 1.5w
6 Architecture specification and review DFT architecture specification 3w

Step 3 is a cost decision disguised as an architecture one. Compression ratio sets pattern volume, pattern volume sets tester memory and test time, and test time is a per-unit cost for the life of the product.

Watch out for

  • Architecture decided after synthesis starts. Scan insertion and constraints depend on it; deciding late means re-running both.
  • Compression ratio chosen without the test cost model. Ratio trades pattern volume against silicon area, and only TEST-09's cost model says which side to favor.
  • Hierarchical DFT ignored on a large die. Flat scan on a design this size produces pattern volumes and runtimes that become their own schedule problem.
  • Test modes defined without the security architecture. Every test mode is an access path, and ARCH-07 has to lock the ones that should not exist in production.
  • Architecture written and not reviewed by test engineering. A scheme that is elegant in design and unrunnable on the chosen ATE is discovered at TEST-08.

Coverage and test time pull against each other, and neither belongs to DFT alone. Step 3 has a large downstream cost. Cell-aware patterns catch defects the other models miss and multiply pattern count doing it, so the decision belongs here with the cost model in the room rather than at <code>DFT-07</code> when the patterns are being generated.

Watch out for

  • Coverage target set by convention. "99% stuck-at" carried from the last program may be far from what this product's DPPM requirement needs.
  • Test time budget not derived from cost. A test time nobody costed becomes whatever the patterns need, and the per-unit cost is discovered at production.
  • Fault model chosen at pattern generation. Adding cell-aware late multiplies pattern volume against a tester memory budget already fixed.
  • Targets agreed without product engineering. The organization that owns field quality has to own the coverage number, or it will be renegotiated when patterns run long.
  • No per-block differentiation. Memory-dominated blocks and control logic need different approaches, and a single flat target over-tests one and under-tests the other.

Step 6 is the joint decision with <code>AMS-09</code>. Both sides can specify an internally consistent repair scheme that the other cannot implement, and writing the interface together is the only reliable way to avoid it.

Watch out for

  • Repair interface specified separately from the array. Two consistent specifications that disagree, found at pattern generation when both are frozen.
  • Algorithms chosen without the failure modes. March algorithms differ in what they catch; a default choice misses the defect modes this array actually exhibits.
  • Fuse capacity insufficient. Repair data has to be stored, and an allocation made without counting the worst-case repair set produces unrepairable parts.
  • MBIST runtime unbudgeted. Memory test on an array-dominated die can dominate test time, and it is often costed after the architecture is fixed.
  • Repair not verified end to end. A repair path proven in pieces and never exercised from failure through analysis to fuse blow fails at production test.

DFT-04Boundary scan and IJTAG (1149.1 / 1687), TAP and debug access architecture

Takes8ww4–w12 of the stage

Why it exists

Design the access network—boundary scan, IJTAG, TAP controller and the debug paths—that every test, every repair and every silicon debug session runs through.

The TAP is the door into the chip. It is used at wafer sort, at package test, during bring-up and in the field, and it is also the door ARCH-07 needs to lock in production. Designing it is a negotiation between access and security rather than a purely technical exercise.

DFT-05On-chip clock controller design for at-speed testing

Takes7ww8–w15 of the stage

Why it exists

Design the on-chip clock controllers that generate at-speed test clocks—because transition-fault testing needs clock pulses the tester cannot supply at frequency.

Stuck-at testing runs slowly and catches static defects. The defects that matter for a high-frequency part are timing-related, and catching them needs launch-capture pulses at functional speed. The tester cannot produce them, so the chip has to produce them for itself.

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • DFT architecture from DFT-01

  • Transition fault coverage targets from DFT-02

Done when

  • At-speed clocking available on every domain that needs coverage
  • Cross-domain at-speed strategy defined and verified
  • OCC inserted before clock tree synthesis, not after

Step 4 is the difficult part. Single-domain at-speed test is well understood; testing paths that cross domains at speed requires the domains to have a defined phase relationship in test mode, which is a constraint on the clocking architecture rather than on DFT.

Watch out for

  • At-speed test not supported on every domain. Coverage then has a hole exactly where the fastest logic is, which is where transition defects concentrate.
  • Cross-domain paths untested at speed. These are among the most timing-marginal paths in the design and the hardest to cover.
  • OCC interaction with the PLL unverified. A controller that cannot get a clean clock from the PLL in test mode produces patterns that fail on good silicon.
  • Power during at-speed test ignored. Scan shift followed by at-speed capture creates switching activity far above functional, and the IR drop can cause failures on good parts.
  • OCC inserted late. It sits in the clock path, so adding it after clock tree synthesis means redoing the tree.

This is where the architecture becomes logic. DFT DRC violations—uncontrollable clocks, unresettable flops, blocked scan paths—reduce coverage silently, and each one is a set of faults ATPG will never be able to target.

Step 5 is the substance. Every DFT DRC violation is a region of logic ATPG cannot control or observe, and the coverage loss is silent—the tool simply reports a lower number without saying which violation caused it.

Watch out for

  • DRC violations accepted without measuring their coverage cost. Each one silently removes faults from the targetable set, and the total is invisible until ATPG reports a low number.
  • Test points inserted without area budget. They improve coverage and cost area and timing, and adding them late competes with closure.
  • Chain balance ignored. Unbalanced chains set shift time by the longest one, and shift time is most of the test time.
  • Insertion done once and not re-run. Netlist changes after insertion leave chains stale, and the mismatch appears at pattern validation.
  • Chain integrity unverified. A broken chain makes everything behind it untestable, and finding that at ATE rather than in simulation costs a silicon turn.

Step 5 is what makes a coverage number honest. Faults reported as untestable are either genuinely untestable—tied off, redundant—or untestable because of a DRC violation, and only analysis distinguishes a real limit from a fixable one.

Watch out for

  • Coverage target missed and accepted late. The remedies—test points, DRC fixes, architecture changes—all need an RTL or netlist change, and none are available near tapeout.
  • Pattern volume exceeding tester memory. Patterns that do not fit have to be split across loads, which multiplies test time and cost.
  • Untestable faults accepted without analysis. A fixable DRC violation reported as an untestable fault is coverage given away.
  • Cell-aware added late. It multiplies pattern count against a budget already set, forcing a choice between coverage and test time with no room to negotiate.
  • Patterns generated on a netlist that then changes. Any netlist change after generation invalidates the set, and regeneration takes weeks.

Step 3 catches what zero-delay cannot: patterns that violate timing at the capture edge. On an at-speed pattern set this is not a formality—a launch-capture sequence that closes in ATPG and fails in timing simulation would have produced yield loss on good die.

Watch out for

  • Validation skipped for schedule. A pattern failure then appears at ATE bring-up, where the diagnosis competes with everything else happening at first silicon.
  • Only zero-delay simulation run. Timing-related pattern failures are exactly what at-speed patterns are meant to detect, and they are invisible without SDF.
  • Format conversion assumed. STIL and WGL translation has tool-specific quirks, and a set that converts cleanly can still time incorrectly on the tester.
  • Regeneration cost underestimated. A pattern failure requiring regeneration puts the whole set back through DFT-07, which takes weeks not days.
  • Timing sets not validated against the actual tester. A pattern that assumes an edge placement the ATE cannot produce fails on hardware for a reason no simulation shows.

Why it exists

Compression networks connect every chain to a shared decompressor and compactor, which produces long routes across the die competing with functional signals for the same resource. Step 3 is where the two disciplines usually collide. DFT wants chains ordered for balance and diagnosis; physical design wants them ordered for routing. Reordering after placement is the standard compromise, and agreeing it here avoids arguing about it during closure.

Watch out for

  • Compression ratio unroutable. A ratio chosen for pattern volume alone produces a network that consumes routing resource the functional design needs.
  • Chain reordering breaking diagnosis. Physical reordering improves routing and can destroy the chain-to-block mapping diagnosis depends on.
  • Test clock distribution treated as functional. Scan shift clocks reach every flop and have their own skew and power requirements.
  • Feasibility assessed after routing starts. The findings then arrive when the only remaining remedy is to reduce coverage.
  • Hierarchical partition boundaries ignored. Chains crossing physical partitions carry a routing and timing cost that a logical view does not show.

Step 2 is the step that fails silently. Every consumer asks for a modest allocation, the total is set once, and the worst-case repair set—which is a distribution rather than an average—exceeds it on the parts that most needed repairing.

Watch out for

  • Capacity sized to the average repair need. Repair need is a distribution, and the parts needing most repair are exactly the ones the allocation fails.
  • Programming path untested. Fuses are one-time; a programming path that does not work correctly produces parts that are permanently wrong.
  • Fuse read timing in the boot path unconsidered. Repair and trim values have to be distributed before the logic that uses them is released from reset.
  • Traceability scheme designed late. Chip identity is needed for yield analysis and field returns, and retrofitting it means parts that cannot be traced.
  • Lifecycle encoding without a test path. A lifecycle transition that cannot be exercised in test is a transition whose correctness is unknown until the field.

5 Test mode and scan constraintsruns in parallel Test mode constraints 1.5w
6 Constraint validation and quality checking Constraint validation reports 2.5w

Step 6 is not review, it is tooling. Constraint quality checkers find unconstrained paths, conflicting exceptions and clocks that reach nothing, and they find them in minutes—which is why every drop should be re-checked rather than checked once.

Watch out for

  • Unconstrained paths reported as clean. A path with no constraint is a path the tool ignores, and it appears in the report as no violation at all.
  • Exceptions written to close timing. A false path added because the path would not close is a silicon failure being converted into a green report.
  • Constraints diverging between synthesis and signoff. Two constraint sets means optimizing against one and being judged against the other.
  • Test mode constraints written late. Scan shift and at-speed modes have their own timing, and a design closed only in functional mode fails at ATE.
  • IO constraints assumed from the interface specification. Actual budgets come from the package and channel analysis in SIPI-07, not from the protocol document.

SYN-02Technology mapping and optimization — multi-Vt, multi-bit, useful skew

Takes8ww2–w10 of the stage
Costs16.0 M/M~8.7 people while it runs

Why it exists

Map the RTL onto the qualified library and optimize it for the PPA budget—Vt mix, multi-bit banking, useful skew, datapath structure.

Technology mapping is where architecture becomes gates and where most of the achievable PPA is decided. The same RTL mapped two ways can differ by 20% in area and a hundred millivolts in achievable frequency, and the difference is entirely in how this activity is configured.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Qualified libraries from PDK-03
  • Constraints from SYN-01
  • RTL from RTL-02 and RTL-04
  • PPA budgets from ARCH-06
  • Flow and methodology from PDK-09

Done when

  • Area recovered on non-critical paths, not only speed optimized
  • Vt menu used across its range, not defaulted
  • QoR reported normalized so drops are comparable

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Library and mapping strategy selection Mapping strategy and library configuration 1.5w
2 Baseline mapping and optimization Baseline mapped netlist 2.5w
3 Datapath and arithmetic optimizationruns in parallel Datapath optimization results 1.5w
4 Multi-bit banking and useful skew configuration Multi-bit and useful skew configuration 2w
5 Area recovery on non-critical pathsruns in parallel Area recovery results 1.5w
6 QoR analysis and optimization iteration QoR analysis per iteration 2w

Step 5 is where area is won without cost. Most of a design is not on the critical path, and recovering area and leakage there is free performance-wise—but it only happens if someone configures the flow to do it rather than optimizing everything for speed.

Watch out for

  • Everything optimized for speed. Area and leakage on non-critical paths are given away for performance nobody asked for, and the die grows.
  • Multi-bit banking configured late. Clock power depends heavily on it, and adding it after closure means re-timing the design.
  • Useful skew used to hide a timing problem. It buys real margin and also makes the clock tree harder to build; using it to rescue a path that should be restructured moves the problem to PD-07.
  • Library subset used without knowing it. Synthesis using only part of the Vt menu produces avoidable leakage, and nobody notices because the design closes.
  • QoR compared drop to drop without normalizing. A netlist with more RTL in it is not directly comparable to the last one, and the trend becomes noise.

Why it exists

Release the N0 flow-flush netlist—functionally incomplete, structurally representative—so physical design can build and debug its flow against a real database months before the design is ready.

N0 exists to be wrong in the right way. It has the right hierarchy, the right macros and roughly the right size, and it does not need to work. Its entire purpose is to let PD-01 find its flow problems on a throwaway netlist rather than on the one the schedule depends on.

Step 1 is the whole activity. N0 has to be representative in the dimensions PD's flow cares about—hierarchy, macro count, instance count, pin count—and can be arbitrarily wrong in everything else. Getting that distinction right is what makes it cheap.

Watch out for

  • N0 delayed until it is good. The point is to be early; a correct N0 delivered late has become N1 and left PD's flow undebugged.
  • Not representative in the dimensions that matter. A netlist with a tenth of the instances exercises none of the runtime and capacity problems PD needs to find.
  • Limitations not stated. Physical design chasing timing on a stubbed netlist wastes a week before someone explains it was never going to close.
  • Stub strategy that changes the hierarchy. A hierarchy that differs from the real one means the flow is set up for a structure that will not arrive.
  • Treated as a milestone rather than a tool. N0 is scaffolding; celebrating it as progress distracts from the fact that no real design has been synthesized.

Why it exists

Synthesize with the floorplan in the loop—physical-aware mapping, congestion feedback, placement-driven restructuring—so the netlist that reaches physical design is already routable.

Logic synthesis without physical information optimizes for a wire model that does not exist. On a large die the difference between estimated and actual wire delay is large enough to invalidate the optimization, and the correction happens either here or as weeks of congestion work at PD-06.

Step 6 answers whether the added runtime is worth it. Physical-aware synthesis is slower; comparing its QoR against the wire-load-model result is what justifies the cost, and occasionally shows the floorplan is the problem rather than the logic.

Watch out for

  • Floorplan too immature to synthesize against. Physical-aware synthesis against a floorplan that then changes produces optimization for a layout that never exists.
  • Congestion feedback one-directional. Synthesis restructures and physical design re-places; without both, each optimizes against the other's stale result.
  • Runtime cost not justified. Physical-aware flows are slow, and without the QoR comparison nobody knows whether the extra hours bought anything.
  • Restructuring breaking hierarchy. Aggressive cross-boundary optimization improves QoR and makes the netlist harder to close hierarchically and harder to equivalence-check.
  • Blockages not modelled. Macros and their keep-out regions dominate placement on this die, and synthesis blind to them produces logic that cannot be placed where it assumed.

SYN-06Power optimization — clock gating, operand isolation, Vt mix

Takes7ww9–w16 of the stage
Costs12.0 M/M~7.4 people while it runs

Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Reduce power where it is actually spent—clock gating, operand isolation, Vt mix—driven by real switching activity rather than by defaults.

Power optimization without activity data is guesswork. Clock gating inserted everywhere costs area and saves little; inserted where the data says the logic is idle it saves a meaningful fraction of dynamic power. The activity data comes from verification, which makes this a cross-stage dependency more than a synthesis setting.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Switching activity from DV-04 workload simulations
  • Power budgets from ARCH-06
  • Mapped netlist from SYN-02
  • Library Vt menu from PDK-03
  • Clock architecture from ARCH-05

Done when

  • Optimization driven by real activity data, not defaults
  • Clock gating efficiency measured, not assumed
  • Power reported at the operating point the product uses

4 Operand isolation and datapath gating Operand isolation implementation 2w

Step 5 is what separates power optimization from power decoration. Switching activity from the <code>DV-04</code> workload simulations tells the tool which logic is actually idle; without it, gating is inserted by structural heuristic and saves a fraction of what it could.

Watch out for

  • Optimization driven by default activity. Uniform switching assumptions produce gating where it saves nothing and none where it would.
  • Clock gating efficiency unmeasured. Gates inserted without measuring how often they actually gate cost area and leakage for no benefit.
  • Vt mix skewed to low-Vt for timing. Leakage grows non-linearly, and a design closed on low-Vt everywhere blows its static power budget.
  • Power measured at the wrong operating point. The number that matters is at the DVFS point the product runs at, not at nominal.
  • Optimization deferred to the final turn. Power changes timing; a design closed on timing and then power-optimized has to be re-closed.

SYN-07Low-power synthesis — isolation and level-shifter insertion against UPF

Takes5ww10–w15 of the stage

Why it exists

Implement the power intent in the netlist—isolation cells, level shifters, retention flops, always-on paths—from the UPF, and prove the netlist and the intent still agree.

UPF describes what should happen; synthesis is where it becomes cells. An isolation cell missing at a domain boundary is a design that corrupts data on power-down, and it is invisible in any functional check that does not model power. The consistency check between netlist and intent is the only reliable detector.

What it delivers

SYN-D7Power intent implementation report

This activity is the deliverable—what was inferred, what was inserted, and where intent and netlist agree.

Needs first

  • Low-power cells from PDK-03
  • Power domain definition from ARCH-05
  • Mapped netlist from SYN-02
  • Low-power flow from PDK-09

Done when

  • Every domain boundary has verified isolation
  • UPF and netlist consistent, checked rather than assumed
  • Retention and always-on requirements handed to physical design

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 5 runs in parallel and is the one that must not be skipped. The netlist and the UPF are two descriptions of the same intent, and any divergence between them propagates into physical design and verification as a defect nobody can attribute.

Watch out for

  • Isolation inferred but not verified. A missing cell at one boundary corrupts state on power-down and appears in no functional test.
  • Retention cells inserted without physical planning. They have a different footprint and power connectivity, and adding them late disturbs the floorplan.
  • Always-on paths not identified. Logic that must survive a domain shutting down and is not marked always-on is powered down with it.
  • UPF and netlist diverging. Two descriptions of the same intent, and downstream tools reading different ones.
  • Level shifters omitted between voltage domains. The design functions in simulation and fails at the voltage extremes in silicon.

Watch out for

Step 1 is a confirmation rather than a formality. If <code>RTL-10</code> has not actually declared freeze, the FFN is a snapshot of a moving design, and the final turn in <code>PD-13</code> will be closing against something that changes underneath it.

Watch out for

  • FFN released against RTL that is not actually frozen. The final turn then closes against a moving netlist, and every change restarts it.
  • Constraints still changing after the FFN. A design closed against one constraint set and signed off against another has not been signed off.
  • Equivalence not proved on the final netlist. The last synthesis run is the one most likely to contain a transformation error, and the least likely to be checked under schedule pressure.
  • Functional freeze declared and not enforced. Post-FFN functional ECOs are sometimes unavoidable and must be exceptional, visible and costed.
  • Handoff package incomplete. The final turn needs constraints, UPF, DFT collateral and abstracts together; a missing item stops closure at its start.

Step 5 is where most of the difficulty lives. Scan insertion and clock gating change the netlist in ways that are correct and not structurally equivalent, and setting up the checker to accept those and reject everything else is the skilled part of the activity.

Watch out for

  • Equivalence run only on the final netlist. A transformation error introduced at N1 is then found at the FFN, when the debug competes with tapeout.
  • Non-equivalences waived to make progress. Each waiver is a place where the netlist may not implement the verified RTL, and they accumulate quietly.
  • DFT transformations not modelled. The checker reports thousands of differences and everyone stops reading the report.
  • Black-box handling too permissive. Boxing out a block to get a clean result excludes exactly the logic that was not checked.
  • Debug capacity underestimated. A single real non-equivalence on a design this size can take a week to localize, and there is rarely a week available.

Why it exists

Report timing, area and power against the budget after every drop, and escalate when a block is diverging rather than when it has already blown its allocation.

QoR reported in absolute terms tells nobody anything. Reported against the ARCH-06 allocation and trended across drops, it says which blocks are converging, which are not, and how much of the gap is still recoverable—which is the only version a program manager can act on.

Step 5 is the part that predicts. A block 10% over budget and improving is a different problem from one 5% over and flat, and only a trend across drops distinguishes them.

Watch out for

  • QoR reported in absolute terms. Numbers with no budget reference cannot be acted on, and everyone forms their own opinion of whether they are acceptable.
  • No escalation rule. Divergence noticed and not escalated becomes a surprise at the final turn, when there is nothing left to do about it.
  • Reports not normalized across drops. More RTL in a later drop makes the trend meaningless unless the comparison accounts for it.
  • Power reported at nominal only. The number that matters is at the product's operating point, and reporting at nominal understates it consistently.
  • Reporting stopping between drops. The interesting question is whether a block is improving, and that needs data between releases as well as at them.

Watch out for

  • Packages delivered without acceptance. Physical design discovers the gap mid-turn, and the turn absorbs the delay.
  • QoR reviewed asynchronously. A report read separately produces two interpretations, and the disagreement surfaces at the next escalation.
  • Issues not tracked between drops. Each handoff then starts fresh, and the same problems are raised at every drop.
  • Package contents changing between drops. Physical design automates against the format, and an inconsistent package breaks their flow.
  • Handoff treated as a synthesis milestone. It is a shared event; a handoff that PD has not accepted has not happened.

This is why SYN-03 releases a netlist nobody expects to close. Every flow problem—a deck that does not load, a scenario that does not converge, a runtime that exceeds the night—is found here on a throwaway database, weeks before the same problem would have cost a turn.

Step 6 is what makes the schedule credible. A flow that runs correctly and takes forty hours per iteration sets a closure cadence nobody planned for, and knowing that number now is what lets <code>PDK-12</code> buy capacity before it is needed.

Watch out for

  • Flow setup on the first real netlist. Every flow problem then costs a turn, and the turns are the schedule.
  • MMMC scenarios incomplete. A corner or mode missing from the setup is one the design is never closed at, and it is found at SO-02.
  • Runtime not measured. A flow that works and takes two days per iteration produces a closure schedule nobody planned, discovered when closure starts.
  • Hierarchical flow deferred. A design this size cannot be closed flat; deferring the block-level flow means building it under pressure.
  • Capacity assumed rather than booked. The flow's peak concurrency is known here, and licences take weeks to procure.

PD-02Floorplan, macro placement and partition definition

Takes9ww5–w14 of the stage
Costs32.0 M/M~15.4 people while it runs
OwnerFloorplan ownerSynthesis liaison approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Decide where everything physically goes—partitions, macros, block boundaries, pins, utilization—and freeze it, because everything downstream is built on it.

The floorplan is the most consequential and least reversible decision in the stage. Macro placement sets routing congestion, block boundaries set what can be closed independently, and pin placement sets the top-level routing burden. A floorplan changed at turn 2 invalidates the clock trees, the power grid and the routing built on it.

What it delivers

PD-D4Floorplan and PDN specification

The floorplan half; PD-03 supplies the power grid it is built against.

Needs first

  • Floorplan intent and bump map from ARCH-08
  • Macro abstracts from AMS-15 and PDK-04
  • Partitioning from ARCH-02
  • Netlist from SYN-05
  • Area budgets from ARCH-06

Done when

  • Floorplan frozen before turn 1 starts
  • Macro placement validated against congestion, not only access
  • Pin placement reviewed for top-level routing cost

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

5 Keep-out, blockage and halo definitionruns in parallel Keep-out and blockage definition 1.5w

Step 2 is where a memory-dominated die is won or lost. Hundreds of macro instances have to be placed so their access paths are short, their power can be delivered and the logic between them can be routed—and moving one late moves everything around it.

Watch out for

  • Macro placement not congestion-aware. Macros placed for access and not for the logic between them produce routing congestion that cannot be fixed at PD-08.
  • Floorplan changed after turn 1. Clock trees, power grid and routing are all built on it, and all of them are invalidated.
  • Utilization set too high. A dense floorplan closes area and cannot be routed or timing-closed, and the discovery comes after weeks of work.
  • Pin placement ignoring top-level routing. Block pins facing the wrong way make top-level routing expensive for the whole rest of the program.
  • Partitions that do not match the design hierarchy. Closing blocks that cut across logical boundaries makes timing budgets and equivalence checking harder for no gain.

PD-03Power delivery network design and early IR analysis

Why it exists

Build the power delivery network—grid topology, straps, switches, decap—and prove by early IR analysis that it can actually feed the die at its power envelope.

The PDN is built early because everything routes around it. Grid density trades directly against routing resource: too sparse and IR drop eats timing margin, too dense and there is nothing left to route with. Getting it wrong is discovered at SO-04, when the fix is a metal change across the whole die.

  • Static IR analyzed on a placed design with real power numbers

Step 4 has to happen while the grid can still change. Static IR on a placed design with real power numbers tells you whether the grid works; running it after routing means any fix competes with a routed design for the same metal.

Watch out for

  • Grid density traded against routing without analysis. Both constraints are real, and choosing by feel produces either IR problems or congestion.
  • IR analyzed only statically. Dynamic IR under real switching is worse, and SIPI-04 with the package model is worse again.
  • Decap placed where there is room. Decoupling works where the current is drawn, not where the floorplan left space.
  • Power switches planned late. They need area, always-on routing and their own control, and retrofitting them disturbs the floorplan.
  • PDN frozen before power numbers are real. A grid designed against estimates and fed a design that draws more is a grid that fails at signoff.

Why it exists

Turn the architecture's bump budget into an actual bump map and RDL, iterating with package design until both sides can build what the other needs.

The bump map is the contract between the die and the package, and it is negotiated rather than declared. Signal escape on the package constrains bump position; power delivery constrains bump count; and the die's floorplan constrains where either can go. All three have to close at once.

Step 6 is a hard date rather than a milestone. <code>PKGD-11</code> freezes package design against this map, and the substrate order that follows has a twenty-week lead time—a late bump map moves wafer-out by moving the substrate.

Watch out for

  • Bump map frozen late. Package design and the substrate order both wait on it, and the substrate lead time makes the delay a wafer-out delay.
  • Escape routing not checked on the package side. A map that is optimal on the die and unroutable on the substrate has to be redone.
  • Power bump count reduced to fit signals. The signals that fit are then fed by a PDN that cannot deliver, and SIPI-04 finds it.
  • RDL treated as free. Redistribution has its own rules and resistance, and a plan that ignores them produces IR and EM problems in the RDL itself.
  • Co-design conducted by file exchange. Two teams iterating asynchronously on the same interface converge slowly or not at all.

Watch out for

  • Turn 1 expected to close. It will not, and treating the gap as a crisis rather than as data produces panic instead of a plan.
  • Feedback not specific. "Congestion is high" changes nothing; "the compute cluster is over 90% utilization in three regions and needs restructuring" changes the next drop.
  • Turn run on an incomplete netlist. A baseline missing blocks understates the difficulty and misleads the closure plan.
  • Congestion mitigated locally. Fixing congestion by rip-up and reroute hides a structural problem that only synthesis or floorplan can solve.
  • Clock tree built before the floorplan is stable. A CTS on a floorplan that then changes is work thrown away.

PD-07Clock tree synthesis with skew and jitter budgeting, refined across turns

Takes12w cont.w10–w22 of the stage

Why it exists

Build and refine the clock trees across turns—skew, insertion delay, jitter budget, power—for a design with dozens of domains and crossings between them.

Clock tree synthesis is rebuilt every turn and improved each time. Skew directly buys or costs timing margin; insertion delay costs power and OCV; and cross-domain paths need a defined phase relationship that only a deliberately built tree provides. It is one of the few areas where a good result is worth several percent of frequency.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Clock architecture from ARCH-05
  • OCC insertion from DFT-05

  • Placement from PD-05 and PD-06
  • PLL characteristics from AMS-02

Done when

  • Clock power inside the ARCH-06 budget
  • Cross-domain relationships defined and closed
  • Clock DRC clean, not only timing-clean

357
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Clock architecture implementation plan Clock architecture implementation plan 1.5w
2 Clock tree synthesis per domain Clock tree implementation plan · Synthesized clock trees per domain 2.5w

6 Cross-domain and useful skew handling Cross-domain and useful skew handling 2.5w
7 Clock DRC and quality checkingruns in parallel Clock DRC and quality reports 2w
8 Continuous refinement across turns Clock tree refinement record across turns 3w

Step 6 is the hardest part and the one that pays. Useful skew moves margin from paths that have it to paths that need it, and cross-domain handling decides whether those paths can be closed at all—but both make the tree harder to build and harder to verify.

Watch out for

  • Clock power ignored. The clock network is a large fraction of dynamic power on a design this size, and a tree optimized only for skew is expensive to run.
  • Useful skew applied without a plan. It buys margin and complicates every subsequent ECO, because moving one path's timing moves its neighbors'.
  • Cross-domain phase relationship undefined. Paths between domains cannot be closed reliably, and the failure appears as intermittent silicon behavior.
  • Insertion delay allowed to grow. Deep trees increase OCV derate and jitter accumulation, consuming the margin the skew balancing bought.
  • Tree quality not checked. Clock DRC violations—transition, capacitance, pulse width—degrade the tree in ways timing analysis reports as margin loss without explaining.

Step 6 takes four weeks because DRC convergence on an advanced node is iterative and asymptotic. The last few hundred violations take as long as the first hundred thousand, and they are the ones that need manual attention.

Watch out for

  • Congestion treated as a routing problem. Structural congestion cannot be routed around, and rip-up cycles spent on it consume time without converging.
  • Antenna violations left late. Fixes need diodes or layer jumps, both of which need space that a fully routed design does not have.
  • DRC convergence assumed linear. The last violations are the hardest, and planning as if the rate is constant produces a schedule that misses.
  • Manufacturability ignored until signoff. DFM-clean routing is cheaper to produce than to retrofit, and SO-08 finds what was not.
  • Layer plan not respecting the PDN. Signals and the power grid contend for the same upper layers, and a plan that ignores the grid produces conflicts everywhere.

Step 7 prevents the worst surprise available. A design closed in the implementation tool and re-analyzed in the signoff tool will show differences; discovering their size early lets the team close with the right margin rather than re-closing after <code>SO-02</code> reports.

Watch out for

  • Closing at some corners and deferring others. The deferred corner is the one that fails, and it fails when there is no time to fix it.
  • Implementation and signoff timing diverging. A design closed in one tool and judged in another can be weeks from closure without anyone knowing.
  • Hold fixed after setup. Hold fixes add buffers that change setup, and doing them sequentially means iterating both.
  • Burn-down not tracked. Without a trend nobody can distinguish a design that is converging slowly from one that is not converging at all.
  • ECO volume exceeding what the database can absorb. Thousands of ECOs degrade the physical result, and at some point a re-run is cheaper than another ECO round.

Step 6 is an iteration rather than a step, because every fix perturbs something else. Widening a wire for EM changes its coupling; adding shielding consumes routing resource; and both change timing, which sends the design back to <code>PD-09</code>.

Watch out for

  • SI analyzed after timing closes. Crosstalk delay is timing, and closing without it means closing against numbers that will move.
  • EM checked only on power. High-toggle signal nets on advanced nodes carry EM exposure too, and they are usually the ones nobody checks.
  • Dynamic IR analyzed with uniform activity. Real switching is bursty and localized, and uniform assumptions understate the worst case badly.
  • Fixes applied without re-timing. Shielding and spacing change delay, and a fix that breaks timing has moved the problem rather than solved it.
  • Package effects excluded. Die-only dynamic IR is optimistic; SIPI-04 with package inductance is the number signoff will use.

Step 3 determines whether the model is useful. A CPM extracted under average activity understates the transient the package has to supply; extracting under the worst realistic burst is what makes <code>SIPI-04</code>'s answer meaningful.

Watch out for

  • Model extracted under average activity. The package has to supply the transient, and an averaged model hides exactly the event that matters.
  • Delivered late. Co-verification is on the critical path to mask release, and it cannot start without this model.
  • Model not validated. A CPM that disagrees with the die's own IR analysis is wrong in one of the two places, and nobody knows which.
  • Single model for all modes. Different DVFS points and workloads draw very differently, and one model cannot represent them.
  • No version control. The package team analyzing against a stale model produces conclusions about a die that no longer exists.

Step 6 is not optional. Reordering rewrites the netlist's scan connectivity, and a chain broken by the reorder makes everything behind it untestable—a failure that would otherwise be discovered at ATE bring-up.

Watch out for

  • Reordering breaking diagnosis. Failure analysis relies on mapping a failing bit to a physical location, and a scrambled chain removes that.
  • Chains not verified after reorder. A break makes everything behind it untestable, and ATE bring-up is a costly place to find that.
  • Patterns generated before the final reorder. Any chain change after DFT-07 invalidates the pattern set and costs weeks of regeneration.
  • Test clock skew ignored. Scan shift reaches every flop, and skew on the shift clock produces shift failures that look like design bugs.
  • Chain imbalance after reorder. Physical reordering can lengthen one chain and shorten another, and shift time follows the longest.

Why it exists

Finish the die as a manufacturable object—seal ring, metal fill, dummy, alignment marks, identification—and verify that none of it broke what was closed.

Chip finishing is mechanical and it is not free. Metal fill changes coupling capacitance and therefore timing; the seal ring consumes die edge; and dummy fill interacts with the analog matching that AMS-12 spent weeks building. Every one has to be applied and then re-verified.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Routed database from PD-08 and PD-13
  • Seal ring and frame rules from PDK-02
  • Fill and density rules from the DRM
  • Analog macro fill exclusions from AMS-12
  • Die identification requirements from MP-09

Done when

  • Timing verified after fill, not before it
  • Analog matching structures protected from fill
  • Die identification present and readable

Step 3 is why finishing is not a formality. Fill adds capacitance to every net near it, and a design closed before fill and taped out after it has been signed off against a database that no longer exists.

Watch out for

  • Timing signed off before fill. The taped-out database has fill and the signed-off one did not, which is a signoff against a different design.
  • Fill applied over analog matching structures. It disturbs the parasitics AMS-12 tuned, and the damage is invisible until silicon characterization.
  • Seal ring area not reserved. Discovered late, it forces the die edge inward and moves the bump map.
  • Die identification omitted. Traceability at yield analysis and field return depends on being able to identify the die, and it cannot be added later.
  • Finishing treated as a checkbox. Each step changes the physical database, and each needs verification against what was closed.

PD-16Hierarchical block closure and top-level assembly

Why it exists

Close the blocks independently and assemble them into a top level that meets timing across their boundaries—the hierarchical discipline a die this size requires.

A design of this size cannot be closed flat: runtime and capacity make it impossible. Hierarchical closure lets blocks converge in parallel, at the cost of interface budgets that have to be right. A block that closes internally and misses its boundary budget has not helped.

What it delivers

PD-D9Signoff-ready database handoff

This activity is the deliverable—the assembled top level signoff and tapeout actually consume.

Needs first

  • Partition definition from PD-02
  • Block databases from each turn
  • Interface budgets from ARCH-06
  • Timing closure status from PD-09
  • Final database from PD-13

Done when

  • Block models correlated against flat analysis
  • Every block closed to one shared criterion
  • Top level assembled and verified before the final turn ends

Step 7 is the check that keeps hierarchy honest. A block's timing model is an abstraction, and if it disagrees with a flat analysis of the same block then the top level has been closed against a fiction.

Watch out for

  • Block models disagreeing with flat analysis. The top level is then closed against an abstraction that does not represent the block.
  • Interface budgets set late. Blocks close internally and fail at their boundaries, and the fix requires reopening blocks that were declared done.
  • Feedthroughs not planned. Signals crossing a block have to be routed through it, and a block closed without feedthrough provision blocks the top level.
  • Blocks closed to different criteria. Without an enforced standard, each block closes to what its owner considered sufficient, and the top level inherits the weakest.
  • Top-level assembly left to the end. Assembly finds interface problems, and finding them after the final turn leaves no time to fix them.

SO-01Signoff flow dry run on the Turn 2 database — decks, runtimes, capacity and violation triage rehearsed

Why it exists

Rehearse the entire signoff flow on the turn 2 database—decks, runtimes, capacity, violation triage—so the final turn is not the first time it runs at full chip.

Signoff is a large, slow, deck-heavy flow, and the first run always finds problems that have nothing to do with the design. Finding them on turn 2 costs a week of a database nobody is waiting for; finding them on the final turn costs a week of the tapeout schedule.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Decks and runsets from PDK-10
  • Corner definition from PDK-11

  • Runtime measured and the campaign scheduled against it

Step 3 sizes the signoff campaign. Signoff runtime on a die this size is measured in days per corner, and knowing the number before the final turn is what lets the schedule be built rather than discovered.

Watch out for

  • Dry run skipped for schedule. The flow's first full-chip run then happens on the critical path, and every problem it finds costs tapeout days.
  • Runtime not measured. A signoff campaign planned without knowing its runtime is planned against a guess.
  • Dry run on an unrepresentative database. Turn 2 has to be close enough in size and structure that the runtimes and violation counts mean something.
  • Triage tooling built during the real campaign. Thousands of violations arrive at once, and sorting them by hand is how a week disappears.
  • Findings not fixed before the final turn. A rehearsal that identifies problems and does not resolve them has only produced a list.

This is the largest activity in the stage and the one Design Freeze most depends on. It differs from PD-09 in that it is judgment rather than optimization: the signoff tool, the foundry-agreed derates and the full corner set, with no ECO loop to fall back on.

Step 6 covers the modes that are easy to forget and expensive to miss. Scan shift, at-speed capture and any low-power mode each have their own timing, and a design signed off functionally and not in test mode produces parts that fail at ATE.

Watch out for

  • Corners deferred to fit the schedule. The deferred corner is the one that fails, and it fails in silicon where there is no fix.
  • Waivers granted without root cause. A waived violation with no understood cause is a silicon risk being accepted blind.
  • Test modes not signed off. Scan shift and at-speed timing failures produce parts that work functionally and fail at ATE.
  • Signoff and implementation disagreeing late. If SO-12 has not correlated the two, the first signoff run can show a design weeks from closure.
  • ECO loop reopening after signoff starts. Each ECO invalidates the analysis it was based on, and uncontrolled iteration never converges.

Why it exists

Run full-chip physical verification—DRC, LVS, antenna, density—to clean, on the database that will become masks.

Physical verification is binary and unforgiving: the foundry will not accept a database with violations it has not waived. On a die this size the runs take days, the violation counts start in the tens of thousands, and the last hundred are the ones that need a human.

Step 4 is where the hardest problems hide. An LVS mismatch on a full chip can take days to localize, and the causes are usually elsewhere—a macro abstract that disagrees with its layout, or an ECO applied to one view and not the other.

Watch out for

  • LVS mismatch traced late. Full-chip mismatches take days to localize, and they are frequently caused by macro views rather than by the design.
  • Runs started too late. Each full-chip run takes days, and the iteration count is what sets the schedule rather than any single run.
  • Antenna fixes needing space that is gone. Diodes and layer jumps need room, and a fully routed design has none.
  • Waivers assumed acceptable. Foundry waivers are granted case by case, and a design that assumes one will be granted may not tape out.
  • Verification on a database that then changes. Any ECO after a clean run invalidates it, and re-running costs days.

Sign off electromigration and IR drop—static and dynamic, with real switching—because a design that meets timing and fails EM will not survive its warranty.

EM and IR are reliability and performance at once. IR drop consumes timing margin the STA assumed; EM limits how long the part will work. Both are analyzed on the final database with real activity, and both can send routing back for changes that reopen timing.

Step 5 closes a loop that is often left open. IR drop lowers the local supply and slows the logic, and unless that is back-annotated into timing the STA has been run at a voltage the die does not actually see.

Watch out for

  • IR not back-annotated into timing. The design is then signed off at a supply voltage it never sees, and the margin was never real.
  • Dynamic IR analyzed with uniform activity. Real switching is bursty and local, and uniform assumptions understate the worst case.
  • Package effects excluded. Die-only IR is optimistic; the number that matters includes the package inductance SIPI-04 models.
  • Signal EM overlooked. High-toggle nets on advanced nodes carry real EM exposure, and checking only power misses them.
  • EM fixes reopening timing. Widening wires changes delay, and a fix applied after timing signoff invalidates it.

Why it exists

Sign off signal integrity—crosstalk delay, noise, glitch—on the final database, and confirm the numbers the timing signoff assumed.

Crosstalk is timing. Coupling between adjacent nets changes delay in both directions and can inject glitches that propagate as functional failures. The analysis is separate from STA and its results feed straight back into it, which makes the two inseparable at signoff.

What it delivers

SO-D3EM/IR and SI/PI signoff reports

The signal integrity half of the deliverable.

Needs first

  • Crosstalk fixes from PD-10
  • Timing analysis from SO-02
  • Noise rules and thresholds from PDK-02
  • PI results from SO-04

Done when

  • Crosstalk delay included in the timing signoff numbers
  • Glitch analysis run, not only delay analysis
  • Noise thresholds set from library data, not defaults

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 4 is where the analysis becomes actionable. A global crosstalk number tells nobody what to fix; a victim-aggressor list on the critical paths tells routing exactly which nets to space or shield.

Watch out for

  • Crosstalk reported and not reconciled with timing. Two separate reports means the design is signed off against timing that excludes coupling.
  • Glitch analysis omitted. Noise on a static net can propagate as a functional failure that no timing analysis would show.
  • Analysis on a subset of nets. Coupling is a property of adjacency, and the critical net set is not the same as the coupled net set.
  • Fixes applied after timing signoff. Spacing and shielding change delay, and a late fix invalidates the timing it was meant to protect.
  • Thresholds set by tool default. Noise thresholds are a library and technology property, and defaults are either optimistic or unnecessarily punitive.

Step 2 is the reconciliation that matters. Die-only IR analysis excludes package inductance, and the difference between the two numbers is margin the design either has or does not—a discrepancy that has to be resolved before mask release rather than explained afterwards.

Watch out for

  • Co-verification treated as a package deliverable. It constrains the die's signoff, and excluding it from the signoff record means freezing without it.
  • Discrepancies explained rather than resolved. Where die-only and system-level disagree, one is wrong, and the difference is real margin.
  • Channel compliance reviewed against internal assumptions. The interface specification's mask is what compliance means, and internal budgets can be more generous.
  • Review scheduled after Design Freeze. The freeze is what gates mask release, and a co-verification finding afterwards has nowhere to go.
  • Power-aware timing not reviewed. STA at nominal voltage and IR analysis showing droop are two views of the same design, and only the reconciliation is the truth.

Step 2 traces the discharge path through the actual layout rather than confirming the strategy. A clamp that exists and a path that reaches it are different claims, and only the full-chip trace establishes the second.

Watch out for

  • ESD verified as a strategy rather than a path. A clamp with no complete discharge path to it protects nothing, and only a full-chip trace finds the gap.
  • Latch-up checked only at the IO ring. Internal structures near power domain boundaries can latch up too, and they are rarely checked.
  • Soft error rate not estimated. FIT is a product requirement in many markets, and estimating it after qualification leaves no mitigation options.
  • Reliability waivers granted without lifetime analysis. A waiver with no quantified impact cannot be defended when qualification fails.
  • Analysis on a database that then changes. Late ECOs can break an ESD path, and nobody re-runs the check.

SO-08DFM and lithography checks, CMP and hotspot analysis

Takes6ww8–w14 of the stage
Costs10.0 M/M~7.2 people while it runs

Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Check the design against manufacturability—lithography hotspots, CMP density, DFM recommended rules—so the foundry can print it at yield.

A DRC-clean design can still be difficult to manufacture. Litho hotspots print differently from what was drawn, and CMP density variation produces thickness variation that moves timing. Both are checked with foundry-supplied models and both are cheaper to fix here than to yield-learn in production.

What it delivers

SO-D5DFM and lithography hotspot report

This activity is the deliverable, and its compliance score is a yield predictor.

Needs first

  • Final database from PD-13
  • DFM decks and litho models from the foundry
  • Rule dispositions from PDK-02
  • Fill and density from PD-15
  • Defect density model from TECH-07

Done when

  • Hotspots fixed or accepted with a yield impact estimate
  • Compliance scored rather than assumed
  • Fixes re-verified against DRC and timing

125

34
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 DFM deck setup and model version confirmation DFM deck setup and model versions 1w

4 Recommended rule compliance scoringruns in parallel Recommended rule compliance score 1.5w

Step 4 quantifies what <code>PDK-02</code> decided. Recommended-rule compliance is a score rather than a pass, and it correlates with yield—a design that scored 60% on the rules it chose to ignore is a design whose yield learning curve starts lower.

Watch out for

  • DFM checked after routing is frozen. Hotspot fixes are layout changes, and a frozen database has no room for them.
  • Recommended rules ignored without scoring. The yield cost of ignoring them is real and unmeasured unless someone scores compliance.
  • Litho models outdated. Foundry models improve through the node's life, and an old model finds the wrong hotspots.
  • CMP variation not linked to timing. Thickness variation changes resistance and capacitance, and the timing impact is rarely fed back.
  • Fixes applied without re-verification. A DFM fix is a layout change, and it can create DRC or timing problems of its own.

Why it exists

Prove for the last time that the database being taped out is the design that was verified—final formal equivalence and netlist-to-layout consistency.

Between the FFN and the tapeout database sit hundreds of ECOs, a scan reorder, fill and finishing. Each was individually correct; the question is whether the composition still implements the RTL that DV signed off. This is the last check that answers it.

Step 3 pairs the formal result with the ECO log from <code>PD-14</code>. Equivalence proves the netlists match; reconciliation proves that every difference between them was an ECO somebody approved rather than a change nobody noticed.

Watch out for

  • Equivalence run against the FFN rather than the RTL. That proves the ECOs preserved the netlist and not that the netlist implements the verified design.
  • ECO log not reconciled. A difference that no ECO explains is an unapproved change, and it is exactly what this check exists to find.
  • Non-equivalences waived under tapeout pressure. Each waiver is a region where the silicon may not do what verification proved.
  • Run before the last ECO. Any change after the equivalence run invalidates it, and re-running takes days nobody has.
  • Layout consistency assumed from LVS. LVS compares layout to netlist; that the netlist is the right one is a separate claim.

Why it exists

Every large design tapes out with waivers. What distinguishes a controlled tapeout from a hopeful one is whether each waiver was understood, quantified and signed, or simply ran out of time. This board is where that distinction is made, and its package is what the Go / No-Go decision reads.

Step 3 has a duration outside the program's control. Foundry waivers are reviewed on the foundry's schedule, and a design that assumes approval and does not receive it cannot release masks—which makes early submission worth more than a complete submission.

Watch out for

  • Waivers accumulated rather than reviewed. A register nobody dispositioned is a set of accepted risks nobody accepted.
  • Foundry waivers submitted late. Their review is on the foundry's schedule, and an unapproved waiver blocks mask release.
  • Risk quantified qualitatively. "Low risk" is not a basis for a tapeout decision; a stated failure mode and probability is.
  • Board without authority. A review that cannot refuse a waiver is a review that approves everything.
  • Residual risk not summarized. The Go / No-Go decision needs one statement of what is being accepted, not a register of two hundred entries.

Takes5ww10–w15 of the stage

Why it exists

Run gate-level simulation with the final SDF—the last dynamic check that the design behaves correctly with real timing on the database being taped out.

Static timing analysis proves paths meet constraints; it does not prove the design works. Simulating with final timing catches what STA structurally cannot—race conditions, reset behavior under real delays, and any place where the constraints described a design different from the one built.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Final database and SDF from PD-13 and PD-09
  • Gate-level environment from DV-11
  • Test patterns and modes from DFT-08
  • Timing signoff results from SO-02
  • Power intent from SYN-07

Done when

  • Simulated against the final SDF, not an earlier one
  • Reset and initialization simulated with real delays
  • X failures fixed rather than forced

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

w10w11w12w13w14w15

Main sequence

125

In parallel

34
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Final SDF generation and simulation setup Final SDF and simulation setup 1w
2 Timing-annotated functional simulation Timing-annotated functional simulation results 1.5w
3 Reset and initialization sequence simulationruns in parallel Reset and initialization results 1w
4 Test mode simulation with final timingruns in parallel Test mode simulation results 1w
5 Failure debug and signoff reporting Gate-level signoff report 2.5w

Step 3 is the check most likely to find something. Reset behavior depends on relative delays across the die, and a sequence that works with estimated timing can fail with the real numbers—a failure that would otherwise appear at first power-on.

Watch out for

  • Skipped because STA is clean. They answer different questions, and the failures gate-level simulation finds are invisible to static analysis.
  • Run on an earlier database. A simulation against pre-final timing says nothing about the database being taped out.
  • Reset simulation omitted. Reset ordering under real delays is a common silicon failure and one of the cheapest to catch here.
  • X failures forced away. Initializing signals to make the simulation run hides exactly the uninitialized state that will fail at power-on.
  • Runtime prohibiting meaningful scenarios. Full-timing simulation is slow, and a scenario set trimmed to fit may exclude the case that matters.

Why it exists

Correlate the signoff flow against the foundry's own decks and the implementation tool, so that a number produced here means the same thing everywhere it is read.

Three parties analyze this design: the implementation tool, the signoff tool and the foundry. If they disagree, the design can be closed in one and rejected by another. Establishing the correlation early is what lets physical design close with the right margin instead of re-closing after signoff reports.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Implementation timing results from PD-09
  • Signoff flow from SO-01
  • Foundry decks and derates from PDK-11
  • Extraction decks from PDK-10
  • Library models from PDK-03

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

w2w3w4w5w6w7

Main sequence

125

In parallel

34
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Correlation methodology and reference case selection Correlation methodology and reference cases 1w
2 Implementation to signoff tool correlation Implementation to signoff correlation results 1.5w
3 Foundry deck and derate correlationruns in parallel Foundry deck and derate correlation 1w
4 Extraction and parasitic correlationruns in parallel Extraction and parasitic correlation 1w
5 Correlation findings and margin guidance Margin guidance for physical design 2.5w

Step 5 is the output physical design actually uses. Knowing that signoff reads 40 ps more pessimistic than implementation on long paths lets <code>PD-09</code> close with that margin built in, rather than closing to zero and discovering the gap at <code>SO-02</code>.

Watch out for

  • Correlation established after signoff starts. The gap is then discovered on the final database, when closing it means re-opening closure.
  • Correlation on unrepresentative paths. Tool differences concentrate on long, heavily coupled paths, and correlating on short clean ones shows agreement that does not generalize.
  • Extraction differences overlooked. Parasitic differences between flows can exceed timing tool differences and are less often checked.
  • Margin guidance not adopted. Correlation that physical design does not close against has produced information nobody used.
  • Foundry decks assumed identical to internal ones. Derates and corner definitions can differ in detail, and the foundry's version is the one that decides acceptance.

14 TO · Tapeout & Mask Release (MTO)

TO-01Final GDSII / OASIS assembly on the FFN closure database, with layer map verification

Takes2ww0–w2 of the stage
Costs6.0 M/M~13.0 people while it runs
OwnerTapeout engineerFoundry liaison approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Assemble the final GDSII or OASIS database from the closed design—every block, every macro, every layer—and verify that the layer map the foundry will read matches the one the design was built with.

This is a mechanical activity with no tolerance for error. A layer misassigned in the stream-out produces masks that are wrong in a way no verification would have caught, because the design was correct and the translation was not.

What it delivers

TO-D1Released GDSII / OASIS database with checksum record

This activity is the deliverable, and the checksum is what makes every later reference unambiguous.

Needs first

  • Frozen signoff database from PD-13 and PD-16
  • Hard macro GDS from AMS-15
  • Foundry layer map and stream-out rules
  • Chip finishing from PD-15
  • Signoff clean status from SO-03

Done when

  • Layer map verified against the foundry's definition, not the internal one
  • Every macro GDS traced to its released version
  • Database checksummed and recorded

How it gets there 4 steps · 2 lanes

w0w1w2

Main sequence

124

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Closure database intake and provenance check Database checksum and provenance record 0.5w
2 GDSII / OASIS stream out from the closed database Streamed GDSII / OASIS database 0.75w
3 Macro and hard IP GDS mergeruns in parallel Merged macro and hard IP GDS 0.5w
4 Layer map verification against the foundry definition Merged macro and IP layers · Layer map verification record 0.75w

Step 4 is checked against the foundry's layer map rather than the internal one. The two are usually identical and occasionally are not, and the difference is only visible at the mask shop—by which point the masks exist.

Watch out for

  • Layer map mismatch. A misassigned layer produces masks that are wrong in a way no design verification would have found.
  • Macro GDS from the wrong version. An abstract that matched and a layout that did not is discovered at LVS, or worse, not at all.
  • Stream-out from an unfrozen database. The design has to stop moving before it is streamed, or the streamed version is not the signed-off one.
  • No checksum. Without one, the question "is this the database we signed off" has no answer.
  • Assembly compressed to hours. Stream-out on a die this size takes real time, and rushing it is how a merge error is missed.

Takes2ww0–w2 of the stage

Why it exists

Re-run full-chip physical verification on the released database—not on the one signoff checked, but on the exact bytes going to the mask shop.

Between the signoff run and the released database sit stream-out, macro merge and possibly a late fix. Each is a chance to introduce something. This re-run is short, expensive in compute and non-negotiable: it is the only check that the thing being released is the thing that was verified.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Released database from TO-01
  • Verification decks from PDK-10
  • Signoff results from SO-03
  • Waiver list from SO-10
  • Compute capacity for full-chip runs

  • Checksums confirmed identical between verified and released

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

w0w1w2

Main sequence

124

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Verification setup on the released database Verification results on the released database 0.5w
2 Full-chip DRC re-run Full-chip DRC re-run results 0.75w
3 Density and fill re-checkruns in parallel Density and fill confirmation 0.5w
4 LVS and antenna re-run LVS and antenna re-run results 0.75w
5 Checksum confirmation against the released databaseruns in parallel Checksum confirmation record 0.5w

Step 5 sounds pedantic and prevents the worst class of error. Verifying one database and releasing another has happened on real programs, and the only defense is confirming the checksum of what was verified against the checksum of what was sent.

Watch out for

  • Skipped because signoff was clean. Signoff checked a different database, and the difference between them is exactly what this run exists to catch.
  • Run on the signoff database rather than the released one. That repeats the earlier check and proves nothing new.
  • Compute capacity unavailable. A full-chip run takes days and needs to be scheduled, not requested.
  • New violations discovered with no time to fix. Which is why SO-03 has to close cleanly rather than nearly.
  • Checksums not compared. Verifying one file and releasing another is a documented failure mode with a trivial defense.

Takes3ww0–w3 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~7.2 people while it runs

Why it exists

Walk the tapeout checklist—every domain, every entry, evidence attached, owner signed—so the Go / No-Go decision is taken on facts rather than on confidence.

The checklist is the program's collected memory of what has to be true before masks are cut. Its value is entirely in the evidence: an entry ticked because the owner believes it is true is worth nothing, and the difference between a checklist and a ritual is whether anyone reads the attachments.

What it delivers

TO-D2Tapeout checklist with signoff matrix

This activity is the deliverable, and the signoff matrix is what makes accountability explicit.

Needs first

  • Signoff results from SO-02 through SO-11
  • DFT signoff from DFT-08
  • DV closure from DV-12
  • Verification results from TO-02
  • Waiver dispositions from SO-10

Done when

  • Every entry carries evidence, not an assertion
  • Signatures from accountable owners, not proxies
  • Gaps escalated with time to close them

Step 3 runs in parallel because it is where the time goes. Chasing an owner who has not signed, or an entry whose evidence does not exist, is the real work—the checklist itself takes an afternoon.

Watch out for

  • Entries ticked without evidence. A checklist of assertions is a ritual, and it produces confidence rather than information.
  • Signoff by proxy. An entry signed by someone other than the accountable owner has moved the signature without moving the accountability.
  • Checklist assembled at tapeout. It should be maintained across the program; assembling it in the last week means discovering gaps with no time to close them.
  • Domains missing from the checklist. Test, package and reliability entries are easy to omit from a design-centred checklist and expensive to miss.
  • Gaps escalated too late. An unsigned entry three days before the Go / No-Go is a decision the meeting cannot take.
