Step 3 is what gives the Go / No-Go meeting something to decide. An item with a mitigation—a test screen, a software workaround, a bin split—is a different decision from one without, and identifying which is which is this activity's contribution.

Watch out for

  • Items carried without assessment. An open issue nobody classified is a risk being accepted without anyone accepting it.
  • Risk stated qualitatively. "Low risk" gives the decision room nothing; a failure mode, a probability and an affected population gives it a decision.
  • Mitigations not identified. Many silicon risks can be screened at test or worked around in software, and the option is worth knowing before the gate.
  • Test and package items excluded. Risk consolidation that covers only design misses the categories that most often cause a late problem.
  • Acceptance without an owner. An accepted risk with no name against it has nobody watching for it at bring-up.

Why it exists

Hold the Go / No-Go decision—the moment the program commits several million dollars of masks and a quarter of schedule to the design as it stands.

Half a week of activity and one man-month, preceded by three weeks of preparation. That ratio is correct: a gate argued in the room rather than before it is a gate whose outcome depends on who attended. The meeting exists to take a decision, record its conditions and name who owns them.

What it delivers

TO-D4Go / No-Go decision minutes

This activity is the deliverable, and the conditions attached are as important as the decision itself.

Needs first

  • Tapeout checklist from TO-03
  • Risk acceptance record from TO-04
  • Verification results from TO-02
  • Foundry readiness from TECH-05
  • Program schedule position from DEF-08

Done when

  • Decision recorded with conditions and their owners
  • Dissent captured in the minutes
  • Conditions assigned before mask data is released

How it gets there 3 steps · 1 lane

123
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Decision pack presentation — checklist, risks, readiness Decision pack 0.2w

3 Minutes, distribution and condition assignment Minutes and condition assignments 0.1w

Step 2 captures dissent deliberately. The objection nobody minuted is the one that resurfaces at first silicon with nothing to point at, and recording it costs a line.

Watch out for

  • Decision taken because the date arrived. A gate that cannot say no is not a gate, and the organization learns that quickly.
  • Conditions accepted verbally. A Go granted "subject to" something unrecorded is an unconditional Go.
  • Wrong people in the room. The decision needs someone who can say no and someone who owns the consequence, and both have to attend.
  • Dissent unrecorded. It is the cheapest insurance available and it is routinely omitted.
  • Material presented for the first time in the room. A pack circulated on the day produces a decision based on whoever speaks most confidently.

Step 1's layer selection has to be exact. A layer released with FEOL that later needs a fix cannot be fixed in the BEOL window, and a layer held back that the mask shop needed delays the whole set.

Watch out for

TO-08BEOL design fix window — metal-layer ECOs and late fixes while FEOL masks are being cut

Takes4ww2–w6 of the stage

OwnerPhysical design leadSignoff lead approves

Why it exists

Use the four weeks between the two mask releases to make metal-layer fixes—the last window in which a design change is possible without a new front-end mask set.

This window is the reason the releases are split. FEOL masks are being cut and cannot change; BEOL is still open, and any fix implementable in metal can still be made. It is a genuine and finite opportunity, and it closes on a date.

What it delivers

TO-D6BEOL ECO log covering the fix window

This activity is the deliverable, and the log is what makes the BEOL database traceable.

Needs first

  • Released database from TO-01
  • Late findings from bring-up preparation, verification and signoff
  • Spare cell and metal-only strategy from PD-14
  • Go / No-Go conditions from TO-05
  • Equivalence methodology from SO-09

Done when

  • Every fix implementable in metal, none requiring base layers
  • Combined database verified, not only individual fixes
  • Window closed on its date, not extended

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w2w3w4w5w6

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Fix window scope and admission rules Fix window scope and admission rules 0.5w
2 Metal-layer ECO implementation Implemented metal-layer ECOs 1.5w
3 Fix prioritization and risk assessmentruns in parallel Fix prioritization and risk record 1w
4 ECO verification per fix Per-fix verification results 1w
5 Equivalence and consistency check per fixruns in parallel Per-fix equivalence and consistency results 1w
6 Window close and BEOL database freeze Frozen BEOL database 1w

Step 1 has to be strict. Every late fix carries risk, and a window with no admission rules fills with changes that individually look safe and collectively make the BEOL database something nobody has verified as a whole.

Watch out for

  • Window used as general contingency. Fixes admitted without rules accumulate into a database that differs from the verified one in ways nobody assessed as a whole.
  • Fix requiring base layers. If PD-14's spare cell strategy was not put in place, the fix cannot be made in metal and the window is useless.
  • Verification per fix but not in combination. Individually correct changes can interact, and the combined database needs a check of its own.
  • Window extended. BEOL mask release has a date; extending the window pushes the whole mask set and with it wafer start.
  • Equivalence skipped for speed. A metal ECO can change function, and the only detector is an equivalence run.

Why it exists

Re-verify the metal stack after the fix window—DRC, LVS, antenna, density on the changed layers—before the back-end data is released.

The BEOL database is not the one that was signed off. It carries the fix window's changes, and every one of them touched routing. This re-verification is what makes the BEOL release as trustworthy as the FEOL one, and it has to fit inside the window's tail.

What it delivers

Step 1 decides between a targeted re-run and a full one. Targeted is faster and risks missing an interaction; full is safe and may not fit the window. The scope decision has to be made on what the fixes actually touched.

Watch out for

  • Scope too narrow. A targeted re-run that misses an interaction between two fixes releases a violation into the mask set.
  • Timing not re-confirmed. Metal ECOs change delay, and a fix that breaks timing has replaced one problem with another.
  • Re-verification not fitting the window. Full-chip runs take days, and a window planned without them cannot accommodate them.
  • LVS skipped because the change was metal-only. Metal changes connectivity, which is exactly what LVS checks.
  • Results arriving after the release. Verifying after submission is verifying something already committed to masks.

Why it exists

EUV mask sets at this node are slow and expensive to produce, and a single mask failing inspection means a remake measured in weeks. The program's role is oversight rather than execution: confirm the data was accepted, review inspection results and escalate when a layer slips.

Step 5 is where a schedule is saved or lost. A mask defect can sometimes be repaired, sometimes waived as non-printing, and sometimes requires a remake—and the three outcomes differ by weeks.

Watch out for

  • Mask defect requiring a remake. Weeks of schedule, and the program has no way to accelerate the replacement.
  • Inspection criteria not understood. Whether a defect is printing depends on layer and position, and the disposition needs design input the foundry does not have.
  • Critical layers not prioritized. Mask shops write in a sequence, and the layers on the critical path can sometimes be pulled forward if anyone asks.
  • Data preparation rejected late. MDP problems surface days after submission and consume the schedule silently.
  • No visibility into progress. A seven-week activity with no status reporting means the first news is either completion or a delay.

Step 2 decides the split strategy—whether all wafers run the same process conditions or some are deliberately skewed. Splits cost wafers and buy information about process sensitivity that no simulation can provide.

Watch out for

  • Start delayed after masks are ready. Every day is a day at the far end of a schedule with no recovery mechanism.
  • Wafer quantity too small. Bring-up, characterization, qualification and customer samples all draw from this lot, and running short means a second lot and a quarter.
  • No process splits. A single condition gives one data point; splits reveal process sensitivity while there is still time to act on it.
  • Hot-lot status not invoked. The priority negotiated in TECH-05 has to be requested at start, not assumed.
  • Starting material not specified. Substrate type and specification affect device behavior, and defaulting is how an unexpected variable enters.

Step 5's date is the one that matters. The masks do not need to exist at wafer start; they need to exist before the lots reach the first metal layer, and that is several weeks of margin the split created deliberately.

Watch out for

  • Masks late against metallization. Lots stop mid-process, which wastes fab capacity and is harder to recover from than a late start.
  • Parallelism assumed rather than tracked. The split only pays off if the BEOL schedule is actively compared against the front-end progress.
  • Defect disposition slower on BEOL layers. There are more of them, and a per-layer process that worked for FEOL can bottleneck here.
  • Metallization start estimate stale. The masks are needed against a moving date, and planning against the original estimate is planning against fiction.
  • No priority on the first metal layers. They are needed first and can often be written first if anyone asks.

Step 5 needs a standing decision framework. When a lot goes out of control limits the choices are scrap, rework, continue at risk or split—and making that decision in the moment, without a framework, tends to produce whichever answer is least disruptive rather than best.

Watch out for

  • Excursion response improvised. Without a framework the decision defaults to whatever is least disruptive rather than what is best for the lot.
  • Inline data not reviewed by the program. The foundry monitors its process; only the design team can say whether a deviation matters for this device.
  • Hot-lot priority lost mid-flow. Priority granted at start can quietly lapse, and nobody notices until the cycle time slips.
  • Scrap decision taken too late. A lot continuing through eight weeks of processing after a fatal excursion wastes capacity that a second lot needed.
  • No second lot in reserve. If the first lot is lost, having no material started means restarting the whole cycle.

Watch out for

  • Monitoring every step equally. Attention spread evenly finds nothing; the design's sensitivities decide where to look.
  • Data reviewed only by the foundry. Process control answers whether the line is in control, not whether this device is affected.
  • Excursions detected after the affected step. Once the lot has moved on, the response options narrow sharply.
  • Defects classified but not attributed. Knowing the count without the source gives no basis for a corrective action.
  • Monitoring stopping at front-end exit. Back-end defects affect yield as much and are often less well monitored.

Step 4 is where the value is. A threshold voltage 30 mV from target changes timing across the whole design, and knowing that before parts arrive lets bring-up be planned around it rather than surprised by it.

Watch out for

  • PCM data not reviewed until parts arrive. It answers process questions weeks earlier and costs nothing extra to read.
  • Comparison against target only. The design was built against models; comparing against the model is what predicts silicon behavior.
  • Variability ignored. Across-wafer parameter spread predicts the bin distribution, and the mean alone does not.
  • Split lots analyzed together. If splits were run, aggregating them averages away exactly the information the splits were for.
  • No link to the test chip results. TC-07 correlated models against silicon; this data either confirms that correlation or contradicts it.

Step 4 can accept a lot that is out of specification. On an engineering lot the priority is usually silicon in the lab rather than perfect silicon, and accepting a marginal lot with the deviation documented is often the right call—but it must be a call.

Watch out for

  • Acceptance by default. A lot released without a decision has been accepted by nobody, and the deviation is discovered later with no record.
  • Criteria not agreed in advance. Negotiating acceptance criteria after the data exists favors whoever is more motivated.
  • Marginal lot rejected on principle. On an engineering lot, silicon in the lab is usually worth more than a lot within every limit.
  • Deviations not documented. A parameter out of specification affects bring-up interpretation, and the bring-up team has to know.
  • Disposition delayed. Every day the lot sits undispositioned is a day of bring-up not happening.

PKGD-01Package architecture selection — 2.5D interposer type, organic substrate, layer count

Takes8ww0–w8 of the stage
Costs10.0 M/M~5.4 people while it runs
OwnerPackage architectChief architect approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Choose the package architecture—interposer type, substrate construction, layer count, body size—and commit to it, because everything from bump pitch to assembly capacity follows.

This decision has the same character as the monolithic-versus-chiplet call in ARCH-02: it looks like an engineering choice and it is a supply chain commitment. A 2.5D silicon interposer is a different supplier, a different capacity queue and a different cost structure from an organic bridge, and switching later is not practical.

What it delivers

PKGD-D1Package architecture specification

This activity is the deliverable, and it is a supply chain commitment as much as a technical one.

Needs first

  • Package architecture assumption from DEF-01
  • Partitioning and die count from ARCH-02
  • Backend supply chain findings from TECH-09
  • Bandwidth and HBM requirements from DEF-05
  • Cost model from DEF-04

Done when

  • Architecture selected with capacity indicated, not assumed
  • At least two options evaluated and costed end to end
  • Specification issued before bump planning starts

3 Capability and capacity screen per optionruns in parallel Architecture options with capability assessment · Capacity screen per option 1.5w
4 Substrate construction and layer count study Substrate construction study 2w

Step 3 can eliminate an option outright. Advanced interposer capacity is allocated quarters ahead to a small number of customers, and an architecture the program cannot get capacity for is not an option however good it looks technically.

Watch out for

  • Architecture chosen without capacity. Advanced packaging capacity is scarce and allocated far ahead; a technically ideal option with no allocation is not an option.
  • Decision taken after the bump map. Package architecture constrains bump pitch and field, and deciding afterwards means renegotiating the die.
  • Cost compared on the package alone. Interposer, substrate, assembly yield and test all differ per architecture, and comparing one line misleads.
  • Thermal requirement not in the selection. Package thermal resistance is architecture-dependent and sets the achievable power envelope.
  • Single option evaluated. Without an alternative the program has no negotiating position and no fallback if capacity is refused.

PKGD-02Bump map, pitch and power-ground planning with physical design

Takes10ww8–w18 of the stage

Why it exists

Negotiate the bump map with physical design—pitch, count, power-to-signal ratio, position—until both the die and the package can build what the other needs.

The bump field is where two design teams share one constraint. The die wants bumps where its logic is; the package wants them where its escape routing can reach; and the power delivery requirement takes most of the field regardless. Convergence takes iteration, and the iteration has to finish before PD-04 freezes.

What it delivers

PKGD-D2Bump map and interposer / RDL database

The bump map half of the deliverable; PKGD-03 supplies the interposer routing.

Needs first

  • Package architecture from PKGD-01
  • Bump budget and intent from ARCH-08
  • Power envelope and delivery requirement from PD-03
  • Interface lane counts from ARCH-04
  • Substrate layer count from PKGD-04

Done when

  • Escape feasibility confirmed on the substrate, not only on the die
  • Power-to-signal ratio meets the delivery requirement
  • Map converged before the PD-04 freeze date

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w8w10w12w14w16w18

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Bump pitch and field definition against the architecture Bump pitch and field definition 2w
2 Power-to-signal ratio derivation from the power envelope Power-to-signal ratio 1.5w
3 Signal bump assignment per interfaceruns in parallel Signal bump assignment per interface 2w
4 Escape feasibility check against the substrate Escape feasibility findings 2w
5 Die-side placement iteration with physical designruns in parallel Die-side placement iteration record 2w
6 Bump map convergence and handoff Converged bump map 4.5w

Step 4 is the check that usually forces the iteration. A bump assignment that works on the die can require escape routing the substrate cannot provide at its layer count, and finding that early is what keeps the map from being redone after freeze.

Watch out for

  • Bump map converged on the die side only. A map that cannot escape on the substrate has to be redone, and by then the die may be placed around it.
  • Power bumps reduced to fit signals. The interfaces then work and the die cannot be fed, which SIPI-04 finds much later.
  • Pitch chosen from the previous program. Pitch depends on the interposer technology and the assembly process, both of which may have changed.
  • Signal assignment ignoring channel quality. Which bump a high-speed signal uses affects its escape path and its crosstalk exposure.
  • Iteration continuing past the freeze date. PD-04 and the substrate order both depend on this closing on time.

Takes14ww16–w30 of the stage

Why it exists

Route the interposer and its redistribution layers—the silicon layer that carries the die-to-HBM channels and everything else the substrate cannot.

On a 2.5D part the interposer carries the highest-density and highest-performance connections in the package. HBM channels alone run to thousands of nets at fine pitch, and their routing quality decides whether the memory interface trains at speed.

The interposer half of the deliverable—the routed silicon layer itself.

  • Power delivery requirement from PD-03
  • SI requirements from SIPI-07

  • Reference planes continuous under high-speed channels

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 2 dominates because HBM channels are numerous, fine-pitch and length-sensitive at once. Getting them routed with matched lengths and clean references is most of the interposer's difficulty and most of its schedule.

Watch out for

  • HBM channel lengths unmatched. Skew across a wide parallel interface eats the training margin, and the failure appears at bring-up as a memory that will not train at speed.
  • Reference plane discontinuities. A channel crossing a plane split has an impedance discontinuity, and on HBM there are thousands of channels to get right.
  • Interposer power distribution underprovisioned. Current for two HBM stacks and the die passes through the interposer, and its resistance is part of the IR budget.
  • Manufacturability checked late. Interposer rules differ from die rules, and a design that violates them is a supplier rejection rather than a warning.
  • Routing started before the bump map converges. Every bump change is an interposer rework, and the rework is expensive at this density.

Why it exists

Design the substrate—stack-up, escape routing, power planes, package DRC—the organic carrier that connects the interposer to the board.

The substrate is the part with the longest lead time and the least flexibility once ordered. Its layer count is fixed by escape routing needs and its cost scales with it, so the design converges on the smallest stack-up that can carry the escape—a trade made once and lived with.

Step 1 is the cost decision. Every substrate layer adds cost across the product's lifetime, and the layer count is set by whether the escape routing fits—which is not known until step 2 is attempted. The two steps iterate.

Watch out for

  • Layer count set before escape is attempted. A stack-up chosen for cost that cannot carry the escape has to be increased, and the cost model was built on the smaller number.
  • Supplier rules obtained late. Substrate rules vary by supplier and technology, and designing to generic rules produces a design one supplier can build.
  • Power planes fragmented by escape routing. Escape vias perforate the planes, and the resulting current path is what SIPI-03 will analyze.
  • Ball map not agreed with the board. The substrate's board-side interface is the board's problem too, and changing it late affects both.
  • Design released before DRC closes. A supplier rejection costs weeks against a twenty-week lead time.

Why it exists

Route the package for signal integrity—length matching, reference continuity, via design, crosstalk separation—so the channels can carry what the interfaces need.

Package routing is where high-speed channels are made or ruined. A via with a long stub, a trace crossing a plane split, or a differential pair routed without its partner all cost margin that the PHY then has to make up. SIPI-07 will measure the result; this activity is what determines it.

The signal half of the deliverable—the design intent SIPI then verifies.

  • Channel budgets from AMS-03 and ARCH-04
  • SI requirements and targets from SIPI-07
  • Interface compliance requirements
  • Supplier via and drill capability

Done when

  • Channel budget explicitly allocated between die, package and board
  • Via stubs managed rather than accepted

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Channel budget allocation to the package Channel budget allocation to the package 1.5w
2 Length matching and skew control per interface Length-matched routing per interface 2.5w
3 Reference plane continuity and return path designruns in parallel Reference plane continuity design 2w
4 Via structure design and stub management Via structures with managed stubs 2w
5 Crosstalk separation and shieldingruns in parallel Crosstalk separation plan 2w

Step 4 is the one most often underestimated. Via stubs resonate at frequencies that matter for the fastest interfaces, and back-drilling or blind via structures are decisions with cost implications that belong to the substrate design rather than to routing.

Watch out for

  • Via stubs unmanaged. They resonate in band for the fastest interfaces, and the remedy—back-drilling or blind vias—is a substrate cost decision made too late.
  • Length matching without reference continuity. Matched traces over a split plane have matched delay and mismatched impedance.
  • Channel budget not allocated. Die, package and board each consume part of the loss budget, and without allocation each assumes the others left room.
  • Crosstalk managed by spacing alone. On a dense substrate there is no spare space, and the answer is usually reference and via design instead.
  • Review after the substrate is released. SI findings then have nowhere to go except into the PHY's margin.

Takes9ww28–w37 of the stage

Why it exists

Design the package power delivery—plane structure, via arrays, decoupling footprints—knowing that its electrical closure belongs to SIPI rather than to this activity.

The package sits between the die's instantaneous current demand and the board's slower supply. Its planes, vias and decoupling determine the impedance in the mid-frequency band where neither the die's on-chip decap nor the board's bulk capacitors help. Designing it is here; proving it works is co-verification.

What it delivers

PKGD-D4Package electrical design intent and model handoff to co-verification

The power half of the deliverable, handed to SIPI for closure.

Needs first

  • Substrate stack-up from PKGD-04
  • Power delivery requirement from PD-03
  • Bump and ball power assignment from PKGD-02
  • Impedance targets from SIPI-03
  • Supplier capability for via arrays and mounting

Done when

  • Decoupling footprints placed for loop inductance, not convenience
  • Plane perforation analyzed rather than assumed away
  • Design intent handed over in a form SIPI can analyze

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w28w30w32w34w36w37

1246

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Package PDN topology and plane allocation Package PDN topology and plane allocation 2w
2 Power via array design and current capability Power via array design 2w
3 Decoupling capacitor footprint placementruns in parallel Decoupling footprint placement 1.5w
4 Plane perforation and current path management Plane perforation and current path analysis 2w
5 Interposer to substrate power transitionruns in parallel Interposer to substrate power transition design 1.5w
6 PDN design intent handoff to co-verification PDN design intent handoff 3w

Step 3 places footprints rather than choosing values. Which capacitors go where is decided by <code>SIPI-05</code> against the impedance target; the package's job is to provide mounting positions close enough to the current draw for those choices to be available.

Watch out for

  • Decoupling footprints too far from the current draw. Mounting position determines the loop inductance, and a capacitor mounted far away is a capacitor that does not help.
  • Plane perforation ignored. Escape vias perforate power planes, and the remaining current path can be far worse than the plane suggests.
  • Via array sized for DC only. Transient current is what the package has to supply, and DC sizing understates the requirement.
  • Closure assumed to be someone else's problem. If the design intent is not analysable, SIPI cannot close it and the iteration comes back here.
  • Interposer to substrate transition overlooked. The power path crosses two interfaces, and the transition is where its resistance concentrates.

PKGD-07Thermal and mechanical simulation — warpage, co-planarity, TIM, lid

Takes12ww20–w32 of the stage
Costs12.0 M/M~4.3 people while it runs
OwnerThermal engineerDie power liaison approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Simulate the thermal and mechanical behavior of the package—heat path, warpage, co-planarity, TIM and lid—before any of it is built.

A package at this power dissipates hundreds of watts through a stack of materials with different expansion coefficients. The thermal path decides the achievable power envelope; the mechanical behavior decides whether the assembly survives reflow. Both are simulated here and measured on real vehicles in PTV.

What it delivers

PKGD-D5Thermal and mechanical (warpage) simulation reports

This activity is the deliverable, and PTV is what validates it.

Needs first

  • Package architecture from PKGD-01
  • Power map and hotspot data from PD-03 and SYN-06
  • Material properties from the supplier
  • Assembly reflow profile from PKGD-10
  • Thermal requirements from DEF-03

Done when

  • Thermal simulated against the real power map, not uniform power
  • Warpage simulated across the full reflow profile
  • Findings handed to PTV as vehicle requirements

How it gets there 7 steps · 2 lanes

w20w23w26w29w32

Main sequence

1257

In parallel

346
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Thermal model construction — die, interposer, substrate, lid Thermal model of the package stack 2w
2 Steady-state thermal simulation and Rjc estimation Steady-state thermal results and Rjc estimate 2.5w
3 Hotspot and transient thermal analysisruns in parallel Hotspot and transient analysis 2w
4 TIM selection and interface resistance studyruns in parallel TIM selection and interface study 2w
5 Warpage simulation across the reflow profile Warpage simulation across reflow 3w
6 Mechanical stress and co-planarity analysisruns in parallel Mechanical stress and co-planarity results 2w
7 Thermal and mechanical design recommendations Thermal and mechanical design recommendations 4.5w

Step 5 predicts what <code>PTV-07</code> will measure. Warpage across the reflow profile is the mechanism behind most 2.5D assembly failures, and simulating it before the vehicles are built is what makes the vehicle results interpretable rather than merely surprising.

Watch out for

  • Thermal simulated at uniform power. An accelerator's power is concentrated in the compute clusters, and uniform assumptions understate the hotspot badly.
  • Warpage simulated at room temperature only. The failure happens at reflow peak, and the room-temperature number says nothing about it.
  • TIM performance taken from the datasheet. Interface resistance depends on bond line thickness and pressure, both of which are assembly properties.
  • Material properties assumed. Substrate and underfill properties vary by supplier and lot, and simulation is only as good as the inputs.
  • Results not fed into the vehicle plan. Simulation identifies which risks to measure, and a vehicle plan built independently measures the wrong things.

Tell PTV what the vehicles have to measure—which risks, which structures, which conditions—early enough that the vehicles can be designed, built and stressed before wafer-out.

The test vehicle program has a fifty-two week window and a hard gate at product wafer-out. Its requirements have to arrive while there is time to act on them, which is why this activity sits at week ten of a fifty-two week stage rather than after the package design is finished.

Step 1 has to be done on an incomplete package design, which is uncomfortable and necessary. The architecture is known, the materials are known and the assembly process is broadly known—enough to say what will be risky, which is all the vehicle plan needs.

Watch out for

  • Requirements issued after the package design completes. The vehicle program then cannot finish before wafer-out, and the gate is missed.
  • Risks identified from the design rather than from experience. The failures that matter are the ones previous programs hit, and they are rarely visible in a design review.
  • Electrical vehicle omitted. Daisy-chain continuity and assembly yield are as important as thermal and mechanical, and they need their own vehicle.
  • Conditions unspecified. A vehicle measured at the wrong temperature or reflow profile answers a question nobody asked.
  • No feedback loop defined. The vehicle results have to change something, and the mechanism for that has to be agreed up front.

Watch out for

  • Order placed after wafer-out is committed. A twenty-week substrate against a fixed wafer-out date means wafers waiting for a package.
  • Supplier rules obtained after design starts. A substrate designed to generic rules may be unbuildable by the chosen supplier.
  • Capacity assumed. Advanced substrate capacity is constrained, and a supplier who can build it may not be able to build it when needed.

  • Lead time quoted without a commitment. An indicative lead time is not a date, and the difference appears when the schedule depends on it.

Step 5 runs in parallel and can send the design back. Suppliers review for manufacturability against their own process, and their acceptance is what makes the order placeable—a design frozen internally and rejected by the supplier has not frozen anything.

Watch out for

  • Freeze slipping. Twenty weeks of substrate lead time follow it, and the delay lands after wafer-out where nothing can absorb it.
  • Frozen before co-verification completes. A SIPI finding after freeze is a package change against an order already placed.
  • Supplier acceptance assumed. A design frozen internally and rejected on manufacturability has not frozen anything except the schedule.
  • Tooling data incomplete. Manufacturing data is more than the design files, and a missing item stalls the order after it is placed.
  • Late bump map change from the die side. PD-04 has to be frozen first, and a die-side change after this point is extremely expensive.

17 PTV · Package Test Vehicle (CPI / TTV)

PTV-01Test vehicle strategy and risk item definition — CPI, warpage, thermal, ULK/BEOL stress

Takes6ww0–w6 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~3.6 people while it runs
OwnerPTV leadOSAT liaison approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Decide which package risks the vehicles will actually retire—chip-package interaction, warpage, thermal, assembly yield—and what evidence would count as retiring them.

The vehicle program has one shot and a hard gate at product wafer-out. Its value depends entirely on measuring the risks that would otherwise be discovered on real dies, and a vehicle plan built from what is easy to measure rather than from what is risky produces reassurance instead of information.

What it delivers

PTV-D1Test vehicle plan and risk coverage matrix

This activity is the deliverable, and the matrix is what every later result is reported against.

Needs first

  • Vehicle requirements from PKGD-08
  • Thermal and warpage predictions from PKGD-07
  • CPI and ULK risk from TECH-03
  • Assembly process direction from PKGD-10
  • Wafer-out forecast from FAB-09

Done when

  • Every carried risk has defined retiring evidence
  • Programme schedule closes before the wafer-out gate
  • Plan reflects prioritized risk rather than measurement convenience

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w0w2w4w6

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Risk intake from package design and previous programs Risk intake from package design and previous programs 1w
2 Risk prioritization against product impact Package risk list with product impact 1.5w
3 Evidence definition — what would retire each riskruns in parallel Evidence definition per risk 1.5w
4 Vehicle type allocation per risk Vehicle type allocation 1.5w
5 Schedule feasibility against the wafer-out gateruns in parallel Schedule feasibility finding 1w
6 Vehicle plan and risk coverage matrix Test vehicle plan and risk coverage matrix 2w

Step 5 checks the whole program against one date. Fifty-two weeks of vehicle work has to finish before product wafers come out at week 98, and if the arithmetic does not close then the plan has to shrink rather than the gate move.

Watch out for

  • Plan built from what is measurable. Easy measurements produce data; the risk list produces information, and the two are not the same set.
  • Schedule not checked against the gate. A fifty-two week program that finishes after wafer-out has validated nothing in time to matter.
  • Evidence undefined. Without agreeing in advance what would retire a risk, the results become an argument rather than a conclusion.
  • Previous-program failures not consulted. The package failure modes that recur are known, and they are the ones worth measuring.
  • Vehicle count driven by budget rather than by risk. Fewer vehicles means fewer risks retired, and the trade should be explicit.

Why it exists

Design the mechanical test vehicle—dummy die stack, representative bump array, substrate coupon—that carries the package's mechanical behavior without any of its electronics.

The MTV exists to be stressed. Its die are blank, its interposer is representative and its purpose is to reproduce the mechanical stack faithfully enough that warpage, co-planarity and CPI measured on it predict what the product will do.

What it delivers

PTV-D2MTV, TTV and daisy-chain vehicle designs

The mechanical vehicle of the three.

Needs first

  • Vehicle plan from PTV-01
  • Package architecture from PKGD-01
  • Mechanical predictions from PKGD-07
  • Die thickness and bump specification from PD-04
  • Material specifications from suppliers

Done when

  • Mechanically representative in the dimensions that drive warpage
  • Measurement features integrated, not added externally
  • Released against a settled product stack

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w5w7w9w11w13w14

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Mechanical representativeness requirements Mechanical representativeness requirements 1.5w
2 Dummy die and die stack design Dummy die and stack design 2w
3 Bump array design representative of the productruns in parallel Representative bump array 2w
4 Interposer and substrate coupon design Interposer and substrate coupon design 2.5w

Step 1 defines what "representative" means for mechanics, which is narrower than it sounds. Die thickness, bump metallurgy, underfill and substrate construction matter; the circuitry does not. Getting that distinction right is what makes the MTV cheap.

Watch out for

  • Vehicle not mechanically representative. Different die thickness or underfill produces warpage that does not predict the product's.
  • Measurement features omitted. A vehicle with no reference marks or strain features can be measured externally and not internally.
  • Bump array simplified. Bump density and distribution drive local stress, and a uniform array does not reproduce the product's concentrations.
  • Design released before the product's stack is settled. A vehicle built on an assumption that changes measures the wrong package.
  • Coupon size unrepresentative. Warpage scales with body size, and a smaller coupon understates it.

17 PTV · Package Test Vehicle (CPI / TTV)

PTV-03Thermal test vehicle (TTV) design — embedded heater array and RTD sensor placement

Takes9ww5–w14 of the stage
Costs8.0 M/M~3.9 people while it runs
OwnerThermal engineerOSAT liaison approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Design the thermal test vehicle—embedded heaters and temperature sensors laid out to match the product's power map—so the package's thermal path can be measured rather than simulated.

A TTV is a die that only makes heat, in the pattern the real die will make it. Uniform heaters measure an average the product will never experience; heaters matched to the compute cluster distribution measure the hotspot that decides the achievable power envelope.

What it delivers

PTV-D2MTV, TTV and daisy-chain vehicle designs

The thermal vehicle of the three.

Needs first

  • Vehicle plan from PTV-01
  • Power map and hotspot distribution from PD-03 and SYN-06
  • Thermal predictions from PKGD-07
  • Package architecture from PKGD-01
  • Sensor and heater process capability

Done when

  • Heater zones match the product's real power distribution
  • Sensors placed to see gradients, not only a peak
  • Calibration approach defined before build

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w5w7w9w11w13w14

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Power map translation into heater zones Heater zone map from the power distribution 1.5w
2 Heater array design and drive requirements Heater array design and drive requirements 2w
3 RTD and temperature sensor placementruns in parallel Sensor placement plan 2w
4 TTV die and interposer integration TTV die and interposer integration 2.5w
5 Calibration approach for the sensorsruns in parallel Sensor calibration approach 1.5w
6 TTV design release Released TTV design 3w

Step 3 decides what the vehicle can see. Sensors placed only at the die center measure a number the datasheet can quote; sensors distributed across the zones measure the gradient that determines whether the hotspot is survivable.

Watch out for

  • Uniform heaters. They measure an average power distribution the product will never have, and the hotspot goes unmeasured.
  • Sensors too few or badly placed. Thermal gradients are what matter, and a single center sensor cannot see one.
  • Sensor calibration not planned. An uncalibrated RTD gives a relative number, and thermal resistance needs an absolute one.
  • Heater drive capability underspecified. Reproducing hundreds of watts through a test vehicle needs real power delivery, and the setup has to supply it.
  • Power map taken from an early estimate. The distribution changes through implementation, and a TTV built on the architecture-era map measures the wrong hotspot.

17 PTV · Package Test Vehicle (CPI / TTV)

PTV-04Daisy-chain electrical vehicle design — interconnect continuity and bump yield structures

Takes8ww6–w14 of the stage
Costs6.0 M/M~3.3 people while it runs
OwnerPackage test engineerYield engineer approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Design the daisy-chain electrical vehicle—continuity structures through every interconnect level—so assembly yield and interconnect integrity can be measured electrically.

Daisy chains turn assembly quality into a resistance measurement. Every bump, every via and every ball becomes part of a chain that either conducts or does not, which makes an otherwise invisible assembly process observable and quantifiable.

What it delivers

PTV-D2MTV, TTV and daisy-chain vehicle designs

The electrical vehicle of the three.

Needs first

  • Vehicle plan from PTV-01
  • Bump map and interconnect structure from PKGD-02 and PKGD-03
  • Assembly process from PKGD-10
  • Substrate ball map from PKGD-04
  • Measurement capability at the OSAT

Done when

  • Chains segmented finely enough to localize a failure
  • Every interconnect level covered by at least one structure
  • Measurement possible with equipment the OSAT actually has

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w6w8w10w12w14

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Interconnect level inventory — bump, TSV, via, ball Interconnect level inventory 1w
2 Daisy chain topology and segmentation design Daisy chain topology with segmentation 2w
3 Kelvin structures for resistance measurementruns in parallel Kelvin resistance structures 1.5w
4 Chain-to-location mapping for defect localization Chain-to-location mapping 1.5w
5 Probe and measurement access designruns in parallel Probe and measurement access design 1.5w
6 Daisy-chain vehicle design release Released daisy-chain vehicle design 3.5w

Step 2's segmentation decides the diagnostic resolution. One long chain says whether the assembly worked; many short segments say where it failed, and the difference is what turns a yield number into a corrective action.

Watch out for

  • Chains too long. A single break makes the whole chain open, and the yield number carries no information about where or why.
  • No Kelvin structures. Two-wire resistance includes the probe path, and marginal interconnects are exactly where the difference matters.
  • Chain-to-location mapping omitted. A failing chain that cannot be located gives no basis for a process change.
  • Not all interconnect levels covered. Bump, TSV, via and ball each fail differently, and a vehicle covering only bumps misses the rest.
  • Measurement access not planned. A vehicle that can only be measured with equipment the OSAT does not have is a vehicle that is not measured.

Why it exists

Assemble the vehicles at the OSAT across a designed experiment—bond force, reflow profile, underfill, cure—so the assembly process window is measured rather than assumed.

The process window is what ASSY will run to. Establishing it needs deliberate variation: units assembled at the edges of each parameter, not just at nominal, so that the window's boundaries are known rather than the center being confirmed.

Step 6 is what makes the DOE usable. Every unit has to be traceable to the exact conditions it was assembled under, and an assembly traveler that records the lot but not the condition turns a designed experiment back into a single build.

Watch out for

  • Assembly at nominal only. That confirms the center and says nothing about the boundaries, which is where production will occasionally operate.
  • Condition traceability lost. Units that cannot be attributed to their assembly conditions turn the DOE into an expensive single build.
  • DOE too large for the unit count. Varying every parameter needs units the build did not produce, and an under-powered DOE gives ambiguous results.
  • Inline inspection omitted. Assembly defects found only at final characterization cannot be attributed to a process step.
  • OSAT running its standard process. The point is deliberate variation, and an assembler defaulting to its recipe produces no window information.

17 PTV · Package Test Vehicle (CPI / TTV)

PTV-07Warpage and co-planarity measurement across the reflow profile (shadow moiré)

Takes7ww38–w45 of the stage
Costs8.0 M/M~5.0 people while it runs
OwnerMechanical engineerQuality engineer approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Measure warpage and co-planarity across the reflow profile—not at room temperature, but at every point in the thermal cycle where the package deforms.

Warpage is the mechanism behind most 2.5D assembly failures. A package flat at room temperature can bow by more than a hundred microns at reflow peak, opening joints that then re-close as it cools—leaving a unit that looks fine and has intermittent connections.

What it delivers

PTV-D4Warpage and co-planarity data across the reflow profile

This activity is the deliverable, and the reflow-profile part is what distinguishes it from a room-temperature check.

Needs first

  • Assembled units with condition traceability from PTV-06
  • Warpage simulation from PKGD-07
  • Reflow profile from PKGD-10
  • Measurement equipment and capability
  • Co-planarity specification from the assembly requirements

Done when

  • Warpage measured across the full reflow profile
  • Simulation correlated against measurement
  • Results attributed to assembly conditions

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w38w40w42w44w45

Main sequence

1236

In parallel

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Measurement setup — shadow moiré or equivalent Measurement setup and method 1w
2 Room-temperature baseline across units Room-temperature warpage baseline 1.5w
3 Warpage measurement across the reflow profile Warpage across the reflow profile 2w
4 Co-planarity and ball flatness measurementruns in parallel Co-planarity and ball flatness results 1.5w
5 Condition-to-warpage correlation from the DOEruns in parallel Condition correlation from the DOE 1.5w
6 Comparison against the PKGD-07 simulation Simulation comparison 2.5w

Step 6 is what makes the measurement reusable. A warpage number is one package; a validated simulation model predicts the next one, and correlating the two is what turns a measurement into a capability.

Watch out for

  • Measured only at room temperature. The failure occurs at reflow peak, and the room-temperature number is not predictive of it.
  • Simulation comparison skipped. Without correlation the model stays unvalidated, and the next package has to be measured from scratch.
  • Co-planarity ignored. Ball flatness determines whether the package mounts to the board reliably, and it is a separate property from warpage.
  • Too few units to see condition effects. Warpage varies unit to unit, and distinguishing a condition effect from noise needs population.
  • Results not linked to assembly conditions. Knowing the warpage without knowing which condition produced it gives no basis for a window.

PTV-08Chip-package interaction stress evaluation — low-k / ULK crack, bump and BEOL integrity

Takes11ww37–w48 of the stage
Costs14.0 M/M~5.5 people while it runs
OwnerReliability engineerDie liaison approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Evaluate chip-package interaction—the stress the package puts into the die's low-k dielectric stack, and whether the bumps and back-end metal survive it.

CPI is the failure mode that makes 2.5D packaging risky at advanced nodes. Ultra-low-k dielectrics are mechanically weak, the package expands differently from the silicon, and the resulting stress concentrates exactly where the bumps meet the top metal. It cracks or it does not, and simulation alone is not enough to know.

What it delivers

PTV-D5CPI stress assessment report — ULK, bump and BEOL integrity

This activity is the deliverable, and it is the most consequential result the vehicle program produces.

Needs first

  • Assembled MTV units from PTV-06
  • Die stack and ULK information from TECH-03
  • Warpage results from PTV-07
  • Thermal cycling capability
  • Underfill and material properties

Done when

  • Stress applied to a cycle count that would reveal accumulation
  • Failures cross-sectioned and localized, not only detected
  • Findings delivered before the package design freeze

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w37w40w43w46w48

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 CPI stress evaluation plan and structure selection CPI evaluation plan and structure selection 1.5w
2 Thermal cycling stress application Thermal cycling stress results 3w
3 Bump and BEOL integrity inspectionruns in parallel Bump and BEOL integrity findings 2.5w
4 Low-k and ULK crack detection ULK crack detection results 2.5w
5 Cross-section and failure analysis on affected unitsruns in parallel Cross-section and failure analysis 2w
6 CPI assessment and design implications CPI assessment with design implications 4w

Step 5 is destructive and necessary. Electrical and acoustic methods say something is wrong; only cross-sectioning shows what failed and where, and the design implication depends entirely on which layer cracked.

Watch out for

  • CPI evaluated by simulation alone. Material behavior at these dimensions is not predictable to the accuracy the decision needs.
  • Insufficient thermal cycles. CPI failures accumulate; a short cycle count shows nothing and reassures wrongly.
  • Cross-sectioning skipped. Detection without localization gives no design implication, and the implication is the output that matters.
  • Only nominal units stressed. The DOE's edge conditions are where CPI is most likely, and testing only the center misses it.
  • Findings arriving after package design freezes. A CPI problem needs an underfill, bump or design change, none of which are available after PKGD-11.

Why it exists

Characterize the package's thermal performance—junction-to-case and junction-to-ambient resistance, TIM behavior, hotspot mapping—and correlate it against the simulation.

The thermal path decides the achievable power envelope, and the product is sold on that envelope. Measuring it on a TTV that reproduces the real power distribution is what turns a simulated Rjc into a number the datasheet can carry.

What it delivers

PTV-D6Thermal characterization report with model correlation (Rjc, TIM, hotspot map)

This activity is the deliverable, and the correlation is what makes the model reusable.

  • Sensor calibration approach from PTV-03

  • TIM material options

  • Hotspot mapped rather than averaged
  • Thermal model correlated and updated

Step 4 measures the interface nobody can simulate reliably. TIM performance depends on bond line thickness, pressure and pump-out over time, and the datasheet value is a starting point rather than an answer.

Watch out for

  • TIM performance taken from the datasheet. Bond line thickness and pressure are assembly parameters, and the achieved performance differs from the specification.
  • Hotspot not measured. The average junction temperature is not what limits the part; the hottest zone is.
  • Simulation not correlated. The model then remains unvalidated, and every future thermal question needs another vehicle.
  • Transient response ignored. An accelerator's power is bursty, and the transient behavior determines whether the package can absorb a workload spike.
  • Measured at a single ambient condition. Rja depends on airflow and ambient, and one condition does not characterize the range the product will see.

Takes14ww36–w50 of the stage

Why it exists

Stress the vehicles through board-level reliability—temperature cycling, drop, bend—because the package has to survive being mounted in a system, not only being assembled.

Board-level reliability is where the package meets the customer's manufacturing process. Solder joints crack under thermal cycling, boards flex during handling, and a package that passes component qualification and fails board-level testing is a package the customer cannot use.

What it delivers

PTV-D7Board-level reliability data on vehicles

This activity is the deliverable, and characteristic life is what customers will ask for.

Needs first

  • Assembled units from PTV-06
  • Board-level reliability standards (JEDEC)
  • Customer board and mounting requirements
  • Coupon board design capability
  • Reliability chamber capacity

Done when

  • Testing run to failure, with characteristic life established
  • Coupon boards representative of customer mounting
  • Failure modes identified, not only counted

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

5 Bend and flex testingruns in parallel Bend and flex results 2w

Step 3 runs to failure rather than to a pass criterion. Characteristic life—the cycle count at which a defined fraction fails—is what a customer needs to assess the package in their system, and a pass at a fixed cycle count does not provide it.

Watch out for

  • Testing to a pass criterion rather than to failure. A pass tells the customer nothing about margin; characteristic life does.
  • Coupon board unrepresentative. Board thickness and pad design affect solder joint stress, and a test board unlike the customer's predicts poorly.
  • Started too late to finish. Temperature cycling to failure takes months, and it is the longest test in the vehicle program.
  • Failure modes not analyzed. Knowing units failed at a cycle count without knowing how gives no route to improvement.
  • Only one mounting condition. Different customers mount differently, and the package's sensitivity to that is worth knowing.

Why it exists

Measure assembly yield electrically through the daisy chains, localize what failed, and turn that into process learning before the product is assembled.

Assembly yield on a 2.5D package with hundreds of thousands of interconnects is not guaranteed. The daisy chains make it measurable, and the segmentation makes it attributable—which is what lets the OSAT fix a process problem rather than accept a yield number.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Done when

  • Failures localized to interconnect level and position
  • Marginal joints identified by resistance, not only by continuity
  • Feedback delivered before the process window freezes

Step 5 is why the DOE was run. Yield varying with bond force or reflow profile identifies the parameter that matters, and that is the parameter the process window in <code>PTV-12</code> will be built around.

Watch out for

  • Yield measured without localization. A number with no location gives the OSAT nothing to act on.
  • Marginal interconnects passing continuity. A high-resistance joint conducts and will fail in the field; Kelvin measurement is what distinguishes it.
  • Condition correlation not performed. The DOE's whole purpose is to link yield to parameters, and skipping the analysis wastes the build.
  • Feedback arriving after the process freezes. Learning that cannot change the process window is learning with no consequence.
  • Sample size too small for yield estimation. Assembly yield is a rate, and estimating it needs enough units for the rate to be meaningful.

This is the activity the whole stage exists for. It converts a large body of measurement into two things: a process window ASSY will run to, and a statement that the package has been validated. Step 2 is the honest accounting. Some risks in the matrix will not have been retired—a vehicle failed, a measurement was inconclusive—and the declaration has to say which, rather than declaring completion because the date arrived.

Watch out for

  • Completion declared because the date arrived. The gate exists to be capable of holding wafer-out, and a declaration that cannot say no is not a gate.
  • Unretired risks not stated. A validation record that implies full coverage when some risks remain open misleads exactly the decision it informs.
  • Feedback arriving after PKGD-11. Package design changes are not available after the freeze, so vehicle findings have to land before it.
  • Process window frozen too wide. A window that accommodates every observed condition is not a window; the boundaries have to exclude what produced failures.
  • Window not transferred to the OSAT as a specification. A window that exists in a report and not in the assembly instructions will not be followed.

SIPI-01Chip power model (CPM/CPS) extraction per power domain and operating mode

Takes7ww0–w7 of the stage
Costs8.0 M/M~5.0 people while it runs
OwnerPower modeling engineerConfiguration manager approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Get a chip power model that represents the die's current demand honestly—per domain, per mode, under the switching the product actually produces.

Everything in this stage depends on this model. A CPM extracted under averaged activity understates the transient the package must supply, and every downstream conclusion inherits that error without any indication that it did.

What it delivers

SIPI-D1Chip power model (CPM/CPS) release per domain and mode

This activity is the deliverable, and everything else in the stage consumes it.

Needs first

  • Placed and routed database from PD-05 and PD-06
  • Chip power model extraction from PD-11
  • Switching activity from DV-04 and SYN-06
  • Power domain definition from ARCH-05
  • Model format requirements from the analysis tools

Done when

  • Model built on the worst realistic transient, not an average
  • Separate models per domain and mode
  • Validated against die-level IR before release

Step 2 decides everything the stage can conclude. The worst realistic transient—a workload burst arriving after an idle period—is what the package has to absorb, and a model built on steady-state activity cannot represent it.

Watch out for

  • Model built on averaged activity. The transient is what the package must supply, and averaging removes exactly the event of interest.
  • Single model for all modes. DVFS points and workloads draw very differently, and one model represents none of them well.
  • Not validated against die-level IR. A CPM that disagrees with the die's own analysis is wrong somewhere, and nobody knows where.
  • Delivered late. The stage cannot start without it, and the stage gates mask release.
  • Version drift. Analysis run against a stale model produces conclusions about a die that has since changed.

Why it exists

Extract electrical models of the package and the board—3D field solution, S-parameters, RLC networks—so the system can be analyzed as one circuit rather than three assumptions.

Each of the three parties has been designing against a model of the other two. Extraction replaces those assumptions with a solved answer: what the interposer, substrate and board actually do electrically, at the frequencies the design cares about.

This activity is the deliverable, and it is what turns three design intents into one analysable circuit.

Step 1's frequency range decides the extraction cost and its usefulness. PDN analysis needs DC to the switching harmonics; channel analysis needs far higher. Extracting once for both is efficient and extracting for the wrong range wastes the effort entirely.

Watch out for

  • Frequency range too narrow. A model extracted for PDN analysis cannot support channel simulation, and re-extraction is expensive.
  • Extraction on an unfinished design. Package routing changes invalidate the model, and re-extraction is measured in weeks.
  • Board model omitted. The board is part of the PDN and part of the channel, and excluding it makes the analysis die-and-package only.
  • Models not validated. A 3D extraction has convergence and meshing choices, and an unvalidated result can be confidently wrong.
  • Socket and connector effects ignored. The bring-up platform includes them, and channel margin measured at bring-up will reflect them.

SIPI-03Die-package-board PDN co-simulation — DC and AC impedance versus target

Takes9ww8–w17 of the stage
Costs12.0 M/M~5.8 people while it runs
OwnerPower integrity engineerSI/PI lead approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Simulate the die, package and board as one power delivery network and check its impedance against target across the frequency range that matters.

The three levels each cover a different band: on-die decap handles the highest frequencies, package decoupling the middle, board bulk capacitance the lowest. Analyzed separately each looks adequate; analyzed together the gaps between them appear, and those gaps are where the supply actually sags.

What it delivers

SIPI-D3PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report

The impedance half of the deliverable; SIPI-04 supplies the dynamic IR half.

Needs first

  • Chip power model from SIPI-01
  • Package and board models from SIPI-02
  • Die PDN from PD-03
  • Package PDN design from PKGD-06
  • Board power design from EVB-05

Done when

  • Impedance analyzed across the full frequency range as one network
  • Anti-resonances identified and addressed
  • Findings carry recommendations naming which level to change

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w8w10w12w14w16w17

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Impedance target derivation per domain Impedance targets per domain 1.5w
2 Combined die-package-board PDN assembly Combined PDN model 2w
3 DC resistance and static drop analysisruns in parallel DC resistance and static drop results 1.5w
4 AC impedance analysis across frequency AC impedance across frequency 2.5w
5 Anti-resonance identification and analysisruns in parallel Anti-resonance analysis 1.5w
6 PDN findings and improvement recommendations PDN findings and recommendations 3w

Step 5 finds what separate analyses cannot. Anti-resonances form between the package's inductance and the die's capacitance, at frequencies neither level would identify alone, and they are where impedance peaks far above target.

Watch out for

  • Levels analyzed separately. Each looks adequate in isolation and the transitions between them are where the impedance peaks.
  • Anti-resonances missed. They occur at frequencies no single level would examine and can exceed target by a large factor.
  • Impedance target derived from a rule of thumb. The target follows from the current step and the allowable ripple, and a generic value is either wasteful or inadequate.
  • DC analysis only. Static drop is the easy half; the frequency-dependent behavior is where the problems are.
  • Findings without recommendations. An impedance plot that exceeds target tells the team there is a problem, not which level to fix.

Takes8ww12–w20 of the stage

Why it exists

Analyze dynamic voltage droop with the package's inductance included, under the switching profiles the product actually produces—the number the die-only analysis is optimistic about.

Die-only dynamic IR excludes the package's series inductance, which is the dominant impedance at the frequencies a workload burst excites. The difference between the two numbers is real margin, and it is the reason this stage exists rather than trusting SO-04.

What it delivers

SIPI-D3PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report

The dynamic IR half of the deliverable, and the number signoff should be using.

  • Die-only and co-analysis numbers reconciled
  • Findings delivered before timing signoff closes

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

Main sequence

1236

In parallel

45
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Transient scenario selection from the workload profiles Transient scenario selection 1.5w

6 Dynamic IR findings and margin assessment Dynamic IR margin assessment 2w

Step 4 is the comparison the program most needs. Where die-only analysis says 4.1% and the co-analysis says 5.0% against a 5% budget, the design has no margin—and the two numbers have to be reconciled before <code>SO-04</code> signs off on the optimistic one.

Watch out for

  • Package inductance excluded. It dominates at the frequencies a burst excites, and excluding it produces a comfortable and wrong answer.
  • Transient scenario too gentle. The worst case is a burst after idle, and a scenario built from steady-state activity never reaches it.
  • Droop duration ignored. A deep short droop and a shallow long one have different timing consequences, and only the magnitude is usually reported.
  • Die-only comparison not made. Without it nobody knows whether SO-04's number is optimistic, and the two signoffs disagree silently.
  • Findings arriving after timing signoff. Droop consumes timing margin, and a late finding invalidates closure.

SIPI-05Decoupling capacitor budget and placement optimization across die, package and board

Takes7ww14–w21 of the stage
Costs7.0 M/M~4.3 people while it runs
OwnerPower integrity engineerProgram manager approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Allocate the decoupling budget across die, package and board—how much capacitance, of what type, mounted where—so the three levels cover the frequency range between them rather than overlapping.

Decoupling is a system-level allocation that is usually made three times independently. On-die capacitance is expensive in area, package capacitors are limited by mounting positions, and board bulk is cheap and slow. Optimizing them together is what covers the band; optimizing them separately leaves the middle uncovered.

What it delivers

SIPI-D4Decap budget and placement specification across die, package and board

This activity is the deliverable, and it is the only place the three levels are allocated together.

Needs first

  • PDN impedance results from SIPI-03
  • Dynamic droop results from SIPI-04
  • On-die decap capability and area cost from PD-03
  • Package mounting positions from PKGD-06
  • Board capacitance options from EVB-05

Done when

  • Bands allocated so the three levels cover the range without gaps
  • Package capacitors placed for loop inductance
  • Allocation verified against the impedance target before handoff

5 Combined impedance verification with the allocation Combined impedance verification 1.5w
6 Decap specification and handoff to each level Decap specification per level 2.5w

Step 2 carries a real cost. On-die decoupling consumes die area that could have been logic, and the trade between area and package capacitors is a system decision rather than a physical design one.

Watch out for

  • Each level decoupled independently. The bands overlap in places and leave gaps in others, and the gaps are where the impedance peaks.
  • Package capacitors placed where there is room. Mounting position determines loop inductance, and a capacitor far from the current draw contributes little.
  • On-die decap area not costed. It is die area, and treating it as free produces a design that traded logic for decoupling without anyone deciding to.
  • Allocation not verified. A budget that has not been re-simulated against the impedance target is a proposal rather than a solution.
  • Specification not handed to each level. A system allocation that stays in a report is not implemented by anyone.

SIPI-06SSN / SSO and simultaneous-switching noise analysis at the IO ring

Takes5ww15–w20 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~4.3 people while it runs
OwnerSI/PI engineerInterface architect approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Analyze simultaneous switching noise at the IO ring—the supply disturbance many outputs switching together inject into their own reference.

SSN is a local problem with system consequences. When a wide interface switches together, the current through the shared return path moves the reference the receivers are measuring against, and the resulting noise appears as jitter and reduced eye margin on the very interface that caused it.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Package and board models from SIPI-02
  • IO library characteristics from PDK-07
  • Bump and ball assignment from PKGD-02
  • Interface switching patterns from ARCH-04
  • On-die IO power distribution from PD-03

Done when

  • Worst-case simultaneous switching simulated per interface
  • Reference shift included in the interface eye budget
  • Mitigations identified before the bump map freezes

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w15w16w17w18w19w20

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 SSN analysis scope — which interfaces switch together SSN analysis scope 1w
2 IO ring power and ground network modeling IO ring power and ground models 1.5w
3 Simultaneous switching simulation per interfaceruns in parallel Simultaneous switching simulation results 1.5w
4 Ground bounce and reference shift analysis Ground bounce and reference shift analysis 1.5w
5 Mitigation assessment — bump assignment, decouplingruns in parallel Mitigation assessment 1w
6 SSN findings and interface impact SSN findings per interface 1w

Step 5 usually points back at the bump map. The most effective SSN mitigation is more or better-placed power and ground bumps for that interface, which is a <code>PKGD-02</code> decision—and one that has to be made before the map freezes.

Watch out for

  • SSN analyzed per pin rather than per interface. The problem is simultaneity, and a single-pin analysis cannot see it.
  • Reference shift not included in the eye budget. Ground bounce moves the receiver's threshold, and excluding it overstates the margin.
  • Mitigation identified after bump map freeze. The most effective remedy is bump assignment, and it is unavailable after PKGD-02 closes.
  • Worst-case switching pattern not simulated. All outputs switching the same direction simultaneously is the worst case and is rarely the default pattern.
  • IO ring modelled as ideal. The ring's own power distribution is what carries the return current, and idealizing it removes the effect being analyzed.

Step 6 is the reconciliation that matters. The PHY in <code>AMS-03</code> closed against a channel budget; this activity says what the channel actually is, and any gap between them is margin the interface does not have.

Watch out for

  • Channel simulated on nominal models only. Manufacturing variation moves impedance and loss, and the compliance margin has to survive it.
  • PHY assumption not reconciled. The PHY closed against a budget; if the real channel is worse, the interface has no margin and nobody has noticed.
  • Crosstalk analyzed only at the near end. Far-end crosstalk on a long dense channel can dominate, and it behaves differently.
  • Socket and connector excluded. The bring-up platform includes them, and margin measured at bring-up will reflect them.
  • Findings after the package design freeze. Channel improvements are routing changes, and they are unavailable after PKGD-11.

Why it exists

Close the eye, jitter and BER budget per interface—combining channel loss, crosstalk, SSN, PHY equalization and jitter into one number that either meets the compliance mask or does not.

This is where all the electrical work resolves into a pass or a fail. Every contribution—the channel from SIPI-07, the noise from SIPI-06, the PLL jitter from AMS-02 and the PHY's own equalization—lands in a single budget, and the interface either has margin or it is shipping on hope.

Step 2 is where interfaces are usually lost. Jitter contributions from the PLL, the PHY, the channel and the SSN do not add linearly, and a budget that sums them naively either over-designs or, more often, over-promises.

Watch out for

  • Jitter contributions summed naively. Random and deterministic components combine differently, and getting it wrong produces a budget that is confidently wrong.
  • Equalization assumed at its maximum. A PHY closing only with full equalization has no adaptation range left for a worse-than-nominal channel.
  • Variation sensitivity ignored. The budget has to hold across manufacturing spread, not only at nominal.
  • SSN excluded from the budget. It is a real contribution and it degrades the interface that generates it.
  • Interface failing the mask with no route to fix. Late findings leave only channel changes, PHY changes or a rate reduction, and all three are expensive.

Why it exists

Back-annotate the voltage droop into static timing analysis—because a design signed off at nominal voltage was signed off at a voltage the die does not see.

Timing and power are analyzed by different teams with different tools, and the connection between them is usually a margin someone assumed. This activity replaces the assumption: the droop map from SIPI-04 applied to the timing analysis, so that closure reflects the supply the logic actually has.

What it delivers

This activity is the deliverable, and it connects two signoffs that otherwise run independently.

Needs first

  • Dynamic droop results from SIPI-04
  • Timing analysis from PD-09 and SO-02
  • Voltage-aware timing tool capability
  • Region and instance mapping from PD-02
  • Operating point definitions from ARCH-05

Done when

  • Droop applied regionally rather than as a flat margin
  • Reconciled with the SO-02 signoff assumption

Step 5 is the reconciliation. If timing signoff already carries a flat voltage margin and this analysis shows the droop is worse in some regions and better in others, the flat margin was both too generous and insufficient—and the recommendation is regional rather than global.

Watch out for

  • Flat voltage margin used instead. Droop is regional, and a flat margin is simultaneously wasteful where droop is low and inadequate where it is high.
  • Analysis run after timing closure. Findings then require reopening closure, which is expensive at this point in the schedule.
  • Droop map too coarse. Region granularity determines whether the analysis can distinguish a hot spot from an average.
  • Reconciliation skipped. Two signoffs with different voltage assumptions produce a design that satisfies neither cleanly.
  • Recommendations global rather than regional. The remedy is usually local—more decoupling or a PDN change in one region—and a global response over-corrects.

SIPI-10Electro-thermal co-analysis coupled with the package thermal model

Takes5ww18–w23 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~4.3 people while it runs
OwnerThermal engineerSI/PI lead approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Couple the electrical and thermal analyses—because leakage rises with temperature, temperature rises with power, and the two feed each other until they settle somewhere the isolated analyses did not predict.

Electro-thermal coupling matters at this power density. A hotspot raises local leakage, which raises local power, which raises the hotspot. Analyzing power at a fixed temperature and temperature at a fixed power finds an equilibrium that is optimistic in exactly the region that matters.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Package thermal model from PKGD-07
  • Thermal characterization from PTV-09
  • Chip power model from SIPI-01
  • Leakage characterization from PDK-03
  • Power map from PD-03

Done when

  • Coupled analysis converged, or non-convergence investigated
  • Compared against the isolated analyses to quantify the difference
  • Gradients assessed alongside peak temperature

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w18w19w20w21w22w23

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Coupling methodology and iteration scheme Coupling methodology and iteration scheme 1w
2 Thermal model integration with the package model Integrated electro-thermal model 1.5w
3 Leakage-temperature feedback modelingruns in parallel Leakage-temperature feedback model 1w
4 Coupled electro-thermal iteration to convergence Coupled analysis results 1.5w
5 Hotspot and gradient assessmentruns in parallel Hotspot and gradient assessment 1w
6 Findings against the isolated analyses Comparison against isolated analyses 1w

Step 4 iterates to convergence, and whether it converges is itself information. A design where the leakage-temperature loop does not settle is a design with a thermal runaway risk, which is a different and more serious finding than a high temperature.

Watch out for

  • Analyses run at fixed temperature and fixed power. The equilibrium the coupled analysis finds is worse, and it is the one that occurs.
  • Leakage-temperature model too coarse. The feedback is exponential, and a linear approximation understates the hotspot.
  • Non-convergence dismissed as a numerical issue. It can indicate a real thermal runaway risk and deserves investigation rather than a damping factor.
  • Package thermal model unvalidated. If PTV-09 has not correlated it, the coupled analysis inherits an unknown error.
  • Gradient ignored in favor of peak temperature. Gradients drive mechanical stress and timing variation across the die, and the peak alone does not capture them.
