19 ASSY · Assembly & Package Build

ASSY-01Known-good-die sort and selection

Takes3ww23–w26 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~7.2 people while it runs
OwnerProduct engineeringQuality engineer approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Sort the wafers and pick the known-good die that will go into packages—because on a 2.5D part a bad die does not fail alone, it takes an interposer, two HBM stacks and an assembly with it.

Known-good-die screening is what makes multi-die packaging economically viable. The coverage achieved at sort determines how many assembled units fail for reasons that were detectable on the wafer, and each of those is a package's worth of material lost.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Accepted wafers from FAB-08 and FAB-10
  • Wafer sort program from TEST-05
  • Probe card from TEST-03
  • KGD criteria from PKGD-10
  • Assembly quantity requirement from ASSY-09

Done when

  • Coverage sufficient for the assembled unit's economics
  • Marginal criteria set against package cost, not die cost
  • Every released die traceable to wafer and position

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

w23w24w25w26

Main sequence

1245

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Wafer receipt and sort setup on the probe station Wafers received with sort setup complete 0.5w
2 Wafer sort execution against the KGD criteria Sort execution results 1w
3 Marginal die dispositionruns in parallel Marginal die disposition record 0.75w
4 Known-good-die selection and wafer mapping Known-good-die map per wafer 1w
5 Die release to assembly with traceability Die released to assembly with traceability 0.5w

Step 3 is where the economics live. A marginal die is cheap to scrap and expensive to assemble; the criteria for rejecting one have to be set against the assembled unit's cost rather than against the die's.

Watch out for

  • KGD coverage below what the package economics need. Every escaped die costs an assembled unit, and the coverage target follows from that cost rather than from a test convention.
  • Marginal criteria set against die cost. On a 2.5D part the assembled unit is worth many times the die, and the reject threshold should reflect that.
  • Traceability lost between wafer and package. An assembly failure that cannot be traced back to a die and its wafer position cannot be attributed.
  • Sort program not ready. The probe card and program come from TEST, and a delay there stops assembly rather than delaying test.
  • Sorting only for function. Parametric marginality—leakage, Vmin—predicts field failure and is worth screening even when the die functions.

Why it exists

Procure and inspect the HBM stacks—bought components that go into the package alongside the program's own die, and that fail in ways the program does not control.

HBM is a purchased part with its own supply constraints and its own quality distribution. Incoming inspection matters because an HBM stack that fails after assembly costs the whole unit, and the supplier's outgoing quality is not the program's to verify after the fact.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • HBM purchase orders from MP-10 and procurement
  • Supplier test data and certificates
  • HBM specification and requirements from ARCH-03

Done when

  • Stacks confirmed against the package specification
  • Lot traceability maintained into assembly

Step 3 costs almost nothing and catches a class of problem inspection cannot. Supplier test data shows the distribution the delivered lot came from, and a lot at the edge of specification is worth knowing about before it is bonded in.

Watch out for

  • HBM supply constrained. It is a scarce component with long lead times, and a shortage stops assembly regardless of how many die are ready.
  • Incoming inspection skipped. A marginal stack bonded into a unit costs the whole unit, and the fault is only visible afterwards.
  • Supplier data not reviewed. The distribution the lot came from predicts its behavior, and the data is provided at no cost.
  • Lot traceability not maintained. An HBM-related failure that cannot be traced to a supplier lot cannot be escalated usefully.
  • Specification mismatch discovered at assembly. Stack height, bump pitch and thermal characteristics all have to match the package design.

ASSY-03Die attach, micro-bump and thermo-compression bonding

Takes3ww25–w28 of the stage
Costs6.0 M/M~8.7 people while it runs

Why it exists

Bond the die and HBM stacks to the interposer—micro-bump preparation and thermo-compression bonding—inside the process window the vehicles established.

This is the step the whole PTV program existed to de-risk. Bond force, temperature and time were characterized on vehicles; here they are applied to real die, and the process window is either followed or the vehicle work was wasted.

What it delivers

ASSY-D2Assembly travelers and process data

This activity is where the traveler starts and where the actual bond conditions are recorded.

Needs first

  • Known-good die from ASSY-01
  • Qualified HBM stacks from ASSY-02
  • Interposers from PKGD-09 supply
  • Frozen process window from PTV-12
  • Assembly process flow from PKGD-10

Done when

  • Every unit bonded inside the frozen window
  • Actual bond parameters recorded per unit
  • Post-bond inspection coverage sufficient to catch localized defects

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

Main sequence

1245

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Process setup to the frozen window Process setup to the frozen window 0.5w

Step 3 records what actually happened. The frozen window says what the parameters should be; monitoring says what they were, and a unit that failed can only be attributed if its actual bond conditions were captured.

Watch out for

  • Running outside the frozen window. The PTV program established boundaries; operating outside them discards the evidence it produced.
  • Bond parameters not recorded per unit. A failed unit cannot be attributed to its conditions, and the yield analysis loses its most useful variable.
  • Bump preparation inconsistent. Flux and surface condition affect joint formation, and variability here shows up as scattered yield.
  • Post-bond inspection sampled too thinly. Bonding defects are localized, and a sample that misses them lets them through to underfill where they are unfixable.
  • Process drift across the run. Long runs drift, and without monitoring the drift is only visible in the yield trend afterwards.

19 ASSY · Assembly & Package Build

ASSY-04Interposer and substrate assembly, underfill, molding

Takes3ww26–w29 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~7.2 people while it runs
OwnerOSAT process engineerReliability liaison approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Attach the interposer to the substrate and underfill and mold the assembly—the steps that make it mechanically robust and that lock in whatever went before.

Underfill is irreversible. Once it has flowed and cured, a bonding defect underneath is permanent and invisible to everything except acoustic imaging. The step's quality—void-free flow, complete fillet, correct cure—determines whether the mechanical stress the package will see is distributed or concentrated.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Bonded assemblies from ASSY-03
  • Substrates from PKGD-09 supply
  • Underfill and mold compound specifications
  • Frozen process window from PTV-12
  • Warpage data from PTV-07

Done when

  • Void and fillet inspected before cure, not after
  • Cure profile within the frozen window
  • Warpage during the process inside the validated range

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

w26w27w28w29

Main sequence

1245

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Interposer to substrate attach Interposer-to-substrate attached assemblies 0.5w
2 Underfill dispense and flow Dispensed and flowed underfill 1w
3 Void and fillet inspectionruns in parallel Void and fillet inspection results 0.75w
4 Underfill cure and molding Underfilled assemblies 1w
5 Post-mold inspection Cured and molded units · Post-mold inspection results 0.5w

Step 3 is the last chance to catch a bonding problem. Acoustic imaging before cure can still identify a void or an incomplete fill; after cure the unit is what it is, and the defect surfaces during thermal cycling months later.

Watch out for

  • Underfill voids. They concentrate stress and are the mechanism behind delayed CPI failures, and they are invisible after cure without acoustic imaging.
  • Incomplete fillet. The fillet distributes stress at the die edge, and an incomplete one puts that stress into the die corner instead.
  • Cure profile deviation. Under-cured underfill has different mechanical properties, and the difference appears as reliability rather than as a visible defect.
  • Warpage during cure exceeding the window. The vehicle program measured it; running outside that window reintroduces the risk that was retired.
  • Inspection only after molding. Once molded the assembly cannot be examined usefully, and the inspection has to happen before.

Takes2ww28–w30 of the stage

Why it exists

Finish the package—TIM, lid and ball attach—and produce units that can be mounted, cooled and tested.

These are the last steps and they determine two things the product is judged on: the thermal interface that decides the achievable power envelope, and the ball array that decides whether the package mounts reliably. Both were characterized on vehicles and both are executed here.

What it delivers

ASSY-D1Assembled units — bring-up, qualification and sample lots

This activity is where a unit becomes a finished package.

Needs first

  • Molded assemblies from ASSY-04
  • TIM material and lid components
  • Ball attach process from the frozen window
  • TIM characterization from PTV-09
  • Dimensional specification from PKGD-11

Done when

  • TIM bond line within the characterized range

How it gets there 4 steps · 2 lanes

w28w29w30

Main sequence

124

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 TIM application and lid attach Lidded units with applied TIM 0.5w

Step 1 sets the thermal performance the product will actually have. Bond line thickness under the lid is a process parameter, and the difference between the characterized value and the achieved one is watts of headroom.

Watch out for

  • TIM bond line thicker than characterized. Thermal resistance rises, and the power envelope the product was sold on shrinks.
  • Lid flatness out of specification. The cooling solution then contacts unevenly, which produces hotspots the thermal design did not predict.
  • Ball co-planarity outside the mounting window. The package does not mount reliably, and the customer discovers it during their assembly.
  • Dimensional drift from the specification. The package has to fit sockets, heatsinks and board footprints that were designed to the drawing.
  • Final inspection sampled rather than complete. On an engineering build every unit is precious, and a defect shipped to bring-up costs lab days.

ASSY-06Assembly inline inspection — X-ray, CSAM, warpage metrology

Takes2ww26–w28 of the stage
Costs3.0 M/M~6.5 people while it runs
OwnerQuality engineerPackage engineer approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Inspect the assemblies without taking them apart—X-ray for joints, acoustic imaging for delamination and voids, metrology for warpage—because most assembly defects are invisible from outside.

A 2.5D package hides everything that matters. The joints are under the die, the underfill is under the interposer, and the only way to see any of it non-destructively is through imaging. What this activity catches is what does not reach bring-up as an unexplained failure.

What it delivers

ASSY-D4Package-level inspection and test data

This activity is the deliverable—the non-destructive record of what is inside each unit.

Needs first

  • Assemblies at each process stage from ASSY-03 to ASSY-05
  • Inspection criteria from PTV vehicle results
  • X-ray and CSAM capability at the OSAT
  • Warpage limits from PTV-07
  • Defect classification scheme

Done when

  • Inspection at each process step, not only at the end
  • Defects classified against a consistent scheme
  • Findings fed back to the process that created them

How it gets there 4 steps · 2 lanes

w26w27w28

Main sequence

124

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Inspection plan and sampling strategy Inspection plan and sampling strategy 0.5w
2 X-ray inspection of joints and voids X-ray inspection results 0.75w
3 Defect classification and dispositionruns in parallel Defect classification and disposition 0.5w
4 Acoustic imaging and warpage metrology Acoustic imaging and warpage results 0.75w

Step 1's sampling strategy is a real decision on a small build. Full inspection is affordable at engineering-lot quantities and not at production volume, and starting with full coverage is what tells you what sampling would have missed.

Watch out for

  • Sampling too thin on an engineering build. Full inspection is affordable at these quantities, and a defect reaching bring-up costs far more than the inspection would have.
  • Defects classified inconsistently. Without a scheme the same feature is a defect on Monday and acceptable on Tuesday, and the yield data becomes noise.
  • Inspection only at the end. Defects are cheapest to catch at the step that created them, and end-of-line inspection cannot attribute them.
  • Warpage limits not applied. The vehicle program set them; a unit outside them is a reliability risk regardless of whether it functions.
  • Findings not fed back to process. Inspection that produces a pass/fail and no process signal wastes most of its value.

ASSY-07Assembly yield analysis and process tuning

Takes5ww26–w31 of the stage
Costs6.0 M/M~5.2 people while it runs
OwnerYield engineerProduct cost analyst approves

Why it exists

Analyze the assembly yield, build the failure pareto, find the root causes with the OSAT and tune the process inside the window the vehicles defined.

First-build assembly yield on a 2.5D part is rarely what the cost model assumed. This activity turns the gap into a set of attributed causes and process adjustments—and compares the result against what the vehicle program predicted, which is how the vehicle work gets validated in turn.

What it delivers

ASSY-D3Assembly yield report and failure pareto

This activity is the deliverable, and the pareto is what the OSAT acts on.

Needs first

  • Yield data from every assembly step
  • Inspection results from ASSY-06
  • Continuity results from ASSY-08
  • PTV yield prediction from PTV-11
  • Frozen process window from PTV-12

Done when

  • Failures attributed to process steps, not only counted
  • Tuning kept inside the validated window
  • Yield compared against the vehicle prediction

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w26w27w28w29w30w31

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Yield data collection across process steps Yield data by process step 0.75w
2 Failure pareto by mode and process step Failure pareto by mode 1.25w
3 Comparison against the PTV yield predictionruns in parallel Comparison against vehicle prediction 1w
4 Root cause analysis with the OSAT Root cause findings 1.5w
5 Corrective action trackingruns in parallel Corrective actions and their tracking 1w
6 Process tuning inside the frozen window Process tuning record 1.5w

Step 6 stays inside the window deliberately. Tuning beyond the validated boundaries would abandon the evidence the vehicle program produced, and a yield improvement bought that way carries an unquantified reliability risk.

Watch out for

  • Yield reported without attribution. A number tells the program it has a problem; a pareto by process step tells the OSAT what to change.
  • Tuning outside the validated window. It may improve yield and it discards the reliability evidence the vehicles produced.
  • Vehicle prediction not compared. The comparison is what validates or invalidates the whole PTV program, and it is cheap to make.
  • Root cause pursued without the OSAT. Process knowledge sits with the assembler, and analysis without them produces hypotheses rather than causes.
  • Corrective actions untracked. An agreed action that nobody follows up is an action that did not happen.

Why it exists

Test the assembled packages electrically for opens, shorts and marginal joints before they go anywhere—the cheapest possible screen on the most expensive units the program has.

A package-level continuity test costs minutes and catches assembly failures that would otherwise consume lab days at bring-up. On units this expensive, screening before shipping is not optional economics.

The electrical half of the deliverable, alongside the imaging from ASSY-06.

124

Step 3 separates working from reliably working. A joint that conducts with elevated resistance passes a continuity test and fails in the field, and screening for it here is far cheaper than a field return.

Watch out for

  • Screening skipped because units are scarce. A failed unit consumed at bring-up costs more lab time than the whole screen would have.
  • Continuity only, no resistance. Marginal joints conduct and fail later, and only a resistance measurement distinguishes them.
  • Criteria not derived from vehicle data. PTV-11 measured what good and marginal look like, and the criteria should come from there.
  • Failures not fed to yield analysis. An electrical failure is yield data and belongs in the pareto.
  • Test fixture damaging units. On packages this expensive the fixture itself has to be qualified.

Watch out for

  • Allocation decided by whoever asks first. The three consumers have different downstream consequences, and the trade belongs to the program.
  • Qualification starved. Reliability stress runs for months; starting it late moves mass production directly.
  • Customer samples cut. They are frequently contractual, and missing them has commercial consequences the program may not see.
  • Build quantity below the sum of needs. Which is normal, and it means the shortfall has to be decided rather than discovered.
  • Traceability lost per allocation. A qualification failure has to be traceable to its lot and its assembly conditions.

Why it exists

Build the production interposer the assembly consumes—a silicon wafer run of its own, with its own mask set, started the week the package design freezes and finished before a single die is attached.

On a 2.5D part the interposer is not a purchased commodity; it is a second silicon product on a second schedule. Nothing in the assembly window can begin without it, and its lead time is measured in months rather than weeks, so it is started against the frozen database rather than against the wafers coming out of FAB.

Step 2 is the one that cannot be compressed. The interposer needs a mask set like any other silicon, and ordering it is gated on the same design freeze as the substrate—which is why both start in the same week and why that week, not the tapeout, is the real commitment point for the package.

Watch out for

  • Started against wafer-out rather than against the design freeze. The interposer takes months, and a program that orders it when the die is ready has already lost the assembly slot.
  • Mask tooling treated as part of the die tapeout. It is a separate mask set on a separate release, and it is gated on PKGD-11 rather than on TO-11.
  • Warpage screened only at assembly. An interposer that warps outside the window fails at bonding, where the die it takes with it is already expensive.
  • Capacity booked but not converted to a wafer start. A reservation is not a lot; the start date is what has to be tracked.
  • No known-good screening before handover. An unscreened interposer moves the yield loss into the assembly, which is the most expensive place to find it.

20 EVB · Validation Hardware / EVB

EVB-01Validation platform requirements and topology definition

Takes5ww0–w5 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~4.3 people while it runs
OwnerValidation leadProgram manager approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Decide what the silicon will be validated on—how many platforms, in what configuration, at what quantity—before anyone draws a schematic.

The board is the only way to touch the silicon, and its capability bounds everything bring-up and characterization can do. A platform that cannot reach a rail, cannot socket a part, or cannot be temperature-soaked closes off measurements that the qualification plan assumes are available.

Why it exists

Lay out the PCB with signal and power integrity simulated on the critical channels, because a validation board carrying PCIe Gen6 or CXL is itself a high-speed design.

The board is in series with every interface measurement bring-up will make. A channel with a marginal board contribution produces link failures that look like silicon problems, and separating the two costs weeks of debug time that the simulation would have avoided.

Steps 3 and 5 run against the routing rather than after it. A channel simulated after the board is routed produces a report; simulated during, it produces a routing change.

Watch out for

  • Board channel contribution not budgeted. The SIPI channel budget covers package and board together, and a board that consumes more than its share leaves the silicon nothing.
  • SI simulated after routing. The result is a report rather than a design change, and fixing it costs a revision.
  • Board PDN inadequate for the transient. The silicon's di/dt is on the package model; a board PDN sized without it droops.
  • Stack-up chosen for cost before impedance. Controlled impedance on the high-speed layers is not negotiable, and a cheaper stack-up that misses it is not cheaper.
  • Mechanical constraints applied last. The cooling solution and socket need space, and finding that out after routing costs a revision.

Takes7ww8–w15 of the stage

Why it exists

Design and bring up the power delivery, VRM and telemetry on the platform—the rails the silicon runs on and the instrumentation that measures them.

Characterization is mostly a power measurement. Shmoo needs rails that can be swept, power validation needs rails that can be measured accurately, and both need protection that trips before an expensive part is destroyed rather than after.

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Board PDN design from EVB-03

Done when

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w8w10w12w14w15

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Power tree requirement from the die and package Power tree requirement 1w
2 VRM selection and design VRM design 1.5w
3 Transient response design against the SIPI budgetruns in parallel Transient response design 1.5w
4 Telemetry and monitoring design Telemetry and monitoring capability 1.5w
5 Protection and sequencing designruns in parallel Protection and sequencing design 1.5w

Step 5 is what protects the units. A sequencing error or an overcurrent event on a first-silicon part costs a package worth many thousands, and the protection has to be validated before a real part is ever inserted.

Watch out for

  • Rails not sweepable across the shmoo range. Characterization then cannot reach the corners the qualification plan requires.
  • Protection untested before a real part goes in. A sequencing fault destroys a first-silicon unit, and there are very few of them.
  • Telemetry accuracy insufficient. Power measurements at the resolution characterization needs demand real instrumentation, not a rough monitor.
  • Transient response inadequate. The die's di/dt is known from SIPI; a VRM that cannot follow it produces droop that looks like a silicon failure.
  • Sequencing not matching the silicon's requirement. The power-up order comes from the design, and getting it wrong is a common first-board fault.

Why it exists

Build the debug access—JTAG and trace pods, interposers, probe points—because silicon debug is bounded by what can be observed.

When first silicon does something unexpected, the difference between a day and a month is whether the state that explains it can be read out. The DFT infrastructure provides the internal access; this activity provides the physical path to it.

Step 6 validates the debug path before it is needed. A trace pod that does not work is discovered during the crisis it was meant to resolve, which is the worst possible moment.

Watch out for

  • Debug access designed without DFT. The internal observability comes from DFT-08, and the board access has to match what it exposes.
  • Trace bandwidth insufficient. Trace is only useful if it can keep up with the events being traced, and the bandwidth is a board design parameter.
  • Probe points unreachable once the cooling solution is mounted. The thermal solution and the probe access compete for the same physical space.
  • Debug path unvalidated before silicon. It is then debugged during the emergency it exists to resolve.
  • Software tooling not integrated. A hardware debug path with no software to drive it is not a debug path.

Why it exists

Bring the board itself up—with dummy parts or a socketed loopback—so that when silicon arrives, every failure is the silicon's.

This is the single highest-leverage activity in the stage. A board debugged before first silicon means bring-up starts on a known-good platform; a board debugged alongside first silicon means every anomaly has two possible causes and each takes days to separate.

The whole activity is scheduled to complete before silicon arrives. Every hour spent here is an hour not spent, at ten times the cost, debugging a board while first silicon waits on the bench.

Watch out for

  • Board bring-up deferred until silicon arrives. Every anomaly then has two candidate causes, and separating them costs days each.
  • Known issues not documented. The bring-up team then rediscovers each board quirk independently, once per engineer.
  • Dummy parts not representative. A loopback that does not load the rails or exercise the channels validates less than it appears to.
  • Only one board brought up. Board-to-board variation is real, and a fleet where only one is characterized is a fleet with unknown members.
  • Thermal fit checked after silicon insertion. A cooling solution that does not fit is discovered with an irreplaceable part underneath it.

Step 5 is what makes qualification-adjacent measurement possible. Characterization needs the part held at a temperature, not merely kept cool, and a solution that only cools cannot produce a hot-corner shmoo.

Watch out for

  • Cooling sized to the product's solution rather than to the lab's need. The lab platform can be oversized, and measurement validity is worth more than realism.
  • No temperature control, only cooling. Characterization needs the part held at a set point, including a hot one.
  • Throttling during characterization. The data then describes the cooling rather than the silicon, and it is often not noticed.
  • Mounting competing with probe access. The debug points and the heatsink want the same space, and the conflict has to be resolved in layout.
  • Thermal validated only at nominal power. The interesting measurements are at maximum power, which is where the solution is stressed.

  • Instrument bandwidth below the signal rate. A scope that cannot resolve the edge produces a plausible and wrong measurement.

Why it exists

Provide the minimum host-side software needed to power on and talk to the part—boot, register access, enumeration, logging—without taking on the product's software stack.

SW/FW is outside this program's scope, but silicon cannot be brought up without something on the other end of the link. The boundary matters: this activity delivers exactly enough to reach first register read and no more, and where that line sits should be agreed rather than discovered.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Boot sequence from ARCH-06

Step 1 is the activity's most valuable hour. Without an explicit boundary, hardware validation writes software the firmware team is also writing, and each assumes the other is doing it.

Watch out for

  • Boundary with firmware left implicit. Either the work is duplicated or nobody does it, and both are discovered at power-on.
  • Register map drifting from the RTL. A diagnostic tool built against a stale map reads the wrong addresses and reports plausible nonsense.
  • Scope creeping into the product stack. Minimal enablement becomes a driver project, and the validation team stops validating.
  • Logging insufficient for post-mortem. A failure that cannot be reconstructed from the log has to be reproduced, which on first silicon may not be possible.
  • Enablement unvalidated before silicon. Software bugs then present as silicon bugs during the most expensive week of the program.

21 TEST · Test Development

TEST-01Test plan and coverage strategy — wafer sort, final test, system-level test

Takes8ww0–w8 of the stage
Costs12.0 M/M~6.5 people while it runs
OwnerTest architectCost analyst approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Decide what will be tested, where, and to what defect level—the plan every other activity in the stage implements.

Test is where quality is bought and where cost per unit is set, and the two trade directly. The plan is the document where that trade is made explicitly: a DPPM target implies coverage, coverage implies content, content implies test time, and test time is money on every unit ever shipped.

What it delivers

TEST-D1Test plan and test coverage matrix

This activity is the deliverable, and every other TEST activity implements part of it.

Needs first

  • Product specification and quality target from DEF-04
  • DFT coverage from DFT-03 and DFT-05
  • Package pin map from PKGD-04
  • Quality and reliability requirement from MP-01
  • Cost target from DEF-06

Done when

  • DPPM target derived from actual coverage, not asserted
  • Test time budgeted before content is written
  • Sort and final coverage split deliberately

How it gets there 8 steps · 2 lanes

w0w2w4w6w8

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Coverage requirement from the specification and DFT Coverage requirement 1w
2 Test flow architecture — sort, final, characterization Test flow architecture across insertions 2w
3 Tester resource estimationruns in parallel Tester resource estimate 1.5w

5 DPPM target derivation from the coverageruns in parallel DPPM target derivation 1.5w
6 Test insertion and binning strategy Test insertion and binning strategy · Reviewed test plan 1.5w
7 Burn-in and screening decisionruns in parallel Burn-in and screening decision 1w
8 Plan review and release Reviewed and released test plan 1.5w

Step 5 is the one that closes the loop. Coverage without a DPPM target is an engineering preference; a DPPM target derived from the coverage is a commitment the customer can be given.

Watch out for

  • Coverage chosen without a DPPM target. There is then no way to say whether the test is sufficient, only whether it is thorough.
  • Test time not budgeted at plan time. Content accumulates and the cost per unit is discovered at production readiness when it is expensive to change.
  • Burn-in decided late. It is a capital and cycle-time commitment, and reversing it after qualification planning is expensive.
  • Sort and final coverage overlapping without intent. Testing the same thing twice costs money on every unit and often happens by accretion.
  • DFT coverage assumed rather than measured. The plan then promises a DPPM the actual pattern set cannot deliver.

Why it exists

Choose the ATE platform and book the tester time—a capital and capacity decision that has to be made long before there is anything to test.

Tester capacity is a shared, scheduled resource. Program development time, characterization time and production capacity are all booked against the same pool, and a program that has not committed its slots competes with programs that have.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Pin count and interface rates from PKGD-04
  • Available ATE platforms and their capability
  • Test capacity and capital budget
  • Production volume forecast from DEF-05

Done when

  • Development, characterization and production slots all booked
  • Instrument set covering the highest interface rate
  • Pin count supporting the planned multi-site conversion

Step 6 is why this runs early. Development, characterization and production all draw on the same testers, and slots that are not booked are taken.

Watch out for

  • Tester time not booked ahead. Capacity is shared, and a program without commitments waits behind programs with them.
  • Instrument options short of the interface rate. High-speed content cannot be run, and the shortfall is discovered when the program is written.
  • Pin count insufficient for parallel sites. Multi-site conversion later becomes impossible, and test cost stays where it started.
  • Platform chosen on capital cost alone. Cost per tested unit depends on throughput as much as on the tester's price.
  • Development capacity not separated from production. Program debug then competes with the ramp it is meant to enable.

TEST-03Probe card design, fabrication and qualification

Takes20ww10–w30 of the stage
Costs16.0 M/M~3.5 people while it runs
OwnerProbe engineerOperations planner approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Design, fabricate and qualify the probe card—the physical interface between the tester and the wafer, and the longest lead time in the stage.

Nothing can be sorted without it, and sort gates assembly. Twenty weeks of design and fabrication sit in front of the first wafer, which means the card has to be committed against a bump map that is frozen far earlier than most people expect.

What it delivers

TEST-D2Qualified probe card and load board

The probe card half of the deliverable.

Needs first

  • Bump map from PD-15 and PKGD-03
  • Test plan and sort content from TEST-01
  • ATE platform and interface from TEST-02
  • Wafer sort touchdown plan
  • Probe card vendor capability

Done when

  • Card qualified on the tester before wafers arrive
  • Contact resistance and planarity inside specification
  • Spare card available against the sort volume

How it gets there 8 steps · 2 lanes

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Probe card requirement and bump map extraction Probe card requirement and bump map 2w
2 Probe card design Probe card design 3w
3 Contact resistance and planarity analysisruns in parallel Contact resistance and planarity analysis 3w
4 Probe card fabrication Fabricated probe card 8w
5 Touchdown life and cleaning strategyruns in parallel Touchdown life and cleaning strategy 3w
6 Qualification on the tester Tester qualification results 4w
7 Spare card and repair planruns in parallel Spare card and repair plan 2.5w
8 Release to wafer sort Probe card released to sort 3w

Step 4's eight weeks are pure vendor lead time and cannot be compressed. Step 1's bump map therefore has to be frozen roughly five months before sort, which is well before most people believe the design is stable.

Watch out for

  • Bump map changing after card release. Eight weeks of fabrication are lost, and sort—and therefore assembly—moves by that much.
  • Contact resistance out of specification. Marginal contact produces failures that look like silicon defects and corrupts the whole sort yield.
  • Planarity insufficient across the touchdown area. Some probes contact and some do not, and the pattern is subtle enough to be missed.
  • No spare card. A damaged card with a ten-week replacement stops sort entirely, and cards are damaged routinely.
  • Touchdown life below the wafer volume. Card degradation then appears as a yield trend that gets chased as a process problem.

TEST-04Load board / DUT board design, fabrication and bring-up

Takes17ww12–w29 of the stage

Why it exists

Design, build and bring up the load board and socket—the package-level equivalent of the probe card, and what every final-test and characterization measurement passes through.

The load board carries the tester's signals to the package at full rate and delivers its power at full current. It is a high-speed board design in its own right, and its own contribution to a measurement has to be small enough that what is measured is the silicon.

What it delivers

TEST-D2Qualified probe card and load board

The load board half of the deliverable.

Needs first

  • Package pin map and ball map from PKGD-04
  • Test plan and final content from TEST-01
  • ATE platform interface from TEST-02
  • Power envelope from ARCH-08
  • Socket vendor capability

Done when

  • Power delivery adequate at maximum test current
  • Socket insertion life above the planned test volume
  • Board channel contribution small against the measurement margin

How it gets there 8 steps · 2 lanes

Step 5 is routinely underestimated. A high-power part draws current through the socket, and a load board whose power delivery droops produces failures at speed that are indistinguishable from silicon marginality.

Watch out for

  • Load board power delivery droop. It produces at-speed failures that look exactly like silicon marginality and consume weeks of debug.
  • Socket insertion life below the test volume. Contact degrades, yield trends downward, and the cause is looked for in the process.
  • Board channel loss consuming the measurement margin. The interface test then fails on the board rather than on the part.
  • Socket selected before the package is dimensioned. A socket that does not fit the finished package is discovered very late.
  • No correlation fixture. ATE and bench results then cannot be reconciled, and both are distrusted.

Why it exists

Write the wafer sort test program—the screen that decides which die are worth assembling into a package.

On a 2.5D part, sort is the most economically consequential test in the flow. Everything it lets through carries an interposer, two HBM stacks and an assembly with it, so its coverage is measured against package cost rather than against die cost.

Step 7 is where the program's economics are set. Limits too tight throw away good die; too loose and packages are built on bad ones. The guard bands should come from measurement uncertainty and package cost, not from convention.

Watch out for

  • Guard bands set by convention. On a part where an escape costs an assembled package, the limits should be derived from that cost.
  • Coverage below what the package economics need. Assembly yield then absorbs the difference, at many times the price.
  • Program debugged only in simulation. Tester behavior differs from the model, and the difference is found on the first wafer.
  • Wafer map output not matching the assembly requirement. KGD selection depends on the map format, and a mismatch stops assembly.
  • Test time growing without check. Sort time multiplies across every wafer ever run, and content accretes silently.

Why it exists

Write the final test program that runs on the assembled package—at speed, at temperature, across every interface the product ships with.

Final test is the last screen before a customer sees the part. It exercises what sort could not: the assembled interfaces, the HBM stacks, the full power envelope, and the at-speed behavior of a part that is now mechanically complete.

What it delivers

TEST-D3Wafer sort and final test programs, release-tagged

The final-test half of the deliverable.

  • Load board from TEST-04
  • ATE patterns from TEST-08

  • Binning strategy from TEST-01

Done when

  • At-speed content run across the temperature range
  • Test time inside the cost model's allowance

Step 6 is where the 2.5D part differs most from a monolithic one. The HBM interfaces exist only after assembly, they cannot be tested at sort, and they are the most likely thing to be wrong about an assembled unit.

Watch out for

  • HBM interface content insufficient. The interfaces only exist after assembly, and a marginal one shipped is a field failure.
  • At-speed content not run at temperature. Timing marginality appears at the hot corner, and testing only at room temperature misses it.
  • Binning content added late. Grading is how the product line is built, and retrofitting it changes the flow and its cost.
  • Test time not tracked against the cost model. Final test dominates per-unit test cost and grows quietly.
  • Program debugged without real assembled units. The first units are precious, and the program has to be ready when they exist.

Why it exists

Build the characterization content—shmoos, corners, parametric sweeps, datasheet parameter measurement—that turns silicon into a specified product.

Production test asks whether a part passes. Characterization asks what the part actually does, across voltage, frequency and temperature, over a statistically meaningful sample. Every number in the datasheet comes from here, and so do the guard bands production test uses.

Step 5 decides whether the results mean anything. A datasheet number from three units is an anecdote; the sample size follows from the distribution being characterized and the confidence the specification claims.

Watch out for

  • Sample size too small for the claim. A datasheet parameter from a handful of units is a number without confidence behind it.
  • Corners not spanning the qualification range. Qualification then stresses conditions characterization never measured.
  • Sweeps not automated. Manual shmoo consumes engineer-weeks per corner, and the corners get quietly reduced.
  • Datasheet parameters not traceable to a measurement. A customer question about a number then has no answer.
  • Analysis pipeline built after the data. Data is collected in a format nobody can analyze, and the campaign is re-run.

TEST-08DFT pattern porting to ATE format and pattern debug

Takes10ww22–w32 of the stage
Costs16.0 M/M~7.0 people while it runs
OwnerTest engineerProduct engineering approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Port the DFT patterns to the tester's format and debug them there—the step between a pattern that simulates and a pattern that runs.

ATPG produces patterns against an idealized model. The tester has finite memory, real timing resolution, protocol constraints and a specific pin electronics behavior. Every one of those turns a pattern that passes in simulation into one that fails on hardware, and finding out which is the work.

What it delivers

TEST-D5ATE-ready pattern set with debug log

This activity is the deliverable.

Needs first

  • ATPG patterns from DFT-03
  • Compression architecture from DFT-04
  • ATE platform and memory depth from TEST-02
  • Timing constraints from SO-03
  • Tester timing model

Done when

  • Pattern set fitting tester memory without coverage loss
  • Timing mapped within the tester's resolution
  • Patterns simulated against the tester model before silicon

How it gets there 8 steps · 2 lanes

w22w24w26w28w30w32

Main sequence

12468

In parallel

357
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 ATPG pattern handoff from DFT Pattern handoff record 1.5w
2 Pattern translation to the tester format Translated tester-format patterns 2w
3 Pattern volume and memory-depth reductionruns in parallel Volume and memory reduction 1.5w
4 Timing and protocol mapping Timing and protocol mapping 2.5w
5 Compression and streaming setupruns in parallel Compression and streaming setup 1.5w

7 Pattern regression and version controlruns in parallel Pattern regression under version control 1.5w
8 Pattern debug on silicon or emulation Debugged ATE-ready pattern set 2w

Step 3 is a hard constraint, not an optimization. Tester pattern memory is finite, and a pattern set that exceeds it simply cannot be loaded—which is discovered at translation, not at ATPG.

Watch out for

  • Pattern volume exceeding tester memory. The set cannot be loaded at all, and reduction after ATPG loses coverage.
  • Timing not mappable to the tester's resolution. At-speed patterns then run at the wrong speed, silently.
  • Patterns not simulated against the tester model. Failures are then debugged on silicon at tester rates rather than in simulation.
  • Pattern set not versioned. A yield excursion cannot be correlated to a pattern change nobody recorded.
  • Debug deferred until first silicon. Pattern problems and silicon problems then arrive together and cannot be separated.

Why it exists

Reduce test time and test cost per unit—an activity that starts early, because content is far cheaper to not write than to remove.

Test time is paid on every unit for the product's whole life. A second saved at final test on a million units is real money, and the savings available at plan time are much larger than the ones available after the program is written and qualified.

What it delivers

TEST-D6Test time and test cost model

This activity is the deliverable.

Needs first

  • Test plan and flow from TEST-01
  • Sort content from TEST-05
  • Final content from TEST-06
  • Tester cost per hour from TEST-02
  • Expected yield and failure distribution

Done when

  • Optimization done before qualification freezes the content
  • Coverage trades made explicitly against the DPPM target
  • Cost model including a yield assumption

Step 4's reordering is often the largest single win and costs nothing. Running the tests that fail most first means failing parts leave the tester early, and the average test time drops without any coverage change.

Watch out for

  • Optimization started after qualification. Any content change then requires re-qualification, which is why this starts early.
  • Coverage traded away silently. Time reduction that loses coverage has to be an explicit decision against the DPPM target.
  • Reordering not done. It is free and it is the largest single lever, and it is routinely overlooked.
  • Multi-site assumed without pin count. The tester configuration from TEST-02 has to support it, and retrofitting it does not work.
  • Cost model without a yield assumption. Cost per good unit depends on yield, and a model without it understates the cost.

TEST-10Correlation between ATE, bench and system results

Takes8ww32–w40 of the stage
Costs10.0 M/M~5.4 people while it runs
OwnerProduct engineeringQuality engineer approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Correlate ATE, bench and system results so that a part passing on the tester behaves the same way in a customer's system.

Three measurement environments produce three numbers for the same parameter, and they never agree exactly. What matters is whether the disagreement is understood: an unexplained gap between tester and system is either an escape path or an over-screen, and both are expensive.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Final test results from TEST-06
  • Bench measurements from BU-08
  • System-level results from BU-05
  • Measurement uncertainty from TEST-07
  • Load board and correlation fixture from TEST-04

Done when

  • Every material discrepancy root-caused, not accepted
  • Golden units retained and re-measurable
  • Guard bands updated from what correlation found

How it gets there 8 steps · 2 lanes

w32w34w36w38w40

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Correlation plan and unit selection Correlation plan and unit selection 1w
2 ATE-to-bench correlation ATE-to-bench correlation results 2w
3 Measurement uncertainty budgetruns in parallel Measurement uncertainty budget 1.5w
4 ATE-to-system correlation ATE-to-system correlation results 2w
5 Golden unit designation and retentionruns in parallel Designated golden units 1.5w
6 Discrepancy analysis and root cause Discrepancy analysis and root causes 1.5w
7 Correlation regression setupruns in parallel Correlation regression 1w
8 Guard-band adjustment and release Adjusted guard bands 1.5w

Step 5 is what makes correlation repeatable. A retained set of golden units re-measured after any change is how tester drift, load board degradation and program regressions are caught before they become yield excursions.

Watch out for

  • Discrepancy accepted without root cause. The gap is either an escape or an over-screen, and 'they just differ' resolves neither.
  • Correlation on too few units. Two units that agree prove very little about the population.
  • No golden units retained. Drift in the tester, the load board or the program then has nothing to be measured against.
  • System correlation skipped. ATE-to-bench is the easy half; ATE-to-system is the one the customer experiences.
  • Guard bands not updated. The correlation produced the information and nothing acted on it.

  • Pipeline built after the first lots run. The first silicon's data is the most informative the program will ever have, and it is the data most often lost.
  • Retention policy absent. Field returns arrive years later, and the test record for that unit has to still exist.
  • Dashboards without an alerting layer. A yield excursion is noticed at the weekly review rather than the same day.
  • Schema not covering characterization. Characterization data has a different shape, and a sort-only schema forces it into a separate silo.

Why it exists

Receive the first units, check them and mount them—a short activity whose only job is to make sure the most valuable objects the program has ever produced are not damaged before they are powered.

There are very few first-silicon units and each represents the whole program's schedule. A unit destroyed by a mounting error or an unnoticed shipping defect is not replaceable inside any useful timeframe.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Brought-up boards from EVB-07

  • ESD and handling procedures

Done when

  • Every unit inspected before mounting
  • Units mounted only on validated boards
  • Unit register started and maintained

Step 4 is the reason board bring-up happened first. The checklist is only meaningful because <code>EVB-07</code> already established which board behaviors are normal and which are faults.

Watch out for

  • Handling damage on an irreplaceable unit. ESD or mechanical damage at mounting costs a unit the program cannot replace.
  • Mounting onto an unvalidated board. A board fault then destroys the part, and EVB-07 exists to prevent exactly this.
  • No unit tracking. Every subsequent result has to be attributable to a specific unit and its history.
  • Incoming inspection skipped in the rush. Shipping damage is real and is much cheaper to find before power than after.
  • All units mounted at once. A systematic board or handling fault then takes the whole fleet rather than one unit.

BU-02Power-on, power sequencing and basic health check

Takes3ww1–w4 of the stage
Costs8.0 M/M~11.6 people while it runs
OwnerBring-up leadProgram manager approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Apply power for the first time—sequenced, current-limited and instrumented—and establish that the part is alive.

First power-on is the moment the whole design becomes physical. It is also the moment a shorted rail or a sequencing error can destroy a unit in milliseconds, which is why it is done with limits, with measurement, and with the ability to stop.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Mounted units from BU-01
  • Power subsystem and protection from EVB-05
  • Power sequencing specification from ARCH-08
  • Expected rail currents from PD-08
  • Telemetry from EVB-05

Done when

  • Current limits in place before first application
  • Rail currents profiled against expectation
  • No unexplained anomaly carried into the next milestone

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

w1w2w3w4

Main sequence

1245

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Power sequencing verification against the specification Power sequencing verification 0.5w
2 First power application with current limits First power application record 1w
3 Anomaly triage on the first applicationruns in parallel Anomaly triage findings 0.75w
4 Rail voltage and current profiling Rail voltage and current profiles 1w
5 Health check and go/no-go for the next step Health check and go/no-go decision 0.5w

Step 2's current limits are what turn a fatal event into a diagnostic one. A rail that draws far more than expected trips the limit and the part survives to be investigated; without the limit it is destroyed and the information goes with it.

Watch out for

  • Power applied without current limits. A short then destroys the unit instead of revealing itself.
  • Sequencing not verified against the specification. A wrong power-up order damages the part and the fault is the platform's, not the silicon's.
  • Rail currents not profiled. The first real power data is available at exactly this moment and is easy to not capture.
  • Multiple units powered before the first is understood. A systematic fault then takes several units instead of one.
  • Anomalies pushed past to reach the next milestone. Something unexplained at power-on rarely stays harmless.

BU-03Reset, clocking and PLL lock validation

Takes3ww2–w5 of the stage
Costs8.0 M/M~11.6 people while it runs
OwnerBring-up engineerValidation engineer approves
Critical pathnohas float

Why it exists

Validate reset, clocking and PLL lock—the infrastructure everything else depends on, and the layer where a fault masquerades as a fault somewhere else.

A PLL that locks unreliably or a reset domain released in the wrong order produces symptoms all over the chip: boot failures, interface training failures, sporadic functional errors. Clearing this layer first means the failures found later are real.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Powered units from BU-02
  • PLL specifications from AMS-04
  • Clock architecture from ARCH-05
  • Reset architecture from RTL-04
  • Clock instrumentation from EVB-09

Done when

  • PLL lock verified across the full operating range
  • Reset domain release order confirmed against the architecture
  • Jitter measured with the board's contribution separated

How it gets there 5 steps · 2 lanes

w2w3w4w5

Main sequence

1245

In parallel

3
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Reference clock and input validation Reference clock validation 0.5w
2 PLL lock across the frequency range PLL lock results across the range 1w
3 Reset sequence and domain release verificationruns in parallel Reset sequence and domain release verification 0.75w
4 Clock tree and domain verification Clock tree and domain verification 1w
5 Jitter and stability measurement Jitter and stability measurements 0.5w

Step 5's jitter measurement is easy to skip because the part appears to work without it. It matters because interface training margin depends on clock quality, and a jitter problem found here explains a class of failures that would otherwise be chased in the SerDes.

Watch out for

  • PLL lock validated only at nominal. The lock range matters because shmoo and characterization will operate outside nominal.
  • Reset domain release order not verified. The resulting failures appear anywhere on the chip and are attributed to the wrong block.
  • Jitter unmeasured. Interface training margin depends on it, and a jitter problem is then debugged inside the SerDes.
  • Clock tree assumed correct because the part boots. A misconfigured divider is compatible with booting and incompatible with performance.
  • Clock quality measured through the board without accounting for it. The board contributes jitter and its contribution has to be separated.

Why it exists

Boot the part—ROM, firmware load, register access, first functional response—and confirm that the design does what it was written to do.

First boot is the milestone that turns a powered die into a working processor. It is also the point at which the design, the firmware, the board and the host software are all exercised together for the first time, which is why it is the milestone most likely to expose an integration assumption nobody wrote down.

What it delivers

BU-D1Bring-up report with per-milestone health status

  • Host enablement from EVB-10

  • Register map from RTL-06
  • Debug access from EVB-06

  • Boot-time deviations captured as errata candidates

Step 4's first successful register read is the moment the program knows the silicon is fundamentally sound. Everything before it is infrastructure and everything after it is degrees of correctness.

Watch out for

  • Boot failure with no state visible. Without debug access the failure is a symptom with no information, and debug access comes from EVB-06.
  • Firmware and hardware assumptions differing. The handoff is where two teams' expectations meet, and nobody wrote them down.
  • Register map drift. The tool reads addresses the silicon does not implement and reports plausible garbage.
  • Smoke test too shallow. A part that boots and does nothing else has passed a milestone without demonstrating much.
  • Status not broadcast. First boot is the news the whole program is waiting for, and silence is read as failure.

Why it exists

Bring up the interfaces—PCIe/CXL link training, HBM training, die-to-die—which on this part is the largest single body of bring-up work and the most likely to produce a respin decision.

Interfaces are where design, package, board and protocol all meet. Training failures are notoriously hard to attribute because every layer can cause them, and the margin measurements taken here are what tell the program whether the part is comfortable or on the edge.

This activity is the deliverable, and the margins are what say whether the part is comfortable.

  • SIPI channel budget and predictions from SIPI-04 and SIPI-05
  • Debug and trace access from EVB-06
  • Lab instrumentation from EVB-09

Step 3 is not optional even when training succeeds. A link that trains with no margin trains today and fails at temperature or on a different host, and only the eye measurement distinguishes the two.

Watch out for

  • Training success accepted without margin measurement. A zero-margin link works on the bench and fails in the field.
  • Failures not attributable across layers. Design, package, board and protocol can all cause the same symptom, and the SIPI predictions are what separate them.
  • HBM training treated as a vendor problem. The interface is the program's, and its training parameters have to be understood locally.
  • Interoperability tested against one host. Customers use many, and a link that only works with the lab's host is not compliant.
  • Compliance run deferred. Formal compliance is a gate for certification and takes lab time that has to be booked.

Why it exists

Validate the memory subsystem—controller, address map, bandwidth, latency, ECC—because on an AI accelerator the memory system is most of the performance.

HBM training establishes that the links work; this establishes that the memory system delivers. Bandwidth and latency against the architecture model is the measurement the product's performance claims rest on, and it is where architectural assumptions meet a real memory controller.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Trained HBM interfaces from BU-05
  • Memory subsystem model from ARCH-04
  • Address map from RTL-05
  • Memory test content from TEST-06
  • Thermal capability from EVB-08

Done when

  • ECC validated by injected errors, not by absence of failures
  • Bandwidth and latency compared against the architecture model
  • Efficiency characterized, not only peak

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w8w10w12w14

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

35
#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT
1 Memory controller initialization and configuration Controller initialization and configuration 1w
2 Address map and pattern validation Address map and pattern validation 1.5w
3 ECC and error handling validationruns in parallel ECC and error handling validation 1.5w
4 Bandwidth measurement against the model Bandwidth measurements against the model 1.5w
5 Refresh and thermal behaviorruns in parallel Refresh and thermal behavior data 1.5w
6 Latency and efficiency characterization Latency and efficiency characterization 2w

Step 3 has to be done deliberately by injecting errors. ECC that has never corrected anything is ECC that has never been shown to work, and a broken correction path is silent until it matters.

Watch out for

  • ECC never exercised. A correction path that has never corrected an injected error has not been validated.
  • Bandwidth measured without the model to compare against. A number without a target says nothing about whether the design met its intent.
  • Refresh behavior at temperature not checked. HBM refresh scales with temperature and the effect on bandwidth is real.
  • Address map validated only at the boundaries. Aliasing errors sit in the middle of the map and pass boundary tests.
  • Efficiency ignored in favor of peak. Peak bandwidth is a datasheet number; achieved efficiency is what workloads see.

Why it exists

Shmoo the part across voltage, frequency and temperature—the measurement that establishes how much margin the design actually has.

Every operating condition the product will be specified at comes out of this. The shmoo shows where the part stops working, and the distance between that boundary and the nominal operating point is the margin the datasheet, the guard bands and the qualification plan all depend on.

What it delivers

BU-D2Characterization data set — V/F/T shmoo and power measurements

  • Characterization content from TEST-07

  • Temperature corners included, not only room

How it gets there 6 steps · 2 lanes

w9w11w13w15w16

Main sequence

1246

In parallel

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 5 is what separates a characteristic from an anecdote. One unit's shmoo is that unit; the fleet's spread is what the population looks like, and the specification has to be set against the population.

Watch out for

  • Shmoo on a single unit. The result describes that unit and is used as if it described the population.
  • Room temperature only. The hot and cold corners are where the margin is smallest and where qualification will operate.
  • Manual sweeps. The corner count then gets reduced to fit the available engineer time, silently.
  • Thermal throttling inside the sweep. The shmoo then maps the cooling solution rather than the silicon.
  • Margin measured but not fed into guard bands. The data exists and production test still uses convention.

Measure real performance against the architecture model—the check on whether the product does what it was sold as doing.

The whole program was justified by a performance projection. This is where that projection meets a physical part running real workloads, and any gap has to be attributed: to the model, to the design, to the memory system, or to the software driving it.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

Needs first

  • Functional units from BU-04 through BU-06
  • Architecture performance model from ARCH-02
  • Workload definitions from DEF-03
  • Power measurement from BU-07
  • Lab instrumentation from EVB-09

Done when

  • Every material gap attributed to a cause
  • Efficiency measured alongside throughput
  • Software's contribution to the measurement established

Step 6 is where the program learns something durable. A gap attributed to the model improves the next program's projections; a gap attributed to the design becomes an errata or a respin input; an unattributed gap teaches nothing.

Watch out for

  • Performance measured on unrepresentative workloads. A benchmark that is not what customers run produces a number that does not predict their experience.
  • Gap reported without attribution. Nobody can act on it, and the next program repeats the modeling error.
  • Software limiting the measurement. An immature stack understates the silicon, and the difference has to be established rather than assumed.
  • Efficiency ignored. Performance per watt is the metric this product class is bought on, and raw throughput alone misleads.
  • Measured at a single operating point. Real deployment spans conditions, and performance at nominal is not the whole picture.

Why it exists

Debug what is wrong—reproduce it, isolate it, extract the internal state, find the root cause, and get failure analysis where physical evidence is needed.

This is the activity the whole DFT and debug infrastructure investment exists to serve. It runs alongside every other bring-up activity because anomalies arrive from all of them, and its throughput largely determines how long bring-up takes.

Step 3 is the highest-leverage step in the activity. An anomaly reproduced in simulation can be examined with full visibility and unlimited retries, which is an environment no amount of silicon debug can match.

Watch out for

  • Symptoms treated instead of causes. A workaround without a root cause hides a mechanism that resurfaces in the field.
  • No path back to simulation. Debug then happens only on silicon, with limited visibility and long turnaround per hypothesis.
  • Design team engaged late. The people who wrote the logic can often recognize a symptom in minutes, and validation debugs alone for days first.
  • Units consumed by destructive FA too readily. Physical analysis destroys the unit, and there are very few.
  • Findings not captured. The same anomaly is then debugged twice by different engineers.

Step 4's validation is the part that gets skipped. A workaround that has been described but never run is a hypothesis, and shipping it as a mitigation is how a known issue becomes a field failure anyway.

Watch out for

  • Workarounds documented but never validated. The mitigation then fails in the field and the errata gave false comfort.
  • Severity assessed by engineering alone. Customer impact depends on use models, and the assessment needs that perspective.

  • Errata list not versioned against silicon revision. Which errata apply to which stepping becomes ambiguous the moment a second stepping exists.
  • Documentation deferred to the end. The context is freshest at root cause, and reconstructing it months later loses detail.

BU-11Respin versus metal-fix decision analysis — ECO scope, cost, schedule

Takes4ww13–w17 of the stage
Costs5.0 M/M~5.4 people while it runs

Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Decide whether the silicon needs a respin, a metal fix, or nothing—the single most consequential decision the program makes after tapeout.

A full-mask respin costs a mask set and roughly a quarter of schedule. A metal fix costs far less but can only reach defects in the routing layers. Shipping as-is with workarounds costs nothing now and possibly a great deal later. The decision has to weigh all three against evidence rather than optimism.

What it delivers

This activity is the deliverable, and the record is what the program is held to.

  • Root causes from BU-09
  • Margin data from BU-07
  • Performance gaps from BU-08
  • Mask and fab cost from TECH-08

Done when

  • Metal-fix feasibility established physically, not assumed
  • Margin evidence weighed alongside functional defects
  • Decision recorded with what was known at the time

4 Cost, schedule and risk comparison Cost, schedule and risk comparison 1.25w

Step 2 is bounded by physics rather than by will. A metal fix can only change routing layers, and whether the required change fits inside them is a question with a factual answer that has to be established before the decision is framed.

Watch out for

  • Decision made on schedule pressure alone. Shipping a part with a real defect to protect a date routinely costs more than the delay would have.
  • Metal-fix feasibility assumed. It is a physical question about which layers the fix touches, and it is often answered optimistically.
  • Margin data not weighed. A part with adequate function and no margin fails in the field, and the shmoo already said so.
  • Decision unrecorded. Six months later nobody can reconstruct what was known and what was accepted.
  • Customer input excluded. Whether an errata is tolerable depends on what customers do with the part.

MP-01Qualification plan definition against JEDEC / AEC standards

Takes6ww0–w6 of the stage

OwnerReliability engineerOperations planner approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Define what qualification means for this product—which standards apply, which stresses run, on how many units, and against what acceptance criteria.

Qualification is the evidence that the part survives its intended life. The plan is where that evidence is designed: too little and a customer's own qualification finds what yours did not, too much and months of chamber time are spent on stresses nobody required.

What it delivers

MP-D1Qualification plan and JEDEC-compliant qualification report

The plan half of the deliverable; the report follows from executing it.

  • Package construction from PKGD-11
  • Unit availability from ASSY-09

Done when

  • Sample sizes supporting the reliability claim

#Step, and what it adds to the deliverableTAT

Step 4 is why this activity runs first. HTOL occupies a chamber for a thousand hours, and chambers are shared; a booking made late pushes the whole qualification campaign and therefore mass production.

Watch out for

  • Chamber capacity booked late. Stress duration is fixed and capacity is shared, so a late booking moves mass production directly.
  • Sample sizes below the confidence the claim needs. A reliability claim from too few units does not support the specification.
  • Customer requirements collected after the plan. A customer-specific stress discovered later restarts a months-long campaign.
  • Three lots not planned. Standards generally require multiple production lots, and a single-lot qualification is not accepted.
  • Use conditions assumed rather than specified. The acceleration factors depend on them, and wrong conditions make the whole campaign non-representative.

Step 5's interim readouts are what turn a pass/fail campaign into a learning one. A parameter drifting at 500 hours predicts a failure at 1000 that would otherwise arrive as a surprise at the end of a four-month run.

Watch out for

  • Campaign started late. The duration is fixed, so every week of delay is a week of mass production delay, one for one.
  • No pre-stress characterization. Drift cannot be measured without a baseline, and a failure cannot be distinguished from a part that was always marginal.
  • Interim readouts skipped. Failures then arrive only at the end, with no time left to respond before the ramp.
  • Stress failures not analyzed. A failure without a mechanism cannot be judged as systematic or as a one-off, and the distinction decides the ramp.
  • Units insufficient for the full matrix. A stress dropped for lack of units is a gap in the qualification the customer will find.

Why it exists

Qualify the part's ESD and latch-up robustness—HBM and CDM discharge, and latch-up immunity—the handling-survival properties every downstream user depends on.

ESD failures happen in assembly lines, in labs and in the field, and they are almost never traced back to the part that could not take them. The classification levels are what tell a customer's manufacturing engineer how to handle the device.

4 CDM ESD characterization CDM ESD classification 1.5w
5 Failure analysis on ESD failuresruns in parallel ESD failure analyses 1w
6 Latch-up test and report Latch-up test results and report 2w

Step 4 matters more than step 2 on a package this size. CDM stress scales with package capacitance, and a large 2.5D package charges to a far higher energy than a small one—the CDM level is usually the binding constraint.

Watch out for

  • CDM underestimated for the package size. A large package stores far more charge, and the CDM level is usually the binding one.
  • ESD failures not analyzed. Which pin and which protection element failed is what makes the result actionable for a fix.
  • Latch-up tested only at room temperature. Latch-up susceptibility increases with temperature, and the hot corner is the real test.
  • Classification below what customer assembly requires. A part that cannot survive a customer's line is a part they cannot buy.
  • Pin classification incomplete. Untested pin combinations are unqualified pins, and there is no assumption to fall back on.

Watch out for

  • MSL classification worse than the assembly process needs. A high moisture sensitivity forces bake-and-handle procedures on every customer line.
  • Board-level reliability short of the application requirement. The joints, not the die, then set the product's life.

  • Warpage measured only before stress. The interesting change is what stress does to it, and that requires measurement through the campaign.
  • Failures attributed to the package without analysis. A CPI failure and a solder joint failure need different fixes and look similar from outside.

MP-05Yield learning, failure pareto and defect analysis

Takes20w cont.w2–w22 of the stage
Costs40.0 M/M~8.7 people while it runs
OwnerYield engineerCost analyst approves
Critical pathyesslipping moves the program

Why it exists

Run yield learning continuously through the ramp—pareto, defect analysis, corrective action, and a yield model checked against the cost target.

Yield is the difference between a product that makes money and one that does not, and first-ramp yield is never where the cost model assumed. This activity runs for the whole stage because yield learning is a rate, not an event: what matters is how fast the pareto's top item is removed and replaced by the next.

What it delivers

Step 5 is the split that decides who acts. Die yield, assembly yield and test yield have different owners and different fixes, and a combined number tells none of them what to do.

Watch out for

  • Yield reported as one number. Die, assembly and test yield have different owners, and a combined figure directs nobody.
  • Spatial signatures not analyzed. Edge, center and radial patterns each point at a different process cause and are visible only on the wafer map.
  • Corrective actions not verified. An action taken without confirming the pareto moved is an action that may have done nothing.
  • Excursions detected at the weekly review. By then a week of material is affected, and detection has to be automatic.
  • Yield model not checked against the cost target. The gap between achieved and assumed yield is the product's margin, and it can go unnoticed for months.

MP-06Production test program release and guard-band validation

Takes9ww10–w19 of the stage

Why it exists

Release the production test program—frozen, guard-band-validated, qualified and version-controlled—for every unit the product will ever ship.

After this release, a change to test content requires re-qualification. That makes the release a genuine freeze, and it makes the guard-band validation that precedes it the last chance to be sure the limits neither throw away good parts nor let bad ones through.

What it delivers

  • Both escape and over-kill quantified

Step 3 quantifies both directions of error. Escapes cost the customer's trust and over-kill costs yield, and a limit set without measuring both is optimizing one at the other's expense without knowing it.

Watch out for

  • Guard bands not validated against characterization. Limits then rest on convention rather than on what the silicon actually does.
  • Over-kill unmeasured. Good parts are discarded on every lot and the loss is attributed to yield rather than to the limits.
  • Flow validated on one lot. Lot-to-lot variation is the thing the flow has to tolerate, and one lot cannot show it.
  • Porting across the tester fleet without correlation. Tester-to-tester differences then present as yield differences by machine.
  • Released without version control. A yield excursion cannot be correlated with a program change nobody can identify.

Why it exists

Single-site testing is fine for a hundred units and ruinous for a million. Multi-site conversion multiplies throughput per tester and divides the capital needed for the ramp, and it is a real engineering exercise because parallel sites interfere with each other in ways single-site testing never reveals.

Step 5 is what makes the conversion trustworthy. Sites differ—in contact, in power delivery, in noise coupling—and a systematic site bias shows up as a yield difference that gets chased as a process problem for weeks.

Watch out for

  • Site-to-site bias undetected. It appears as a yield difference and is investigated as a process problem for weeks.
  • Pin count insufficient for the site count. The tester configuration from TEST-02 bounds this, and it cannot be changed now.
  • Parallel power delivery inadequate. Four parts drawing full current through one load board droop in ways one part does not.
  • Conversion done after the ramp starts. Capital is then committed at single-site throughput and cannot be recovered.
  • Time reduction changing coverage. Any content change after MP-06 requires re-qualification, which is expensive at this point.

MP-08Process corner and split-lot validation

Takes9ww8–w17 of the stage
Costs14.0 M/M~6.8 people while it runs

Why it exists

Validate the design across process corners using split lots—material deliberately fabricated at the edges of the process window.

Production silicon spans the process distribution, and the units bring-up characterized came from one lot near its center. Split lots produce the fast and slow corners on purpose, which is the only way to know whether the design's margin survives the population it will actually be built from.

What it delivers

No key deliverable is owned here — this activity contributes to the ones below.

  • Corner models from PDK-05

Done when

  • Cpk computed against the specification
  • Model-to-silicon correlation established at both corners
